HEADLINE: NAB bulks up business banking
INTRO: National Australia Bank looks set to further bulk up its investment in business banking, as it fends off an attack from rivals betting on a rebound in ­borrowing.
TEXT:
National Australia Bank looks set to further bulk up its investment in business banking, as it fends off an attack from rivals betting on a rebound in ­borrowing.

Chief executive Andrew Thorburn has made business lending a top priority for turning NAB around, after recent market share losses and revenue falls in the segment, which is a key source of its earnings.

After NAB said last year it would boost its business banker ranks with 100 new staff, executive general manager of NAB business Cindy Batchelor said she expected the bank would invest more resources to target small and medium enterprise customers.

But there are few signs of a rebound in credit demand from SMEs, suggesting profit margins from business lending are likely to remain pressured.

Ms Batchelor, who is responsible for SME customers with annual turnover of up to $50 million, expected NAB would invest more in business lending as part of Mr Thorburn's strategy, and this would likely involve hiring more bankers as well as more spending on digital technology.

"Andrew has continued to provide that support to us, and I fully expect there's going to be more investment," Ms Batchelor told Fairfax Media.'Highly competitive' market

With all of the major banks eyeing SME customers, she said the market remained "highly competitive" but would not comment on profit margins before NAB's trading update next month.

Credit demand remained "on the soft side," she said, and this was likely to remain the case over the short term.

"I think that will continue. We're not hopeful that there's going to be a significant turnaround in that in the short term."

The increased focus on business banking at NAB comes as it faces pressure from market analysts to lift returns from its business lending arm.

Macquarie analyst Mike Wiblin this month estimated it would need to hire 400 more frontline bankers and spend $50 million in the division over the next three years.

Lending to small and medium firms has traditionally been lucrative for NAB, which has the largest market share in business banking, but in recent years it has been losing customers and facing skinnier profit margins.Campaign launch

In an attempt to lift its performance, NAB last year pledged to lend $1 billion a month to this segment. This week it is launching a campaign to promote its distinctive model, under which business bankers also provide home loans to customers.

"That's where I think, for NAB, our advantage is. It's actually having more bankers in more places," Ms Batchelor said. Some in the market have suggested NAB had allowed the number of frontline bankers in business lending to fall too low. In response, Ms Batchelor said changes in its number of bankers reflected a change in its internal structure, and it was now investing in areas of the market with the most growth potential.

"This is where we think the opportunity and the potential is, so you're going to invest in that," she said.

The SME segment that Ms Batchelor manages is the largest part of NAB's business lending book, which is, in turn, a key driver of the group's overall performance.

HEADLINE: The central bank dilemma
INTRO: Easing monetary policy around the world is making it harder for the RBA, writes Alan Mitchell
TEXT:
Easing monetary policy around the world is making it harder for the RBA, writes Alan Mitchell

It's a time for central bank surprises. First the European Central Bank caught markets unaware with the size of its quantitative easing, followed by India, the Canadians and the Danes with their rate cuts and the Singaporeans with their monetary easing.

Will Australia's Reserve Bank keep the trend going when its board meets on Tuesday?

On Friday the markets were betting heavily that it would. The Australian dollar took its sharpest dive since the global financial crisis, and at midday was less than US78¢.

The RBA governor, Glenn Stevens, and his board may oblige. The disappointing performance of the Australian economy justifies a cut in short-term interest rates, and the most recent consumer price index confirms that there is no inflation problem standing in the way of easier monetary policy.

A rate cut presumably would see the Australian dollar dip further, whereas a failure to cut might see the currency move back up to around US80¢.

But a rate now cut might not be cost-free  either.

There is a risk that lower interest rates could start a new surge of local and foreign investment in the Australian real estate market, which could leave the RBA having to rely on untested macroprudential policies to protect the economy against overheating property prices. It might not be a silky smooth ride.

If it were not for the problem of the property market, the case for a rate would be pretty strong.

The economy is growing at below its trend rate, unemployment is trending up, and there is little evidence of the sort of new business spending needed to start lifting growth in the second half of this year.

If anything, the headwinds seem to be strengthening: the global recovery is losing momentum, China is slowing, iron prices are plummeting, and the Europeans and Japanese are supporting their economies with monetary policy that makes their currencies more competitive.

This monetary-policy-induced depreciation is what economists and the media are calling currency wars, and it certainly does put pressure on other countries to cut their interest rates to avoid suffering a competitive disadvantage.

For many countries in a weak world economy, that may be no great cross to bear. And in Australia lower interest rates would be a welcome tonic for the macro economy; so too would be stronger growth in our major export markets of Europe and Japan.

While the Australian economy is not rapidly deteriorating, there are few signs of the revival of non-mining business investment that is needed to help offset the downturn in mining investment.

The National Australia Bank's December business survey showed "a patchwork economy with little to no momentum building" with business reporting another month of easing sales, profits and employment and with a fall in forward orders pointing to continuing soft demand in the near term.

Business confidence improved slightly but remains well below long-run averages.

While the official data show employment growing strongly in November, the NAB employment series weakened and is now below average levels.

"With soft business confidence and weak forward orders there is doubt that the strength in the official estimates can be maintained," the NAB economists warn.

A deterioration in the employment outlook would increase the downside risks to other pillars of the expected recovery: consumer spending and housing construction.

Comparing the soft November and December surveys with the stronger business conditions reported in October, the NAB economists have a discouraging answer to the obvious question: it now looks like it was the October survey – and not the subsequent weaker surveys – that was the anomaly.

The potential problem is property.

There have been signs of investor demand cooling off, but we also know from last year's experience that the market can find a second or third wind.

One rate cut and the expectation of at least another cut would generate capital gains and, potentially, raise expectations of further gains.

To the extent that it led to a sustained depreciation of the dollar, the rate cut also could reduce the exchange rate risk faced by foreign investors in the Australian property market.

This is the tension that central bankers have been warning about for years as they have come to terms with the increasing size and frequency of asset price bubbles. It is the circumstance in which the economy demands one interest rate, and the real estate market requires another.

Macroprudential policy – the manipulation of the regulation designed to keep the banks safe – is a compromise answer to the problem, and the Australian prudential regulators' pressure on the banks to be careful appears to have worked pretty well in the past months.

But the test of macroprudential policy could become much more intensive if interest rates are lowered and there is a new surge of speculative demand.

For one thing, people might start circumventing the regulated banking system by borrowing from overseas lenders. This might reduce anxiety about the local banks becoming tangled up in a real estate boom and bust, but it could still leave the borrowers vulnerable and pose an important risk to economy.

At the same time, the politics of rationing money are difficult. The politicians will want to both put too much reliance on the new policy and excuse large numbers of voters (first-home buyers) from it.

In the short term, there is also the problem of discovering how the new macroprudential policies work in the highly charged real estate market.

While central banks have been arming themselves with these instruments, they have been at pains to stress that macroprudential regulations are no magic bullet.

Here is how the US Federal Reserve's Janet Yellen explained problem: "Experience with such tools remains limited, and we have much to learn to use these measures effectively.

"The limitations of macroprudential policies reflect the potential for risks to emerge outside sectors subject to regulation, the potential for supervision and regulation to miss emerging risks, the uncertain efficacy of new macroprudential tools such as a countercyclical capital buffer, and the potential for such policy steps to be delayed or to lack public support."

Concerns about the property market and a reluctance to put too much reliance on macroprudential policies may have been behind the RBA's strong emphasis on having a period of stability in interest rates. But events may now be limiting that option.

78 US cents Friday's new, but brief, low for the Australian dollar.

HEADLINE: Home, motor insurers face tough years ahead
INTRO: After years of mega-profits fuelled by double-digit premium hikes, insurers are bracing for a significant slowdown in revenue growth as aggressive competition hits companies' bottom lines.
TEXT:
After years of mega-profits fuelled by double-digit premium hikes, insurers are bracing for a significant slowdown in revenue growth as aggressive competition hits companies' bottom lines.

Research from JPMorgan and actuarial consultants Taylor Fry shows insurers expect to book an average of just 1 per cent growth in 2015 across their domestic classes of business, which include motor and home cover and compulsory third-party cover.

This is half of the 2 per cent average premium growth recorded last year, and below the 3 per cent claims inflation mark.

It is also a far cry from soaring double-digit revenue growth after a spate of natural disasters such as the Brisbane floods and Christchurch earthquakes in 2010-11 that skyrocketed the price of insurance premiums.

"For the next few years . . . the industry is in for a very tough outlook on the growth [side]. Rates are going to stay low for a long period of time," JPMorgan senior insurance analyst Siddharth Parameswaran said.

"We do think we are at a turning point in the industry," he added.

Heated competition for cost-conscious consumers' business, particularly in home and motor insurance, is a key driver of the predicted handbrake on growth. Insurers are trying to woo new business while household budgets remain constrained.

Companies are also suffering from low investment yields and vehicle repair cost inflation. Lower reinsurance costs benefit insurers because they pay less for catastrophe cover, but they also lose their reason for passing on high reinsurance costs to consumers in the form of premium hikes.

"The 2014 year saw very strong profitability with the trends exceeding the expectations of the insurance industry, primarily due to the impact of previous rate increases, a soft period for natural peril claims and a continuation of reserve releases, though at reduced levels," Mr Parameswaran said.

Taylor Fry senior actuary and director Kevin Gomes said: "Profitability is expected to deteriorate in the coming years for Australian insurers in part driven by soft premium rates, providing downward pressure on growth."

The outlook is even more dire in the commercial insurance sector, where competition among companies is more prevalent.

Premium rates fell 12 per cent in the fire and industrial special risks ­sectors, while rates remained flat in commercial motor cover last year. Professional indemnity insurance rates fell 5 per cent, while directors and officers' cover also posted 2 per cent dips.

Australia's general insurance sector is also notorious for its lapse rates, or the number of customers who allow their cover to lapse at renewal times.

According to the research, the industry was recording lapse rates of about 20 per cent a year – much worse than the beleaguered life insurance sector which is posting 10 per cent drops.

The predictions come as some of Australia's biggest insurers, including Suncorp Group, Insurance Australia Group and QBE Insurance Group, prepare to unveil their profits next month.

HEADLINE: Better way to help low-paid
INTRO: Tax credits may be better at boosting income than fixed wage rates, write Ben Potter and John Kehoe.
TEXT:
Tax credits may be better at boosting income than fixed wage rates, write Ben Potter and John Kehoe.

Here's a barbecue stopper that some economists say would give the working poor a fairer suck of the sauce bottle: cut out minimum wage increases and top up their incomes with a tax credit instead.

But the idea comes with a caveat: it's a guaranteed incendiary device at a time of unusually febrile political debate in Australia, where the minimum wage has occupied hallowed ground since the 1907 decision of arbitration judge Henry Bournes Higgins to set a living wage for a "male breadwinner" with a wife and two kids.

"Tony Abbott still wants to attack the minimum wage and penalty rates in this country," Opposition Leader Bill Shorten said when the Productivity Commission put minimum wages and tax credits on the table in its work-place issues paper for the government.

"It will be a weeping sore for the government,'' ACTU assistant boss Tim Lyons said.

Small wonder the idea has never taken root in Australia. Yet it comes with solid academic backing and is widely used around the world. In Australia in 1999, "The Five Economists" – including Hawke government adviser Ross Garnaut, Bracks government economic guru Peter Dawkins and former public service boss Michael Keating - advocated a minimum wage freeze offset with an "earned income tax credit" to lower entrenched unemployment.

The earned income tax credit or EITC – a payment to low wage earners contingent on them working – was in use in 17 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries in 2010, including the United States, United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands, the commission said. It's been a pillar of the safety net for America's working poor since President Bill Clinton dramatically expanded it in 1996.

Australia hasn't taken it up. But our minimum wage was third highest among 26 OECD nations in 2013-2014, according to OECD data cited by Richard Burkhauser, an Australian economist at Cornell and Melbourne universities, in a 2014 paper (Another look at the Economics of Minimum Wage Legislation).

Only Luxembourg – a tiny tax haven with incomes in the stratosphere – and chronically unemployed France had higher minimums. Adjusted using purchasing power parity rates to smooth out currency fluctuations these worked out at $US10.70 in Luxembourg and $US10.60 in France. Australia came next at $US10.20. These three were far above Britain and Canada (tied at eighth on $US7.90) and tenth-placed United States ($US7.10).

Translated at market rates (which have since fallen) Australia's then minimum was a world-topping $US15.10. By contrast US President Barack Obama is now battling Congress to raise the $US7.25 federal minimum wage to $US10.10.

Proponents say an EITC is a much better way to help the working poor because it costs a lot less than economy wide minimum wage hikes and targets poor households much more reliably. Since it's contingent on working, it boosts employment.

By contrast, many economists say, raising the minimum wage – the price of unskilled labour – reduces demand for unskilled workers and can increase unemployment.

This is hotly contested; just as many economists dispute these negative effects on employment.

Yet the idea should not be pooh-poohed on the basis of a largely US debate, says Deloitte Access Economics partner Chris Richardson, one of The Five Economists. Our minimum wage is not only higher than elsewhere, it is has more bite because of the wide coverage of the award system: "You are dealing with a different beast in Australia," he argues.superiority of the EITC

The superiority of the EITC over minimum wage hikes in reducing poverty is compelling to many economists.The EITC socialises the cost of paying unskilled workers more by shifting some of the burden to the broader taxpayer community. It makes it more affordable for business to hire them.

Burkhauser cites data from a 2014 Congressional Budget Office paper which controversially found Obama's minimum wage hike would destroy about 500,000 jobs – 0.3 per cent of the US labour force – at its best guesstimate. (The White House sent out its economics' advisers to rebut these findings, but applauded the CBO's finding that 16.5 million workers who remained in jobs would benefit from a raise.)

Less noticed, writes Burkhauser, whose paper is doing the rounds of Australia's workplace relations club, was other data showing that only $US5 billion of the $US19 billion economy-wide cost of the minimum wage increase would find its way into poor households. This is because most minimum wage earners live in middle or even high income households, not poor ones, and some working poor earn above minimum hourly wages but "just do not work full time." The EITC is more effective because it only raises the incomes of workers who live in poor households, writes Burkhauser.

"The US could dramatically improve the lives of the working poor if the real economic costs of the minimum wage were used instead to finance an EITC expansion," he writes.

Robin McKinney, director of the Maryland CASH Campaign has seen first hand the positive benefits of the EITC in the US.

Maryland CASH Campaign aims to increase the financial security of low income working families and helps file 18,000 tax returns free of charge each year.

"It really does lift people out of poverty and can become a game changer," McKinney says."It is absolutely an incentive and can help overcome the ' benefit cliff  '. "

One woman McKinney remembers who received the earned income tax credit a few years ago was paid about $US3000 after filing her tax return. "She used it to buy a used car so she didn't have to take the bus anymore. This meant she could drive to get a better job. So the next year she wasn't eligible anymore which was a good thing.

"It gave her that lump sum that she would never have been able to save at her low wage."

The EITC has been part of US policy since 1975 , supported and expanded by Republicans and Democrats from an initial $US400 credit to over $US6000, depending on income and numbers of dependent children.

Bill Clinton made it a major part of his 1993 budget, declaring: "[w]e will reward the work of millions of working poor Americans by realising the principle that if you work 40 hours a week and you've got a child in the house, you will no longer be in poverty."

Twenty-six states as well as Washington DC, New York City, and Montgomery County, Maryland, a liberal suburb of the nation's capital, top up the EITC from their own coffers.

Steve Holt, a veteran consultant on the EITC, calls it "one of the most successful social policy interventions we have seen over the last few decades". "There is strong evidence that it is getting people into and keeping people in the labour market," he says.avoided like the plague

Despite the EITC's wide international use, politicians here have avoided it like the plague. But the Productivity Commission will force them to at least consider it. The commission says that only 30 per cent of minimum wage earners live in the poorest households, and argues that "the cumulative effect of successive increases in the wage may still have impacts on unemployment" and that "while minimum wages do assist some low-income households, they may not necessarily target poverty and inequality very well".

Modern Australian politics lacks an advocate of the quality of Bill Clinton or former prime ministers John Howard and Paul Keating to carry the debate.

"It's not a debate that Australia's politicians are well equipped to handle," Richardson says ruefully.

Still, Richardson and several of the Five Economists remain keen on an EITC / wage trade off. Changes in budgets, taxes and minimum wage and award coverage mean the policy would have less "bite" today than in 1999, and funds are scarce. But effective marginal tax rates are still highest on the lowest earners, and the case is stronger than in many countries.

Society has two noble aims – prosperity and fairness. Australia relies heavily on minimum wages to deliver fairness – co-opting employers into the welfare system – because we tackled the issue early, when government was weak, Richardson says.

But business is much better at creating prosperity than fairness, especially for young workers, who are often the first workers laid off when times get tough because they are the least profitable. "That's the fault of decisions we've taken as a nation rather than the fault of those young workers," Richardson says.

You wouldn't do it this way if you had the luxury of starting with a clean slate, he adds. "Why not use the welfare system?"

For all that,he doesn't sound very optimistic. It's too easy to demonise advocates of such changes as cigar-puffing plutocrats.

"Australian can do better on the economics of the labour market. Where we always fail is in the politics of the labour market," he says.

HEADLINE: Lack of evidence in Downer death
INTRO: A high-profile inquest into the death of teenager Alec Meikle, who was ­allegedly bullied at Downer EDI, ended with the coroner deciding there wasn't enough evidence to blame the bullying for his suicide.
TEXT:
A high-profile inquest into the death of teenager Alec Meikle, who was ­allegedly bullied at Downer EDI, ended with the coroner deciding there wasn't enough evidence to blame the bullying for his suicide.

The Coroners Court in Sydney was told that the teenager Mr Meikle was taunted by ­workmates and his supervisor for three months at the company's ­train-building operations at Bathurst.

Mr Meikle quit and moved to New Zealand to live with his aunt and uncle. He committed suicide 40 days after his arrival. The death triggered a debate about whether workplace bullying can be responsible for suicides.

NSW Deputy State Coroner Paul McMahon said he could not make ­findings or recommendations into the death because of a lack of evidence it was caused in NSW.

Mr Meikle's family said it was deeply disappointed with the ruling.

"We are very concerned it would take over 13 months to come to this conclusion of no finding. We hope the media attention surrounding this matter, and having the evidence heard publicly, leads to a greater awareness of the possible devastating consequences of harassment," the family said.

Mr McMahon said it was ­uncontroversial that Mr Meikle's job was a significant contributing factor that led to the development of his depressive condition but it was not the only factor. "It would be speculation to find that the events at Downer ­precipitated his action. It could just as well have been something else," he ­said.

"I cannot therefore be satisfied to the standard of proof required that the cause of his death occurred in NSW."Egregious incidents

The most "egregious" incidents Alec suffered, the coroner said, was a "sphincter dilation chart" created by his colleagues David Hall and Ben Eagle and endorsed by his supervisor Colin Wiggins. The chart marked Mr Meikle's errors and threatened sexual assault if he reached the top.

Mr Meikle was diagnosed with severe anxiety and depression, and spent a short period at Bathurst Hospital's mental health unit after he quit.

His parents arranged for him to move back to New Zealand after he attempted suicide following his ­discharge from the hospital. He moved to Australia from New Zealand with his parents in 2002.

A Downer EDI spokesman, Michael Sharp, said the death was a tragedy and there was "no excuse" for the behaviour that occurred.

The company strengthened its ­policies and ­procedures in ­relation to bullying, ­harassment and discrimination over the past five years and was continually reviewing them, Mr Sharp said. "We just don't tolerate it, everyone at Downer has the right to work in a workplace that is free from ­bullying, harassment and discrimination," he said.

Key points Alec Meikle endured three months of taunting by his boss and workmates while working in Bathurst, NSW. The teenager died by suicide in New Zealand.

HEADLINE: Tinkler faces deadline to quit ownership of the Jets
INTRO: Former mining billionaire Nathan Tinkler is expected to come under extreme pressure to give up his licence to own the Newcastle Jets A-League soccer club over the weekend.
TEXT:
Former mining billionaire Nathan Tinkler is expected to come under extreme pressure to give up his licence to own the Newcastle Jets A-League soccer club over the weekend.

Football Federation Australia has given Mr Tinkler a deadline of the end of the month to settle debts the club has racked up under his ownership, including superannuation owed to players and funds owned to a local football federation.

During the week Mr Tinkler sacked several assistant coaches and five players after the Jets lost to Adelaide United 0-7 last weekend.

New players have been approached to join the club and Mr Tinkler has said publicly he wants to maintain ownership of the team. But the Jets club runs at a loss of about $1 million annually, a shortfall the former mining magnate has to make up.

Scottish club Dundee United has expressed interest in buying the Jets, but has not met Mr Tinkler's $5 million asking price.

Mr Tinkler owes about $22 million to Harvey Norman chairman Gerry Harvey, who said he was like a "bank" for Mr Tinkler.

John Stensholt

HEADLINE: Asian Cup ticket sales soar ahead of final
INTRO: Australia is in the final, but a French marketing firm will be the biggest winner.
TEXT:
Australia is in the final, but a French marketing firm will be the biggest winner.

The Asian Cup will deliver a $5 million to $10 million surplus for the local organising committee after a surge in ticket sales.

The three-week event will end with a final between Australia and South Korea in front of about 80,000 ­spectators at Sydney's ANZ Stadium.

The result could boost Australian soccer, although most of the broadcast and commercial revenue will flow overseas. But the event could prove to be costly for Football Federation Australia's balance sheet in the short term.

About 650,000 tickets were sold for the tournament, well above the ­organiser's 350,000 break-even figure.

"Any event can get a big boost from the host country making the final of a tournament," said organising committee chief executive Michael Brown.

"But it is fair to say it has exceeded our expectations. What has also been great is to see Tourism Australia and Austrade leveraging off the tournament in promoting closer links with Asia for tourism and business."

Under an agreement with the NSW, Victorian, Queensland and ACT ­governments, who combined ­contributed $61 million in funding, any surplus will be distributed to the ­governments should ticket sales top $14 million and exceed the $75 million total cost of ­holding the event.

The Football Federation is ­lobbying the governments to return the surplus to the sport in the form of grassroots junior programs or facilities upgrades.

Controversially, there is no ­prize money on offer from the Asian Football Confederation for the ­tournament and the FFA faces the ­prospect of paying each of the 23-man Socceroos squad up to $100,000 each should it beat Korea and win the men's team's first major trophy.

The biggest winner is World Sports Group, which owns all of the ­commercial rights to Asian football.

Owned by listed French marketing group Lagardere, Japanese advertising group Dentsu and Saudi Arabian ­conglomerate Dallah Al-Baraka, World Sports Group signed a deal in 2009 that delivers between $US50 million ($64 million) and $US100 million in ­revenue to the Asian Football ­Confederation annually.

In return, World Sports Group is able to sell all broadcast rights, sponsorship and hospitality for big events such as the Asian Cup and Asian Champions League. The World Sports Group deal, which did not go to tender, was described as "undervalued" by a PwC report into the Asian Football ­Confederation's finances in 2012.

WSG receives huge sums for ­broadcast rights in markets such as Japan and Middle-Eastern nations via the Al-Jazeera network.

Lagardere's last full-year report for 2013 showed €409 million ­($595 million) income for the division that owns World Sports Group.

FFA chief executive David Gallop said he hoped the Socceroos' ­performance would boost interest and spectator and commercial numbers.

"We now have a team of youngsters that will be at the peak of their powers over the next few years," he said. "Off the field, the event has shown that ­football can provide more in political, economic and sporting terms in regards to Asia than any other sport."

HEADLINE: BC Iron tips short-term price relief
INTRO: BC Iron managing director Morgan Ball says he expects the iron ore price to rebound to around $US70 after Chinese New Year but believes it will only be temporary relief for the sector.
TEXT:
BC Iron managing director Morgan Ball says he expects the iron ore price to rebound to around $US70 after Chinese New Year but believes it will only be temporary relief for the sector.

Speaking on the release of the junior Pilbara miner's December quarterly production report, Mr Ball said the results show that despite the price fluctuations, the business can "turn a buck" at the new lows the sector is facing.

Mr Ball said the company was only just breaking even during the quarter, selling its ore at an average price of $US60 a dry metric tonne. The benchmark price delivered into China ­averaged $US74 a tonne during the quarter, implying BC Iron took a ­discount on its lower quality product of up to 19 per cent.

The fall in the local currency has boosted the miner's margins during the last month.

"In [today's] environment BC Iron can still run an operation that can make a $3 to $4 margin if everything stays as it is," Mr Ball said.Iron ore price close to half

The iron ore price close to halved in 2014 and is now languishing at levels around $US63 a tonne. Mr Ball said he was surprised the price had fallen so low so early in the year but he expects a rebound following Chinese New Year to a price of about $US70 a tonne in March and April.

But the second half of the calendar year will be more challenging, he said, with a new flood of supply from the ­Pilbara expected to send prices lower, including from Gina Rinehart's Roy Hill mine which plans to start shipping ore from its 55 million tonne per annum operation from September.

During the December quarter BC Iron returned to producing its iron ore product at rate of 6 million tonnes per annum during the last two months of the quarter after remedying the ­production issues which plagued it ­during the prior quarter.

The miner's Nullagine joint venture with Fortescue Metals Group shipped 1.38 million wet metric tonnes, of which BC Iron's share was 1.2 million tonnes.

The producer has been focusing on taking costs out of its business, reducing cash operating costs by $2 to $3 a tonne during the quarter and ­lowering its full year guidance accordingly from between $49 and $53 a wet metric tonne to between $47 and $51 a wet ­metric tonne.

All-in costs are now expected to be between $54 and $61 a wet metric tonne for the full year, down from between $64 and $70 a tonne.

BC Iron revealed in the quarterly that it has decided to exit its Brazilian iron ore exploration joint venture with Cleveland Mining Company. Mr Ball said this was due to current market conditions and the fact that the company had obtained "two great growth assets" through the Iron Ore Holdings acquisition.At the end of the quarter BC Iron had cash of $110 million and debt of $43 million.

HEADLINE: Lihir remains drag on Newcrest
INTRO: Australia's biggest gold miner, Newcrest Mining, continues to be plagued by its troublesome Lihir project in Papua New Guinea, and ­analysts are concerned there is little sign of a turnaround.
TEXT:
Australia's biggest gold miner, Newcrest Mining, continues to be plagued by its troublesome Lihir project in Papua New Guinea, and ­analysts are concerned there is little sign of a turnaround.

On Friday Newcrest increased full-year production guidance due to its Cadia mine in NSW, after releasing strong production figures for the December quarter.

But UBS analyst Jo Battershill said: "The key asset that needs to be turned around is Lihir, and we've seen no signs of that.

"We think they have got major problems on Lihir and they still haven't enunciated a strategy to the market.

"The [Lihir] December quarterly production numbers were horrible. If anything, there has been a continuation of the unplanned maintenance issues that have plagued this operation since 1997."

Newcrest chief executive Sandeep Biswas said that Lihir continued to underperform against its potential, but he was "confident we now have the right strategy and people in place, having recruited some of the best people externally and from our other operations".Gold stocks rally

Newcrest is one of a string of local gold stocks that have enjoyed a huge rally since December. The rising US dollar gold price and fall in the Australian dollar have buoyed the sector.

But while the Australian dollar goes some way to helping on costs and the gold price, Newcrest's debt is US-dollar denominated.

Newcrest is hedged on the oil price, so they won't have the chance to reap any benefit from the recent price collapse until the financial year ticks over in June.

UBS said costs on a per unit basis for Newcrest were higher than the previous quarter, when extra copper by-product was stripped out.

"In an environment where the $A is working in their favour, it's an area that needs to be looked at more deeply," Mr Battershill said.

The gold miner said on Friday that its average gold price – in Australian dollars – achieved in the December half jumped to $1398 an ounce.

It lifted full-year production guidance by 100,000 ounces to between 2.3 million and 2.5 million ounces, and slightly reduced all-in sustaining cost guidance to $2.3 billion to $2.5 billion.

Credit Suisse said the miner has full exposure to spot gold – $1622 an ounce – against its planning price of $1400 an ounce for the financial year.

Newcrest's net debt in Australian dollar terms is tipped to have increased to $4.6 billion as at the end of December, from $4 billion six months earlier, putting gearing at 38 per cent, UBS said.

"Equity issuances to fix its balance sheet should certainly be considered by the board," Mr Battershill told the AFR.

Newcrest has said reducing gearing is a priority.

An update on debt will be provided at the miner's half-year results next month.

Newcrest shares fell 1 per cent to $13.56 on Friday.

HEADLINE: Snowy wraps up Colongra
INTRO: Purchase gives Snowy a vital stake in the electricity market as fourth largest player.
TEXT:
Purchase gives Snowy a vital stake in the electricity market as fourth largest player.

When most NSW Treasury boffins were putting the finishing touches on their Christmas preparations, a select group involved in the Colongra peaking power plant sale were still bunkered down in key meetings.

Snowy Hydro – controlled by the NSW, Victorian and federal governments – was in the final throes of agreeing to buy the plant on Christmas Eve with final approvals being put in place. Snowy chief Paul Broad and his team had dubbed the deal Project Sodium.

Treasury's steering committee chair Tim Spencer spearheaded the government's efforts along with high profile project director Kerry Schott and project manager John Mackay.

There were a few twists and turns to navigate for the vendor, particularly given a limited field of buyers and issues around the competitive landscape. The field initially included players such as Origin Energy, Asian strategic buyers and mid-market energy focused private equity firms. NSW had Goldman Sachs (which had advised on the two-year power privatisation plan including the  sale of Macquarie Generation) in its corner, as were Baker & McKenzie and KPMG. Goldman bankers Nick Forster and Antony Steinberg helped to manage the sale.

Snowy was always well placed.

Broad had hit the ground running since being appointed chief in mid-2013. The dominance of the big three integrated electricity groups – Origin, AGL and EnergyAustralia – had forced Snowy's hand. As the traditional "insurer" in the electricity market – it is able to step in and fill supply shortages elsewhere in the market due to demand surges or capacity outages – Snowy's position had become increasingly exposed as the biggest players were able to reduce their needs to look externally for 'insurance'.

As a result, Snowy looked to lift its presence in retail markets, and is now the fourth largest player in the electricity market. Along with others in secotr, it is believed Snowy looked first at acquiring EnergyAustralia's Tallawarra power station in Wollongong, south of Sydney, but never pursued that asset. Around that time, Infratil flagged the sale of Lumo Energy, its Australian generation capacity and retail book, which provided the first expansion opportunity, a $605 million purchase finished last September.

Also on the market were the remaining assets of Delta Electricity, the NSW government generator, its Vales Point power station and the Colongra plant.

Snowy looked at how to structure a purchase of Vales Point along with Colongra, looking at how to structure a wholesale deal. However, given that Vales Point is a coal-fired power station, and Snowy doesn't operate any coal-fired power stations, this option was quickly ruled out.

Then it was a matter of looking more closely at Colongra. As a peaking power plant, Colongra is operated intermittently – only when wholesale electricity prices rise to a level where it can be operated profitably. And using gas means Colongra can be turned on – and off – quickly to profit from sharp price movements. But it is constrained by having only a limited supply of gas on hand, sufficient to run for several hours.

Also, the rising use of solar and wind power, is changing the demand-supply parameters of the wholesale electricity market, with concerns by some as to just how ''peaky'' the wholesale market will be in the future.

Goldman had organised several site visits with potential buyers shown that the plant could be remotely started from a laptop from anywhere around the world. Snowy still had some work ahead though.

To win internal – and board support – for the deal required extensive modelling, of both the weather and also the outlook for the wholesale electricity market, where prices remain stubbornly depressed.

As with the earlier purchase of Lumo , Snowy did not use external bank advisers, bar industry specialists to carry out the due diligence on the power station assets along with advisers on the gas market.

''We have in-house experts, ex-bankers and the like. But we used specialists on the plant and on the gas market,' Broad says. ''We're still in the market for more capacity."'

Allens and Linklaters helped with the legal work, while on accounting, tax, human relations and superannuation advice Ernst & Young was on hand.

For the technical and environmental work Jacobs Engineering was involved.

One government-controlled entity– Snowy – buying from another government-owned entity triggered wariness in the market about governance and probity, although these concerns were eased by the fact that both Snowy and Delta had boards in place to ensure they focused on their own corporate interests.

Still, slowing the internal approval process to putting forward a bid was the fact that Colongra was not likely to be immediately earnings accretive, since it depends on weather volatility along with the volatility of wholesale electricity prices to make money.

The year-end rush ensued and an announcement was made on December 29. Snowy paid $234 million to win the assets that cost $574 million to build. The deal was completed on Friday and NSW Treasurer Andrew Constance was quick to point out the governments's electricity generation transactions delivered proceeds of $2.1 billion, removing more than $2 billion in liabilities from the balance sheet.

HEADLINE: Don't blame Uber: it is an example of how things change
INTRO: Customers love it, taxi operators hate it and governments just don't get it, writes Ben Potter.
TEXT:
Customers love it, taxi operators hate it and governments just don't get it, writes Ben Potter.

Billions of dollars tied up in traditional metropolitan taxi licences, hundreds of thousands in political donations from the taxi industry. No wonder state governments have been slow to embrace Uber, the upstart ride-sharing company that threatens obsolescence for the taxi industry as Joe and Joanna Public vote with their fingers and smart-phones.

Sydney's 5500 metropolitan taxi licences are taxi licences change hands for about $375,000 apiece, and are worth about $2.2 billion combined. Melbourne's 4300 metro licences have seen their value slashed from a peak of $515,000 a few years ago to about $290,000 as the Victorian government has issued an unlimited number of new licences to qualified drivers for an annual cost of $22,000. They're still worth a combined $1.25 billion, but that's a loss of nearly a billion dollars on the total stock. Brisbane and the Gold Coast account for another hefty chunk of investment.

The industry's tentacles run deep into state governments. The NSW Taxi Council donated $10,000 to the NSW Liberal Party in 2013-14, and $9000 to the Labor Party. Cabcharge – a large owner of taxis and the dominant taxi payment system that shares digs with the Taxi Council – tipped $100,000 into the Liberal Party's coffers in 2012-13. Premier Mike Baird's father Bruce, a former politician, recently stepped down as ­chairman of the NSW Tourism and ­Transport Council, of which Cabcharge and the Taxi Council are members.

Yellow Cabs in Queensland – owned by a supporter of Premier Campbell Newman, Neil Ford – donated $6600 to the state's ­Liberal National Party in 2013-14. There's a lot at stake.

When it comes to ride-sharing services like Uber, one state's meat is another's poison. Victoria's pro-competition tax commissioner Graeme Samuel has quietly found a neat fix for the ride-sharing regulatory puzzle that's stumped officials in other states.

The upshot is that at least 270 Uber drivers can legally ply for business via the powerful, user-friendly Uber app in Melbourne as accredited hire-car drivers. The ACT government has just initiated an "innovation review" of the taxi industry, suggesting it is more open to change, like Victoria.Insuperable problem for some

But policymakers in NSW and Queensland continue to treat the explosive growth of ride-sharing as an insuperable problem requiring some sort of global consensus. Rachel Botsman, co-author of a popular book on the shared economy What's Mine is Yours, told AFR Weekend last April that ­Australian governments would be caught off guard when services like Uber went mainstream because they were "behind the curve in a frightening way".

That's come to pass.

Botsman says governments misjudged everything: Public desire for a better taxi service and scepticism of government ­regulation; Uber's determination – as a ­global start-up that has fought these battles in dozens of countries – to supply that ­service; and how easily the public would connect the well entrenched taxi industry with governments' hostility to Uber.

"Regulators have a role in terms of ­market competition and public safety and so on, but the public didn't buy the ­argument that this was unsafe. There are ways to change regulation and I think what's come to the surface really quickly is, 'whose interests are you really protecting?'" she says. "I think it's a really powerful signal that the public is basically saying the ­existing taxi service is broken or inefficient or not a good experience, and they're ­welcoming Uber into their lives."

That's in spite of some well-publicised safety incidents: An alleged New Year's Day sexual assault by an Uber driver in Victoria; a rape in India, and road deaths at the hands of Uber drivers in the US.

The difficulties illustrate a broader ­problem that governments whose leaders still grew up in the 20th Century are ­struggling to come to grips with. Smart phones are not yet a decade old, but they're already turbo-charging the digital ­revolution in industries from taxis, ­equipment and car hire to accommodation, office rents, deliveries, freelance work, retail, music and media. In future, this digital ­revolution will spread deeper into industries once thought immune, such as universities and manufacturing.Work world turning upside down

Established firms and the whole world of work are being turned upside down by ­freelancing sites and distributed networks, even as the federal government grapples with workplace laws. Further on, ­ride-sharing combined with autonomous cars could make millions of drivers ­redundant, cull the American car fleet by 90 per cent – PwC predicted two years ago – and take with it much of car manu­facturing, an icon of the 20th Century.

"The reason it is so profound is we're in a time where we can move away from highly centralised hierarchical organisations [and] traditional firm structures," Botsman says.

What frightens large organisations and governments is that decentralised networks and marketplaces that don't have ­centralised controls "are really tricky to ­regulate", Botsman says. Or lobby.

That's a shift governments need to get their heads around. The problem is most government leaders still think of markets in the physical sense because that's what they know, says John Riccio, digital change ­partner at PwC.

"It's a natural default position for those people to think in the physical world rather than the totally open, borderless world that we are currently living in or moving towards," Riccio says.

Trying to block Uber is "like Kodak saying, 'we don't want digital photography to evolve'," Riccio says. Much better for ­governments to embrace it and enhance services for the public.

"Anything that introduces competition and delivers a better outcome for consumers has got to be good for the economy," ­Riccio says.

HEADLINE: Indie kids lead the way
INTRO: The big festivals are dead; in their place are specialist events, writes Dominic White.
TEXT:
The big festivals are dead; in their place are specialist events, writes Dominic White.

The 12,500 indie music kids who will throng to Sydney College of the Arts on Saturday for the 10th St Jerome's Laneway Festival perfectly fit the 2015 festival-goer market segment.

While the grand-daddy of Australian music festivals, Big Day Out, was cancelled this year, the more targeted, boutique Laneway has sold out in Sydney, Auckland and Singapore. Its hometown Melbourne is expected to sell out over the weekend.

It's evidence that festivals which corner their niche can still thrive – even as others struggle in the face of the weak Australian dollar, slack consumer sentiment and a historical oversupply of events.

The events that have survived the ­industry's recent carnage are serving a ­market that has splintered into tribes which are spoiled for choice – and reluctant to spend big. "Australia's Laneway will sell more tickets than last year across the board, although sales have been slightly slower in the lead-up and punters are more last minute," says its co-founder Danny Rogers.

Rogers, who co-manages Grammy-winning artist Gotye, has earned a reputation for showcasing breakthrough international acts such as Florence and the Machine and Mumford & Sons just before they get properly big. Laneway's line-up this year includes critically acclaimed artists such as FKA Twigs, St Vincent and Caribou.

"Strong, clear festival brands with realistic capacities are still doing very well," Rogers tells AFR Weekend.Event shake-out

Laneway's numbers will be well shy of Big Day Out which, in its heyday in 2010, lured 337,000 attendees. But the digital age has made Big Day Out's multi-genre, one-day approach less relevant.

With YouTube, Spotify and file-sharing, fans no longer need to attend a festival to ­discover new acts. They want a tightly curated experience.

It's one reason for a shake-out that has seen a slew of festivals go to the wall in recent years amid ferocious rivalry in a shallow pool of international blockbuster talent.

Harvest Festival, Pyramid Rock and Homebake have all been canned, following in the wake of hippy-fest Peats Ridge, hip hop shows Rap City and Movement, and Sydney's Playground Weekender.

"Sometimes in an industry there is an oversupply and that's perhaps what's gone on," says Peter Noble, founder of Byron Bay Bluesfest, which is held over the Easter long weekend.

"Now we've seen a bit of rationalisation, there is less product available for buyers and that seems from my perspective to work well in respect of Bluesfest."

Noble has pulled in The Black Keys and Lenny Kravitz this year, acts that would not have looked out of place at the Big Day Out, which means his line-up has skewed a little younger than normal.

But the negative reverberations of the Big Day Out flop have continued too. Noble told AFR Weekend that his banks became ­"jittery" about risk last year. "It would seem to be all due to one of the major festivals going out of business," he says.

He will doubtless reassure them if he repeats his 2014 performance. "We had our best ever year last year with sales of 104,000 and we are on target to match it this year," says Noble.The get-away factor

Legions of middle-aged men in overstretched black T-shirts make the annual ­pilgrimage to Tyagarah Tea Tree Farm – often with their families – for Noble's festival, which has featured legends such as Robert Plant, Crosby Stills & Nash and Paul Simon in recent years. They are discerning music fans – their younger equivalents will go to Laneway.

Promoters claim room remains for the multi-genre festivals. But unlike Big Day Out the ones that have survived are camping festivals. Here the immersive, get-away experience ranks nearly as highly as the line up itself with punters.

New Year's Falls Festival enjoyed its best ever ticket sales, selling out in Lorne, Victoria and Byron Bay – where it increased its capacity to 17,500 – and improving its performance in Marion Bay, Tasmania. The three-state, four-day camping festival's sister event Splendour in the Grass sold out all 27,500 tickets in an hour last May.

But for all promoters, low consumer confidence and the weak Australian dollar will be key challenges in the year ahead.

"The international artists that come out here all trade in US dollars," says Geoff Jones, chief executive of Nine Live, Nine Entertainment Co's fastest-growing division, which toured commercial acts such as One Direction, Ricky Martin and Celtic Thunder last year. "The promoter makes a guarantee, typically in US dollars, so when the Aussie dollar is 80¢ versus parity previously he can't offer as many US dollars,"

Jones says Australia remains one of the healthiest concert markets in the world with an "incredibly strong" spend per capita.

But he has noticed a weakness in the mid-tier market below the true superstar touring acts like Katy Perry, Miley Cyrus and the Rolling Stones, which all visited Australia in 2014. "We've had so many of biggest acts in the world that there may a bit of fatigue, which will recover very quickly," he adds.

The once profligate live music industry is growing up and facing economic reality with alarming professionalism.

HEADLINE: The central bank dilemma
INTRO: Easing monetary policy around the world is making it harder for the RBA, writes Alan Mitchell
TEXT:
Easing monetary policy around the world is making it harder for the RBA, writes Alan Mitchell

It's a time for central bank surprises. First the European Central Bank caught markets unaware with the size of its quantitative easing, followed by India, the Canadians and the Danes with their rate cuts and the Singaporeans with their monetary easing.

Will Australia's Reserve Bank keep the trend going when its board meets on Tuesday?

On Friday the markets were betting heavily that it would. The Australian dollar took its sharpest dive since the global financial crisis, and at midday was less than US78¢.

The RBA governor, Glenn Stevens, and his board may oblige. The disappointing performance of the Australian economy justifies a cut in short-term interest rates, and the most recent consumer price index confirms that there is no inflation problem standing in the way of easier monetary policy.

A rate cut presumably would see the Australian dollar dip further, whereas a failure to cut might see the currency move back up to around US80¢.

But a rate now cut might not be cost-free  either.

There is a risk that lower interest rates could start a new surge of local and foreign investment in the Australian real estate market, which could leave the RBA having to rely on untested macroprudential policies to protect the economy against overheating property prices. It might not be a silky smooth ride.

If it were not for the problem of the property market, the case for a rate would be pretty strong.

The economy is growing at below its trend rate, unemployment is trending up, and there is little evidence of the sort of new business spending needed to start lifting growth in the second half of this year.

If anything, the headwinds seem to be strengthening: the global recovery is losing momentum, China is slowing, iron prices are plummeting, and the Europeans and Japanese are supporting their economies with monetary policy that makes their currencies more competitive.

This monetary-policy-induced depreciation is what economists and the media are calling currency wars, and it certainly does put pressure on other countries to cut their interest rates to avoid suffering a competitive disadvantage.

For many countries in a weak world economy, that may be no great cross to bear. And in Australia lower interest rates would be a welcome tonic for the macro economy; so too would be stronger growth in our major export markets of Europe and Japan.

While the Australian economy is not rapidly deteriorating, there are few signs of the revival of non-mining business investment that is needed to help offset the downturn in mining investment.

The National Australia Bank's December business survey showed "a patchwork economy with little to no momentum building" with business reporting another month of easing sales, profits and employment and with a fall in forward orders pointing to continuing soft demand in the near term.

Business confidence improved slightly but remains well below long-run averages.

While the official data show employment growing strongly in November, the NAB employment series weakened and is now below average levels.

"With soft business confidence and weak forward orders there is doubt that the strength in the official estimates can be maintained," the NAB economists warn.

A deterioration in the employment outlook would increase the downside risks to other pillars of the expected recovery: consumer spending and housing construction.

Comparing the soft November and December surveys with the stronger business conditions reported in October, the NAB economists have a discouraging answer to the obvious question: it now looks like it was the October survey – and not the subsequent weaker surveys – that was the anomaly.

The potential problem is property.

There have been signs of investor demand cooling off, but we also know from last year's experience that the market can find a second or third wind.

One rate cut and the expectation of at least another cut would generate capital gains and, potentially, raise expectations of further gains.

To the extent that it led to a sustained depreciation of the dollar, the rate cut also could reduce the exchange rate risk faced by foreign investors in the Australian property market.

This is the tension that central bankers have been warning about for years as they have come to terms with the increasing size and frequency of asset price bubbles. It is the circumstance in which the economy demands one interest rate, and the real estate market requires another.

Macroprudential policy – the manipulation of the regulation designed to keep the banks safe – is a compromise answer to the problem, and the Australian prudential regulators' pressure on the banks to be careful appears to have worked pretty well in the past months.

But the test of macroprudential policy could become much more intensive if interest rates are lowered and there is a new surge of speculative demand.

For one thing, people might start circumventing the regulated banking system by borrowing from overseas lenders. This might reduce anxiety about the local banks becoming tangled up in a real estate boom and bust, but it could still leave the borrowers vulnerable and pose an important risk to economy.

At the same time, the politics of rationing money are difficult. The politicians will want to both put too much reliance on the new policy and excuse large numbers of voters (first-home buyers) from it.

In the short term, there is also the problem of discovering how the new macroprudential policies work in the highly charged real estate market.

While central banks have been arming themselves with these instruments, they have been at pains to stress that macroprudential regulations are no magic bullet.

Here is how the US Federal Reserve's Janet Yellen explained problem: "Experience with such tools remains limited, and we have much to learn to use these measures effectively.

"The limitations of macroprudential policies reflect the potential for risks to emerge outside sectors subject to regulation, the potential for supervision and regulation to miss emerging risks, the uncertain efficacy of new macroprudential tools such as a countercyclical capital buffer, and the potential for such policy steps to be delayed or to lack public support."

Concerns about the property market and a reluctance to put too much reliance on macroprudential policies may have been behind the RBA's strong emphasis on having a period of stability in interest rates. But events may now be limiting that option.

78 US cents Friday's new, but brief, low for the Australian dollar.

HEADLINE: Low $A driving up price of new motors
INTRO: The falling dollar presents a challenge for luxury car makers and buyers.
TEXT:
The falling dollar presents a challenge for luxury car makers and buyers.

Few industries are watching the fall of the Australian dollar as closely as car sellers, especially at the luxury end of the market.

Maserati, whose cars start at around $140,000, said prices would rise this year as the dollar falls. Maserati Australia managing director Glen Sealey said most luxury car makers traded in US dollars. Given the Australian dollar has slid 26 per cent against the greenback in the last two years, buyers could be wearing the higher import cost. "Currency is one of the biggest determinates of vehicle pricing," he said.

Retailers including car sellers are working out whether they should absorb the fall in the currency, continue buying hedges, or lift their prices and risk losing sales.

Porsche is one company that pledged not to raise prices this year regardless of the movements of the Australian dollar.

Porsche Australia spokesman Paul Ellis said its German parent company would wear the cost of lower margins in Australia.

Mr Sealey said even though Australia was one of the most competitive car markets in the world, with 60 marques competing for just one million vehicle sales, this competition would not stop prices from rising. He also said consumer sentiment, on which Maserati survived, remained weak, and created a bigger threat to sales.

"All that conservatism has resulted in a savings rate for the Australian economy. It is near 15 per cent, so people are keeping their hands in their pockets.

"They will only spend it if there's a good reason," he said.

Meanwhile, makers of upmarket electric cars have an additional problem to the dollar's slide. The fall in the oil price has seen petrol prices dip below $1 for the first time since 2009, making the economics of buying an electric or hybrid vehicle worse on balance.

Porsche has just started delivering its hybrid Cayenne SUV, capitalising on the popularity of the model. But Mr Ellis said the offering was related to the technological developments in the car industry, not the threat from competition of other luxury hybrids such as BMW's i3 and i8 and the arrival in December of Silicon Valley-based fully electric car maker Tesla.

They already don't come cheap. A hybrid Cayenne starts at $160,000, around $40,000 higher than its standard petrol cousin. BMW's compact i3 plug-in hybrid starts at $60,000.

The perceived added costs of buying an electric car do not play on the mind of Simon Hackett.

Mr Hackett took delivery of two Tesla Model S cars last month, and despite paying more than $100,000 a piece, the move to being fully electric was a way of life rather than a financial decision.

"We are completely off the grid now," Mr Hackett, founder of 1990s internet company Internode, said of his Adelaide home.

"[The cars] also have a lower lifetime cost of ownership than a petrol car, in two important respects. One is fuel cost; electricity costs far less than petrol, and you also have the option to make your own fuel on your own roof if you wish," he said.

Tesla Australia spokesman Heath Walker said their buyers were attracted to more than just savings at the bowser.

"There are two things that attract people to the vehicle . . . performance or the fact that it's a nice looking vehicle," he said.

The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries' VFACTS report said while passenger vehicle sales fell 6.1 per cent in 2014, SUV sales grew 5.6 per cent, the only category to report a rise.

HEADLINE: Opposing China's influence
INTRO: A new front has opened up in Indian Ocean ­­­geopolitics: New Delhi is taking a strong stand against expanding Chinese influence, writes Angus Grigg.
TEXT:
A new front has opened up in Indian Ocean ­­­geopolitics: New Delhi is taking a strong stand against expanding Chinese influence, writes Angus Grigg.

When a Chinese diesel-powered submarine docked at the Sri Lankan port of Colombo last September it was seen as a triumph of Beijing's newly acquired naval power. The vessel, known as Great Wall 329, moved from its base near Hainan Island, headed south and made its way though the Straits of Malacca.

In doing so it became only the second ­Chinese submarine to enter the Indian Ocean – the first was a nuclear vessel a year earlier – providing a direct challenge to American naval dominance in the region and unsettling India.

But far from being a triumph for Beijing, the docking of its Song class submarine in Colombo – an event that received little ­attention in Australia – has emerged as the catalyst for a re-alignment of the region's strategic balance.

The events that followed are now being described as Beijing's biggest strategic ­setback in decades.

This was on display in New Delhi during the week when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi gave US President Barack Obama the friendliest of bear hugs.

"He is tough and he's got style," Obama said of the Indian leader who returned the compliment by noting the visit had taken "relations to a new level".

Such is their apparent bromance that the Indian press have even dubbed them "Mobama".

These rapidly warming relations between Washington and Delhi are all about a bulwark against China. For Canberra the emergence of a more assertive India means the injection of additional strategic rivalry in an already crowded region. That leaves ­Australia, once again, caught in the middle – a position requiring the most delicate of diplomatic balancing acts.Managing competing economic interests

The issue, as always, for Australia is how to manage its competing economic ­interests, which are reliant on China, and its security relationships with the US, Japan and now potentially India.

Diplomacy is a rarefied and often abstract world. But as 2014 drew to a close and Modi put his more muscular foreign policy into action theoretical discussions of shifting allegiances took shape. This is now the big strategic game being played in the region.

Known in New Delhi as "Act East" the doctrine is about being a more active player in the region, while developing better ­relations with countries in north and ­south-east Asia.

The more active part of the doctrine envisages standing up to China – a battle that would be played out in neighbouring Sri Lanka, as a rapidly emerging client state of Beijing. This would involve submarines, spies and even interfering in another ­country's election.

According to reports out of the Indian capital this week, it was the appearance of the Chinese sub in Sri Lanka in ­September that prompted Modi to buttress against Beijing.

"Every indication suggests it was a wake-up call for India's policy leadership," says Professor Rory Medcalf, the new head of the National Security College at the ­Australian National University.

"I think the Indian security community saw it as unacceptable that China would not only have a regular submarine presence off its southern flank, but would do this without prior consultation or warning to India."

Indian diplomats, providing briefings before Obama's visit, have said Modi was furious with Colombo at not being told about the sub visit and extracted a pledge from the Sri Lankans that it would not ­happen again.The last straw

Just two months later the same vessel made a return visit without India's ­knowledge. "That was the last straw," a ­senior Indian diplomat told Reuters.

The Chinese naval presence in the Sri Lankan capital also served as a warning to others in the region, as two accompanying ships had docked at the Colombo ­International Container Terminal. As the name suggests this is a civilian port, but is actually part-owned by a Chinese State Owned Enterprise.

The worry was the China was using its commercial infrastructure assets for ­military purposes.

After putting all this together Modi looks to have given a green light to the first ­strategic gamble of his prime ministership, just five months after taking office.

This opportunity was re-enforced itself when Sri Lankan President, Mahinda Rajapaksa, called an early election in ­October seeking a third term in office.

Despite concerns about corruption, ­nepotism and China's growing influence, Rajapaksa, who had brutally put an end to the country's 26-year civil war, was expected to coast back into office. That was until the Indians got involved.

Diplomats and operatives from New Delhi's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW),are said to have been involved in engineering Rajapaksa's demise.

This appears to have been done by ­helping stitch together a disparate ­opposition and convincing, Maithripala Sirisena, to resign as Education Minister and contest the poll. On January 9, he became the country's 7th president – completing the transition from political outsider to ­president in just two months.

India's apparent involvement in his ­elevation was flagged by Sri Lanka's Sunday Times newspaper on December 28, when it reported that the RAW's station chief in Colombo had been expelled for "links with the common opposition".Re-focused foreign service

Whatever Delhi's involvement, the new Sri Lankan president has quickly re-focused his foreign service toward Delhi and ­promised to review all Chinese contracts entered into by the former government.

The most significant of these is Colombo's $US1.5 billion ($1.3 billion) Port City project, to be built on reclaimed land adjacent to the historic Galle Face Green.

The project is part of Beijing's so called Maritime Silk Road, and its construction was launched by Chinese President Xi ­Jinping during his visit in September. The entire project is now in doubt as the review begins.

The new government is concerned about a Chinese state-owned enterprise being given 108 hectares of land in a "high security zone" adjoining the port.

The land was to be granted in return for constructing the precinct, which involves reclaiming 233 hectares.

Delhi has long been opposed to the project, claiming a large number of cargos bound for India pass through the port. "China is certainly viewed in New Delhi with considerable mistrust," Medcalf says.

This mistrust has been around since the Sino-Indian war of 1962, but was rekindled during Xi's visit to Delhi in September.

While promising economic goodies, including $US20 billion to upgrade the country's ageing infrastructure, Beijing's actions indicated other ideas. It staged ­provocative military exercise in the disputed Himalayan border region during Xi's visit and positioned its shiny new submarine in neighbouring Sri Lanka.

"I think Modi would have felt rather betrayed and embarrassed by those actions," Medcalf says.

"China is now going to have to accept India as a major variable in the Indo-Pacific strategic game."Republic Day 'chief guest'

That game was being played in Delhi on Monday, as Obama became the first US ­President to be "chief guest" during India's Republic Day celebrations.

Aside from the pomp and symbolism, the two countries broke a deadlock on civilian nuclear co-operation but more importantly agreed to closer defence ties.

This could see the US sell India drones and advanced maritime surveillance ­aircraft, allowing among other things better tracking of Chinese submarines.

Medcalf says this would be "game ­changing" technology for India.

"It would allow India to monitor its ­maritime approaches and move troops quickly to disputed mountain regions on the border with China," he says.

Beijing was predictably not happy and made its feelings well known via Xinhua, the state news agency.

It noted that Modi was banned from ­travelling to the US just a year ago and labelled the pair's friendship a "superficial rapprochement".

"Three days are surely not enough for Obama and Modi to become true friends, given their hard differences on issues like ­climate change, agricultural disputes and nuclear energy co-operation," Xinhua says.

China made no comment on Modi's most contentious utterance during Obama's visit – a plan to revive the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue between India, Japan, the US and Australia.

This grouping of regional democracies was enacted in the last days of the Howard Government, but was quickly scrapped when Kevin Rudd came to power in 2007.Group revival

When it was convened India was seen as the least enthusiastic of the participants. Now it is proposing the grouping be reformed.

It puts Australian in a difficult position. The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue was fiercely opposed by China, which viewed it was an effort in containment. Those in Canberra who favoured greater engagement with China argued it was not in Australia's interests to divide the region on ideological lines – democracy being the divide – in a throwback to the days of the Cold War.

"We lost the argument then," says one person involved at the time of the Howard government's decision to sign up.

Faced with the same decision again, the outcome may well be different. Australia has softened its language and approach to China in recent months, as trade rather than security issues have dominated the relationship.

And it's not clear if even the US, which is enjoying warmer relationship with Beijing, supports the idea. Politely declining India's invitation might be a setback for India and Modi. But after China over-reached in south Asia, his Act East doctrine has already begun to take shape.

HEADLINE: Rate cut pushes investors into risk
INTRO: Savers including young home buyers, self-funded retirees and debt-free households will be pushed into ever riskier property and costly stock investments to offset slumping deposit rates if the Reserve Bank of Australia cuts official interest rates next week.
TEXT:
Savers including young home buyers, self-funded retirees and debt-free households will be pushed into ever riskier property and costly stock investments to offset slumping deposit rates if the Reserve Bank of Australia cuts official interest rates next week.

The RBA is expected to lower its already record-low 2.5 per cent cash rate in coming weeks to prevent a rebound in the Australian dollar as global currency wars heat up. On Friday a rate cut won endorsement from Treasurer Joe Hockey.

The potential cut has alarmed seniors groups, investment advisers and a prominent real estate figure who says investors may not get the returns from housing that they expect.

"People need to be prepared for lower returns from tenants and for the possibility of vacancy rates rising, impacting on their cash returns," said Charles Tarbey, owner of the Century 21 real estate franchise in Australasia, who is opposed to a further rate cut.

With the search for yield hitting fever pitch, fund manager Brad Potter from Nikko Asset Management said popular equity investments such as banks have become stubbornly expensive as retail and self-managed super funds seek them as safe bets.

Speculation of future rate cuts coincided with predictions that Commonwealth Bank of Australia will become Australia's first $100 stock after rising 74¢ on Friday to touch $90. "[Banks] are expensive on virtually all measures," Mr Potter said, noting 30¢ in every dollar invested by passive or index funds was going automatically into the sector.

Chief executive of seniors group COTA Australia, Ian Yates, warned people on fixed incomes would face a significant drop in revenue if the central bank cuts on Tuesday.

Should a rate cut occur, Mr Yates said he would demand the federal government adjust downwards the so-called deeming rates used to calculate pensions and allowances, boosting government outlays at a time when the budget faces fresh revenue hits.

He said lower rates would further open the door to spruikers, particularly for property. "In a low-interest ­environment there's pressure on people's incomes and therefore they're more vulnerable to the too-good-to-be-true story."

A rate cut would likely add fuel to the property market and spur lending to investors, which the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority has said should not exceed 10 per cent of total household borrowing.

Figures published by the RBA on Friday showed lending growth to investors rose 10.1 per cent last year – the biggest increase in almost seven years.

That figure adds to signs that income-hungry baby boomers are buying residential investment property despite concerns the market is topping and rents could fall.

Eight in 10 people aged in their late 50s with a lump sum from selling their family homes believe an investment property will provide superior capital growth and income , according to the survey by Martin North, principal of Digital Finance Analytics. "It's not easy in the current environment, with volatile stock markets and exchange rates," Mr North said. "An investment property is seen as the most tangible, lower-risk option – especially taking into account tax breaks," he said.

Liam Shorte, from Verante Financial Planning admitted he was struggling to find places for savers to put their money. "Investors are really being squeezed," he said. "It is getting really hard. I am struggling to find where I can get income without taking on too much risk for clients."

With the sharemarket "jumping up and down very day," Mr Shorte said he had looked at recommending hybrid assets of banks such as ANZ which yields 6.3 per cent. "But most clients are already exposed to the banks."

Financial marks have fully priced in a rate cut by early March and see a 69 per cent chance of a reduction on Tuesday. The Australian dollar has tanked this week on speculation of a cut, trading at a 6½-year low US77.86¢.

Mr Hockey – keen for a lower currency to offset the impact on the federal budget of a collapsing iron ore price – said on Friday that exporters would be the big winners from a softer Aussie, even if it hurt consumers and businesses that import goods and services.

The Treasurer noted that financial markets were factoring in further RBA rate cuts. "That's a matter for the Reserve Bank, but obviously when Australians have the opportunity to export more goods and Australian goods are more affordable, that's a good thing for Australian business and you've just got to deal with it."

Financial markets have experienced a sharp surge in currency volatility after a series of dramatic central bank decisions this month. The European Central Bank announced last week it would ramp up a bond-buying programme, prompting counterparts from Singapore to Canada to respond with rate cuts or signal that future increases have been put on hold.

The moves have reignited talk that the globe is facing a fresh round in the so-called currency war, in which countries adopt monetary and other measures to lower the value of their currencies in order to stoke exports.

With Rob Harley, Shaun Drummond, Duncan Hughes and Sally Patten

HEADLINE: Broker let off the hook
INTRO: A last-minute legal U-turn has saved Australian Trent Martin from a conviction in a New York insider trading case, writes John Kehoe.
TEXT:
A last-minute legal U-turn has saved Australian Trent Martin from a conviction in a New York insider trading case, writes John Kehoe.

They were two young Antipodeans, an Australian and a New Zealander, a long way from home in the centre of global capitalism, New York. It may have seemed glamorous, but the work was high pressure and the hours long. In need of a bit of support, one revealed to the other a secret. Then everything unravelled. It began over brunch.

Little did the close friends realise at the time, their catch-up at a Manhattan restaurant almost six years ago would spark a massive insider trading scandal on Wall Street and land Sydney's Trent Martin in jail.
