But in a twist that has redrawn the rules on the nefarious world of insider trading, Martin is now deemed an innocent man.

A New York court threw out the insider trading case against him and four stockbrokers on Thursday. Martin, who had pleaded guilty and was due to be sentenced in April, will be enjoying his first weekend in years free from legal pressures of the scandal.

The shocking U-turn is the result of a shifting of the goal posts in the United States on insider trading laws, after two hedge fund managers successfully appealed their convictions in New York last month. That decision means that in the US, it is not always illegal to trade stocks on inside information.

The story of Trent Martin, a surfer from Sydney's northern beaches, is a tale of how the most extraordinary events can evolve from the most ordinary of circumstances – in this case a casual brunch with a friend.

The astonishing details revealed in court documents also expose the naivety of a young Martin and the greed of US traders for whom Wall Street has become infamous.Fateful brunch

In 2008 Martin, not yet 30 years of age, landed in the US, transferring from Sydney to the Stamford, Connecticut office of the Royal Bank of Scotland where he worked as an equities sales broker and research analyst covering transport. Previously the ­Macquarie University commerce graduate had been a financial analyst at Qantas for five years.

In New York, where he lived, Martin soon formed a close friendship with a New Zealand corporate lawyer. The two single men from neighbouring countries discussed careers, families and relationships. Inevitably conversation strayed to work.

When the pair met for a Sunday brunch in Manhattan on a warm spring day on May 31, 2009, the New Zealander was stressed from working on a major confidential corporate merger.

He had limited experience on big transactions and the boss at his New York law firm was very demanding. The Kiwi told Martin he was acting for computer giant IBM to buy Chicago software company SPSS for a significant premium above the market price.

Martin gave into temptation. Three days after that fateful meeting he bought about 1500 SPSS shares for $US34.20 each. But the secret IBM-SPSS plans soon seeped out to a small network of stockbrokers.

Martin told his Manhattan flatmate, stockbroker Thomas Conradt, about the pending IBM-SPSS deal. Conradt tipped off his colleague and law-school friend David Weishaus who told several others.

Weishaus bought 50 SPSS call option ­contracts at a strike price of $US40 with an expiration date of September 19, 2009. If the SPSS stock price rose above this ­threshold before the expiry he would have the right to buy the shares and be "in the money". Conradt soon acquired 30 SPSS shares for about $US32.67.Horse racing

Messages tendered to the US District Court of New York show how the two American stockbrokers felt thrilled and perhaps a little scared about their investments.

Even more amazing was that these licensed stockbrokers, working for brokerage house Euro Pacific Capital, chose to ­discuss their trades on instant messaging, even though they knew the contents must be kept secret.

Weishaus messaged Conradt saying, "jesus we need spss to run up i need that lexus". He suggested they get another colleague to "buy a f---load" of SPSS shares. Conradt responded: "Jesus don't tell anyone else . . . we gotta keep this in the family".

Weishaus replied that he didn't want to go to jail and noted that celebrity Martha Stewart "spent 5 months in the slammer".

But it was too late. Weishaus had tipped off colleagues Daryl Payton, Benjamin Durant and a perpetrator-turned ­prosecution witness referred to in court ­documents as "co-conspirator 1 (CC-1)". The five colleagues bought SPSS common stock or call options.

Durant even emptied $US50,000 ($64,200) from his retirement savings account to buy the securities, incurring an early-distribution tax penalty, to purchase more than 600 SPSS options. From there on, Conradt, Weishaus and other friends referred to SPSS shares as their "horse".

As IBM and SPSS continued their non-public discussions about a takeover, Martin upped his stake in SPPS. On July 22, Martin bought 29 SPSS call options at a strike price of $US35. In the scheme of things, they were tiny amounts for a finance professional earning a six-figure income. The share price of SPSS began to rise. Weishaus wrote to Conradt, "dude horsey is moving . . . horsey can run! . . .come horsey, come on horsey!!!! ­RUUUUUNNN!!!!!"

Conradt responded: "holy f--- . . . god trent told me not to tell anyone . . . big mistake". Weishaus replied: "eh, we'll get rich".Panic sets in

By now Martin was worried. Seeking advice on July 23, he confessed to his Kiwi lawyer friend that he had bought SPSS stock and options after their brunch. Martin was panicking and looking for a way out.

The lawyer, referred to in court documents as "Attorney-1" after becoming a prosecution witness, was "furious" with Martin, the prosecution alleges.

The pair had a history of sharing work confidences. Martin had once handed the Kiwi his Blackberry to show him an email about the sharemarket which Martin had then sent a colleague. They discussed various ways to cancel or unwind Martin's SPSS options without attracting attention.

Martin sold his 29 call options on July 24 and disposed 1000 of his 1500 SPSS shares on July 27. He tried to wipe his hands clean but for some reason held onto 500 shares.

The following morning, July 28, 2009, IBM and SPSS publicly announced a planned $US1.2 billion transaction at $US50 a share. "IBM to acquire SPSS, adding to acquisitions" read a headline in the Wall Street Journal.

SPSS's share price surged 41 per cent to $US49.45. The brokers had made handsome profits and were eager to discuss their ­winnings. Just hours after the announcement, Durant, Conradt and CC-1 lunched at a Manhattan restaurant near their office. Durant paid for everyone's lunch, saying he would pay in cash so there was no record of the meeting.

Later that night, Durant ,Payton, Conradt, Weishaus and CC-1 met at a hotel. They discussed how much money they had made trading in advance of the announcement. Their combined profits topped $US1 million. Durant profited by about $US625,000, ­Payton $US250,000, Weishaus $US120,000, CC-1 $US44,000 and Weishaus $US2500, prosecutors allege. If anyone asked about their trading, they agreed to simply reply they liked technology stocks.

Their cover-up response contrasted with that of the raw Martin, who did not attend the meeting. More than a year passed and Martin sold his remaining 500 SPSS shares for a profit of about $US7900. His total realised profit from the shares and options was about $US9000.Jail and extradition

But in October 2010, the New Zealander (Attorney-1) learned that the powerful US Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating insider trading on the IBM-SPSS deal. He told Martin, who admitted to profiting from the trades and to tipping his roommate, Conradt.

Sensing his vulnerability, Martin immediately quit his job and packed his bags to leave New York. Martin told Attorney-1 he knew insider trading can result in jail, referring to the criminal prosecution of Martha Stewart. The Australian returned to work at RBS Morgans in his home city of Sydney, before taking a job with investment bank Nomura as an equity sales broker in Hong Kong in September 2011.

More than two years had passed since the Manhattan brunch. Martin and the other traders might have believed the incident had been forgotten. But out of nowhere, three days before Christmas 2012, US authorities swooped on Martin in Hong Kong; they sought his extradition and Martin agreed almost immediately.

However, Martin would languish for three long months in a Hong Kong jail with 90 other inmates.Most of them did not speak English. During that dark period, Martin was temporarily admitted to a psychiatric ward after a prison guard mistook an exercise routine in solitary confinement for a suicide attempt, according to Martin's lawyer.

US marshals eventually escorted Martin to the US in March 2013 and his arrest was trumpeted by US attorney Preet Bharara.

"Like other insider traders, Trent Martin allegedly exploited his access to confidential information to turn an illegal profit," Mr Bharara alleged at the time.

Martin spent the Easter weekend in a Brooklyn jail cell before a New York judge released him on bail for $US250,000. Martin initially pleaded not guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud and one count of securities fraud. The charges carry maximum jail sentences of five years and 20 years. He later switched to a guilty plea to the charge of conspiracy to commit securities fraud and admitted passing the information on to others. "I knew that my actions were wrong [and] in violation of the law," Martin reportedly said in court in New York on September 12, 2013.Shocking ruling

Until this week's U-turn, Martin was due to be sentenced in April. He had been awaiting his fate at his parents' place in Sydney.

Conradt and Weishaus were arrested in November 2012, while Durant and Payton were charged in June 2014. Four of the defendants pleaded guilty. Durant, who allegedly earned the largest profit, pleaded not guilty.

But a shocking separate December court ­ruling, that overturned the convictions of hedge fund managers Todd Newman and Anthony Chiasson, has turned Martin's case on its head.

The decision on their case in New York significantly shifted the goal posts on downstream tipping cases. Successful hedge fund managers Newman and Chiasson traded on tips relayed through professional analysts from corporate insiders.

In a major narrowing of the case law definition of insider trading, the appeals court ruled a conviction can only occur if the person receiving the insider tip knew that the tipper received a personal benefit – such as a payment – in return.

The unprecedented ruling has thrown insider trading prosecutions into turmoil and has broken attorney Bharara's perfect record of 80 insider trading convictions without a single defeat.

New York lawyer Michael Dicke, a former head of enforcement at the SEC, said the decision was "groundbreaking and unexpected". "This is a real murky area of the law that is messy," Dicke says.

As a result of the Newman/Chiasson ­precedent, a New York judge last week reversed Martin's confession and entered a not guilty plea on his behalf.

On Thursday in New York, the prosecution dropped their insider trading charges against Martin and the co-accused. US district judge Andrew Carter threw out the case. The prosecutor reserved the right to refile the charges, if the government's appeal against the Newman decision is successful.

Martin wasn't in court in New York on Thursday. Instead he remained in Sydney – in line with his bail conditions.

A lawyer for Martin, Kimberly Yuhas, said in a statement: "We are very pleased that the court has agreed to grant the government's request to dismiss all insider trading charges against Trent Martin."

Interestingly, insider trading law is stricter in Australia and quite possibly ­Martin would not have been let off the hook on his home turf.

"In Australia the concept centres on whether the information is not public and is price sensitive. It doesn't matter who has the information," says Minter Ellison partner Ross Freeman.

Regardless of the legal situation in ­Australia, it's a sure bet Martin is hitting the waves on Sydney's northern beaches this weekend with a much lighter head and heart.

HEADLINE: Victorian Liberals in a state of panic
INTRO: Latest polling in Victoria is catastrophic for the Coalition, and many are laying the blame firmly at the feet of Tony Abbott, writes Tony Walker.
TEXT:
Latest polling in Victoria is catastrophic for the Coalition, and many are laying the blame firmly at the feet of Tony Abbott, writes Tony Walker.

Tony Abbott spent a lot of time on the phone over the ­Christmas and New Year period "consulting'' fellow parliamentarians and former ­ministerial colleagues, ­seeking their counsel but also taking the opportunity to sound off about a perceived lack of loyalty from his deputy Julie Bishop and Communications Minister, ­Malcolm Turnbull.

Those tensions have now been exposed for all to see following reaction to an ­incomprehensible decision to confer an Australian knighthood on a nonagenarian royal whose connections with this country are sparse at best.

A former Howard government minister told AFR Weekend that, in a phone call before Christmas, Abbott had voiced concerns about Bishop's manoeuvrings and those of her cabinet ally Turnbull.

Bishop's meeting with newspaper proprietor Rupert Murdoch in New York before the latter called for the sacking of Abbott chief of staff Peta Credlin will have done nothing to allay those concerns.

Reports Bishop dined recently at Turnbull's Potts Point mansion will have added to what Liberal insiders are describing as "paranoia" in the leader's office.

Bishop and Credlin have been at each other's throats since the early days of the government over staffing issues and travel arrangements.Unhappy families

Whatever the validity of Abbott's ­concerns about the emergence of a Bishop-Turnbull (or Turnbull-Bishop) leadership duumvirate, the fact a prime minister might be giving voice, if privately, to doubts about the steadfastness of his lieutenants is revealing.

This is an unhappy family that is unhappy to a significant degree, to paraphrase Tolstoy. Abbott's leadership may not be terminal despite overheated speculation about "numbers counting" but it now resides in the casualty ward for a finite period.

Abbott has, at best, until the end of the year to turn things around, or risk the possibility of losing the leadership.

AFR Weekend canvassed views broadly across the Abbott ministry, among backbenchers and former Howard government ministers, and could find no individual who expressed anything but despair over his decision to confer a knighthood on Prince Philip in the latest of what is regarded as a series of missteps.

"There is real anger in the ranks driven by frustration and disillusionment. The feedback is nothing short of brutal," one of the smarter young Liberal Turks told the AFR.

And nowhere is such despair felt more than in Victoria, once regarded as the Liberal Party heartland, home of Robert Menzies and solid Liberal majorities until Gough Whitlam changed all that.

Latest polling in Victoria is catastrophic for the Coalition, and if reflected at an ­election would result in the loss of something like one-third of the 16 seats held by the ­Liberal and National parties out of 37 in the states.

Adding to disillusionment bordering on panic in Victoria is a sense among senior ­Liberals their counsel is disregarded in a NSW-dominated party where no Victorian has a seat at the top table.

Former treasurer, Melburnian Peter Costello may have had a poisonous relationship in the end with John Howard, but his larger-than-life presence could not be disregarded.

In his efforts to shore up his position in Victoria, Abbott has been consulting widely with senior Victorian Liberals.

This includes several face-to-face sessions with Costello and discussions with former Howard-era ministers, Peter Reith and David Kemp. Kemp has been conducting a review of the Coalition's recent state election loss, including the question of likely blame attached to Abbott.Ginger group

Costello, Kemp, Reith and soon-to-be-anointed state president Michael Kroger are referred to by Liberal insiders as a ­"ginger group'' seeking to exert pressure on the federal party. But there is no evidence these individuals have coalesced.

Costello will not have held back in his exchanges with Abbott about the need for budget discipline and a consistent focus on what is important, but the question posed widely in the Victorian branch is whether the Prime Minister listens.

"He rings you up, not to listen but to tell the press he's gone round talking to ­people,'' says another Howard-era minister caustically.

This former minister echoed a view held by some that Abbott's leadership is unsustainable beyond the end of the year unless things change.

"I don't think he's salvageable,'' he says.

Victorian Liberals hope Kroger's elevation to the state presidency – his anointing will take place at State Council at the end of March – will strengthen the branch's voice in federal councils, including proffering strategic advice to Abbott.

These hopes probably border on vainglorious. In the end, as a former Abbott ministerial colleague puts it, Abbott's salvation lies with Abbott, and that is what concerns people.

Tony Walker is a former Political Editor.

HEADLINE: Din from the Gong
INTRO: The federal government asserts that it's in control of the nation's destiny, but the Prime Minister is losing control of his own, writes Laura Tingle.
TEXT:
The federal government asserts that it's in control of the nation's destiny, but the Prime Minister is losing control of his own, writes Laura Tingle.

Just how much trouble Tony Abbott is really in as a result of his decision to bestow a knighthood on the needy figure of Prince Philip was there for all to see at the end of a nightmare week. Treasurer Joe Hockey emerged on Friday to don a hard hat and spruik the value of a federal government spend on roads in western Sydney.

He kept getting asked, instead, about Tony Abbott's leadership door.

When Abbott himself appeared a couple of hours later to spruik the benefits of the government's free trade deals, he faced the same sort of questions.

They are the sorts of questions that drive many voters berserk when leadership becomes a focus (why won't journalists ask about more important issues?) But it was in the answers that the Prime Minister's real problems became most obvious.

Hockey and Abbott were trying to get on with the task of telling voters what the government is doing for them, as much of the gratuitous public advice from conservative commentators has told them they should.

But after the events of the week, their much worked-over political rhetoric sounded particularly sick.

"No one wants to go back to the dysfunction of Labor", the Treasurer opined, leaving open the obvious question about the apparent dysfunction of the current government.

The Treasurer and the Prime Minister also had some new lines to put to work.

The Coalition, Hockey said, "is the only political party with a plan for the future of Australia and we're rolling out that plan". It turns out, according to Hockey and Abbott, that the LNP in Queensland – which is facing a massive voter backlash at the weekend's state election – is also the only party with a plan in that state.No ear for irony

Without apparently any ear for irony, the Prime Minister proclaimed that "all the opposition has is a plan for getting into government". Given that much of the internal and external criticism of the federal Coalition is that it has not been able to transform itself from an opposition into a government, that it only had a plan for getting into government and not for what it would do when it got there, the assertions now about all these plans sounded very lame.

Just as lame seems the fact that the entire edifice of the federal government's rhetoric still seems to be framed in terms of trying to remind people that they didn't like the Labor government much either.

The political warrior who seemed to think he could prod the left by knighting Prince Philip – but only succeeded in losing the right – still seemed to be running strategy. It was all about scoring points off the opposition, not talking about the concerns of voters.

"We do not want to become a carbon copy of a bad Labor government, the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd government", the Prime Minister said in response to questions about the barrage of criticism he has faced over the week.

So armed with "a plan", and also a new line about "the Labor-controlled Senate", the Coalition is now striding into a parliamentary year gamely asserting it is in control of its destiny – and the nation's – after a week in which the Prime Minister's grip on his own destiny weakened.

Health Minister Sussan Ley perhaps unwittingly reflected the extent to which the framework for considering the political outlook has shifted both in the public mind, and within the government itself, when she used a tennis analogy on Thursday to defend the prime minister.

"Sometimes you can be down match point and still recover", she said.

This is the Prime Minister's problem: even within the government, there is an acknowledgement that – somehow – it has found itself and its leader on the edge of a political precipice just 16 months from its election win.

Within the government, the past couple of weeks have seen the framework for considering the Coalition's prospects shift from 'voters don't like Abbott but we can't repeat Labor's mistake and get rid of him" to ,"Actually, we may have to get rid of him. We just have to work out how we can get away with it".Trying to hose down alarm

Senior cabinet ministers were trying to hose down an alarmed backbench calling for something to be done, and arguing that the Prime Minister needed to be given time to recover.

Ominously for Abbott, the argument for giving him time was not just based on sympathy for his predicament but the pragmatic view that, if a change was going to happen, it needed to be done in a way which did not repeat the mistakes of the Gillard coup against Kevin Rudd, with its overtones of a party room suffering a very severe rush of blood to the head. Scenarios involving Julie Bishop as leader and Malcolm Turnbull as deputy and treasurer were suddenly being canvassed, as were more improbable leadership tickets.

Few leaders recover easily from such a breach in their aura of invincibility among their colleagues.

Once the leadership genie is out of the bottle, it is very hard to stop it swirling around everything the government does: the internal relationships, the rhetoric, the strategy considerations, the willingness and capacity to take risks.

Just think how hard it is for a politically wounded Prime Minister to try to launch any new policy debate, let alone contentious ones like, say, industrial relations and tax, or even deal with a stroppy Senate.

And that is even before Coalition MPs start focusing on their own mortality at the next election.

The reaction to the Prince Philip announcement was focused on the more immediate. Beyond simple horror, government frontbenchers and backbenchers were just pleading for the debacle to stop.

The fact that the knighthood issue was such a spectacular own goal, that Abbott conjured up a gong for a Pom in his 90s out of thin air, has caused a collapse in any remaining internal confidence about his political judgment, let alone in his willingness or capacity to learn from earlier mistakes and failures to consult.Lessons unlearned

Abbott now carries the burden of a party room of colleagues who fear that he does not only fail to learn from his mistakes, but indeed, tends to dig in more obstinately under pressure.

Beyond the mistrust of his party room, the Prime Minister faces the difficulties of relaunching a range of already deeply flawed policies from the paid parental leave scheme, to health funding changes, to education funding.

On Monday, he is due to address the National Press Club in the wake of the events of this week, and following a Queensland election campaign where he was asked to stay away.

His Treasurer says he will outline the 'plan' the government has for Australia. He has already talked about how he wants this year to be about families.

Despite an apparently convincing election victory, the Coalition and Abbott never enjoyed a honeymoon and has recorded levels of voter support of unprecedented levels  – and not in a good way. Its two-party preferred vote, when compared with that of the first term Howard and Rudd governments, is positively sick.

The revival of criticism of Abbott's chief of staff, Peta Credlin, this week – and its public outing by Rupert Murdoch – reflects not just a frustration with the Prime Minister's perceived refusal within the government to consult his colleagues or attempts to criticise Abbott without doing so directly.

The criticisms of Credlin point to a broader dysfunction in the way governments are working – or not working – in Canberra.

When people criticise Peta Credlin – just as they previously criticised the senior staff of former Labor prime ministers – they were reflecting both on flaws in political and policy management which seem to have now trapped both sides of politics.

One veteran conservative observer argued this week that these flaws ultimately reflect a political class that has become increasingly distant from voters.

"The whole 'inside the beltway/outside the beltway' divide has become quite real," he said. "We try and bridge it through research and polling, but if there is one thing that illustrates the problem it is the decision-making process in the last budget".

"There was no one looking at the cumulative impact of the decisions, who actually asked or wanted to understand how these decisions would affect voters..

"And just like Rudd and Gillard, the current crop think in more day-to-day terms of tactics – they haven't morphed from opposition".

Tony Abbott was lionised as the great and unlikely opposition leader who tore down two prime ministers.

But now he is wounded and under savage public attack from his own noisiest public backers who are frustrated by his incapacity to grow into the prime ministership and increasingly uncertain that he ever will.

HEADLINE: Squashed by property prices
INTRO: The iconic sport of the 80s is feeling the pressure from rising land values.
TEXT:
The iconic sport of the 80s is feeling the pressure from rising land values.

It was the sport of the 1980s. Squash, and its cousin racquetball, seemed to be in every film set in New York. An aggressive Gordon Gekko, played by Michael Douglas, put a young Bud Fox, played by Charlie Sheen, through his paces on the racquetball court in the classic Wall St reet. Squash was played by Woody Allen in his movie Manhattan. John Candy gave up after five minutes of ­racquetball with Tom Hanks in Splash.

Now squash itself is reaching for the towel. The sport is being squashed by high property prices.

The number of squash centres in Australia has more than halved in the past 30 years, with soaring property prices in urban areas one of the main reasons for the demise.

When tennis is in the spotlight as the finals of the Australian Open approach, squash is battling a sharp slide in the number of courts and a diminishing public profile. The sport's custodians face an uphill battle to stem the tide.

Gary O'Donnell, the chief executive of Squash Australia, the over-arching body which runs the sport, estimates there were more than 1000 squash ­centres in Australia in the 1980s, ­compared with 421 now.

"A lot of centres were built privately and as property values have marched on, a lot of that value is locked up in the land,'' O'Donnell says. "Developers and others have been unlocking that value."Private funding

The rise of squash in the 1970s and 1980s as a popular sport came on the back of free enterprise, with most squash centres being funded by private backers built around a business model which paid its way through court hire. Squash was the ultimate private sector sport and many leisure entrepreneurs funded squash centres at the height of the squash boom.

"Those operations were subject to a more commercial footing,'' says O'Donnell. Australian legend Geoff Hunt was a world champion in squash and won the last of his British Opens in 1981 which helped to drive the boom.

But a sharp rise in property prices and the prime location of many centres means many squash centres have made way for apartments and ­commercial development. The land they sat on was simply too valuable.

Cricket ovals and many tennis courts funded by government and local councils were spared the impact of rising property prices. They also have a much longer history and provision of ovals and tennis courts as pieces of infrastructure for local communities went hand-in-hand with the development of Australian cities. The latest figures from an Australian Sports Commission survey, last updated in 2012, estimated 325,000 people played squash in Australia, compared with 240,000 in 2001.

Mr O'Donnell says even at its most popular squash did not have the big ­television presence of tennis or ­Australian rules football. It had no ­flagship televised event, and was mainly a ­community-based activity.New technology

But new technology and equipment is enabling it to expand its presence in fitness centres, and for busy executives it represents a very efficient workout.

There are movable wall courts and lightweight materials which enable ­fitness operators to offer it amongst other exercise choices, and retain ­flexibility in the centre layout.

"It's a great fitness offering."

And in a time of widening waistlines, squash has an ace up its sleeve.

Forbes business magazine says it delivers the best all-round workout based on cardio-respiratory ­endurance, muscular strength, ­muscular endurance and flexibility, and its ­calorie burning ability.

"You don't waste a lot of time. There's not a lot of rest between points.''

HEADLINE: High Court slaps down CFMEU
INTRO: The High Court threw out a bid by the Victorian construction union to delay a long-awaited trial over allegations it imposed a cement boycott on Boral.
TEXT:
The High Court threw out a bid by the Victorian construction union to delay a long-awaited trial over allegations it imposed a cement boycott on Boral.

Judge Kenneth Hayne said the ­Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union should have gone to the Supreme Court to seek a stay on the trial over the union being in contempt of a Supreme Court injunction.

"In this particular case I do not ­consider this court should grant any stay on the orders in which the CFMEU seeks to have this stayed, without­ ­knowing first if an application for stay has been made in the Supreme Court of Victoria, but also knowing the outcome of that application," Justice Hayne said.

"This court should not make a stay without an application first being made in the Supreme Court."

The CFMEU also failed in its bid to have costs reserved, claiming they should be because the matter could return to the High Court if further ­material was gathered.

It is alleged the CFMEU began a ­secondary boycott against Boral in 2013 to pressure the cement maker to stop supplying building group Grocon, with which the CFMEU has had an ­ongoing industrial feud since a 16-day blockade in central Melbourne in 2012.

The company claims the union ­pressured other customers not to buy cement from Boral and claims the move cost it more than $10 million.

The alleged boycott remains in place after almost two years, despite the ­Victorian Supreme Court issuing an injunction against the union, and the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission launching legal action in November against the union and some officials in the Federal court, according to Boral.

This week the Fair Work Building and Construction began legal action against the union and two officials for disrupting a concrete pour at a "major government-funded construction site".

The building watchdog alleges this caused two batches of concrete, ­destined for the $4.3 billion Regional Rail Link Package C Project in ­Footscray, Victoria, to become "cooked" and unable to be used.Multiple law breaches alleged

The FWBC claims union officials Joe Myles broke the law on 10 occasions, colleague Drew MacDonald on four, and the CFMEU on 14 occasions.

FWBC director Nigel Hadgkiss said he was becoming worried by reports of CFMEU officials refusing to obey safety laws while conducting site visits.

"Safety must come first on construction sites," he said. "Safety is a matter for all of us and u Union officials should be leading by example."

As well as disrupting a concrete pour, it is claimed Mr Myles walked beyond yellow safety tape that marked off an unsafe, out-of-bounds area.

The building watchdog alleges Mr Myles blocked a concrete pump from pouring by standing between the truck and the pump, and spoke to the concrete pump operator and other workers, which caused the pouring and laying of concrete to cease in the area.

Mr MacDonald allegedly obstructed another concrete truck by standing in the middle of the access road so the truck could not pass.

The maximum penalties available to the Court in this case, per breach are $10,200 for an individual, and $51,000 for a union.

A directions hearing is scheduled for 6 March, 2015, in the Federal Court.

HEADLINE: Vic embraces UberX NSW, Qld tough it out
INTRO: The Victorian TSC has issued nearly 300 hire-car licences to UberX drivers.
TEXT:
The Victorian TSC has issued nearly 300 hire-car licences to UberX drivers.

Victoria's Taxi Services Commission has paved a way for a thaw in the bitter battle between ride-sharing companies and traditional taxis and slow-moving government policymakers.

In an unheralded move, the TSC has issued nearly 300 hire-car drivers' licences to UberX drivers plying Melbourne's CBD and suburbs, in a move could encourage other states to resolve the impasse. UberX is a ride-sharing service that competes with taxis.

In January the TSC issued about 270 metropolitan hire-car licences to UberX drivers who applied by December 31, with nine months' grace to pass a geographic knowledge test. Drivers must undergo weekly criminal record checks, as do all licensed taxi and hire-car drivers. "Public safety is the highest priority," a TSC spokesman said.

NSW and Queensland are in open warfare with UberX and its drivers, even as residents flock to the user-friendly service and officials worry they are fighting a losing battle.

NSW has issued UberX drivers 33 infringement notices totalling $28,500 using undercover transport police and summonsed 10 repeat offenders to court. "The law is the law, and there are also serious safety issues to consider," said NSW Minister for Transport Gladys Berejiklian.

Campbell Newman's Queensland government, which faces the voters on Saturday, has been most aggressive, ­fining 395 UberX drivers a total of $470,000. Victoria's pro-competition taxi commissioner Graeme Samuel has been less hostile. He told ABC TV's 7.30 Report two weeks ago it was futile for states to try to ban such a popular service.Mr Samuel has pursued a dual strategy. Eighty Victorian UberX drivers face court next Thursday over $136,000 of infringement notices by TSC officers.

Mr Samuel was annoyed Uber started in Victoria without alerting him. But he invited drivers to apply for "point to point" hire-car accreditation. The ACT wants to go in a similar direction.

Hire-car licences cost a few hundred dollars, including medical and police checks and knowledge test fees. Those who have applied since December 31 must complete the knowledge test first.

The licences do not entitle drivers to pick up passengers who hail them on the street or use booking and dispatch systems operated by licensed taxi operators, although these systems have been largely rendered obsolete by ride-sharing apps. But they also mean car owners do not have to buy a costly taxi operators' licence, and the Uber smartphone app renders the licensed taxi radio networks obsolete.

"We welcome the TSC's progressive approach and look forward to policy reviews in NSW and Queensland," an Uber spokesman said.

Traditional taxi operators' licences change hands for about $290,000 in Victoria, down from $515,000 three years ago before new licences were issued on request for a fixed annual fee.

Licensed taxi owners, facing large capital losses and flatlining earnings, have urged state governments to take a hard line. "We are not going to sit quietly by and allow them to roll over the top of our industry," said Victorian Taxi Association CEO David Samuel.

Last month NSW independent pricing and regulatory tribunal chairman Peter Boxall urged the NSW government to embrace ride-sharing, citing a survey showing 11 per cent of NSW ­residents had tried UberX in its first six months.

Ms Berjiklian promised industry consultation and reform in June when she introduced a new transport bill which did not address ride-sharing. But she said this week it was a "complex issue and cities all around the world are grappling with it as we speak".

Uber has thwarted undercover enforcement efforts by blocking credit cards and mobiles of officers booking drivers, forcing governments to issue them new cards and phones to keep up.

HEADLINE: Australia target for illicit China funds
INTRO: A retired Chinese tax official allegedly ordered a businessman to channel money to his daughter in Australia to buy a $2.6 million Sydney property.
TEXT:
A retired Chinese tax official allegedly ordered a businessman to channel money to his daughter in Australia to buy a $2.6 million Sydney property.

The trial of Li Yongheng, former director of Guangdong's State ­Administration of Taxation, has again highlighted the role Australia is playing as a popular haven for illicit funds out of China.

Last October AFR Weekend revealed that a corrupt railway official sent money from bribes back to his family in Sydney, who owned houses and ­apartments worth at least $4.5 million.

The government's anti-money laundering agency, AUSTRAC, confirmed on Friday it was considering a request from China to strengthen the exchange of financial information between the two countries.

At the end of last year, a senior ­Chinese government official said the People's Bank of China was finalising agreements with the US and Australia.

"Once law enforcement officers in the US and Australia identify illegal funds, they will immediately initiate judicial procedures to freeze and confiscate those criminal proceeds in their country," Zhang Xiaoming from the Justice Ministry told the China Daily.

China is ratcheting up pressure on Western countries to co-operate as more cases come to light of money being sent offshore. In the most recent example, Guangdong tax official Mr Li was arrested in January last year, his trial was held in Shenzhen earlier this month and he is currently awaiting a verdict.

According to court documents obtained by AFR Weekend, local ­businessman Zhang Pingbing claims he paid Mr Li bribes of 8.68 million yuan ($1.75 million) over a ten-year period in exchange for introductions to tax officials and favourable treatment.

In early 2013, Mr Zhang said Mr Li told him that he and his daughter, Li Dan, were "interested" in buying a property in Sydney. Even though Mr Li had retired, he asked Mr Zhang to help fund the purchase.

Mr Zhang said he then exchanged 6.5 million yuan into $1 million through "underground banks" and put the money into Ms Dan's Hong Kong account. He claimed she then ­transferred these funds to Australia to buy the property.Multi-million dollar properties

The Southern Metropolis Daily newspaper, which covered the court case, said the property was worth $2.6 million in total.

AFR Weekend has been told the property was sold roughly six months later when it became clear Mr Li was under investigation from China's ­anti-corruption arm, the Central ­Commission for Discipline Inspection.

The CCDI has recently focused on bringing back those officials who have fled overseas or sent their money ­offshore and Australia is said to be a popular destination.

Government-run media outlets in China have speculated for years that Gao Yan, a former high-ranking ­Party official, alleged to have stolen millions of dollars in state assets, fled to ­Australia in 2002.

AFR Weekend reported in October that his son, Gao Xinyuan, who spent five years in a ­Chinese prison for corruption, was a shareholder and director of two ­Sydney-based companies in the late 1990s and early 2000s and involved in a Neutral Bay property deal.

In a separate corruption case last year, jailed railway official, Su Shunhu, was found to have channelled at least $1.2 million to his son and daughter-in-law in Sydney, who owned a number of properties.

While most Western countries ­recognise that China is facing a big ­corruption problem, co-operation is difficult.

China lacks an independent legal ­system and its main anti-corruption organisation is a Party entity and not a government agency. Corruption cases can also attract the death penalty.

AUSTRAC said it received a letter from PBOC's China Anti-Money Laundering Monitoring and Analysis Centre, dated January 6, regarding the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on the exchange of information and was "still in the process of considering the request".

HEADLINE: $1m Chinese bribe helps buy Sydney property, court hears
INTRO: Retired tax official on trial as China crackdown ramps up.
TEXT:
Retired tax official on trial as China crackdown ramps up.

The text message was always going to be hard to explain. From a local Guangdong businessman to a retired tax official, it read: "Boss. Total amount r650, a100. All done. Wish you a happy trip."

In a country where money is counted in the 10,000s, corruption investigators concluded that Zhang Pingbing was referring to the 6.5 million yuan he had just changed into $1 million dollars and put into the Hong Kong bank account of Li Yongheng's daughter. They claim the "r" referred to renminbi (another name for China's currency) and the "a" to Australian dollars.

But according to evidence given by Zhang during Li's corruption trial, which was covered by the Southern Metropolis Daily, the man he called "boss" had a different explanation prepared. If asked, Zhang should simply tell investigators the text was referring to types of tiles that he had given the former tax official's daughter, Li Dan. The Shenzhen Intermediate People's court was told this month that Li Dan was not doing up her kitchen or bathroom. Rather, she was buying a $2.6 million property in Sydney and needed more money.

Li and his wife, Jiang Yuan, who faced her own corruption trial this week, maintain they only borrowed money from Zhang. However, their claims clash with Zhang's evidence that he paid millions of yuan in bribes to the couple over a 10-year period.

And it appears that he was not the only businessman looking to benefit from Li's connections.'Other payments made'

Three other companies claim they, too, paid bribes to Li and his family in exchange for favourable treatment from the local tax department.

Apart from receiving money for the Sydney property, Li's daughter was allegedly paid a salary from a company, Wanmei, who hired her as a financial consultant. Wanmei claims it paid her a total of $HK600,000 ($97,558) over 2½ years in monthly instalments, during which time she did no work for the company.

In all, the elder Li stands accused of accepting almost 10 million yuan ($2 million) in bribes either directly or via his family. But it is the Sydney property that particularly caught the eye of investigators.

As part of President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign there has been a special focus on bringing back those officials who have fled overseas and stashed their ill-gotten gains offshore.

It is known as Operation Fox Hunt and since it was launched in July last year, has reportedly led to 680 repatriations, with 117 "fugitives" having been on the run for more than a decade.

According to the US-based non-profit group Global Financial Integrity, $US2.8 trillion was spirited illegally out of China between 2005 and 2011. And Australia, with Canada and the United States, is often cited by government spokespeople as one of the most popular destinations for corrupt officials.

Tracking down illegal purchases is often difficult because foreign purchasers skirt scrutiny from the Foreign Investment Review Board by buying the property in the name of locally based associates. The median price for houses in Sydney in December – when the Li's are believed to have sold the property – had risen about 18 per cent since April, according to property research group RP Data.

HEADLINE: Better way to help low-paid
INTRO: Tax credits may be better at boosting income than fixed wage rates, write Ben Potter and John Kehoe.
TEXT:
Tax credits may be better at boosting income than fixed wage rates, write Ben Potter and John Kehoe.

Here's a barbecue stopper that some economists say would give the working poor a fairer suck of the sauce bottle: cut out minimum wage increases and top up their incomes with a tax credit instead.

But the idea comes with a caveat: it's a guaranteed incendiary device at a time of unusually febrile political debate in Australia, where the minimum wage has occupied hallowed ground since the 1907 decision of arbitration judge Henry Bournes Higgins to set a living wage for a "male breadwinner" with a wife and two kids.

"Tony Abbott still wants to attack the minimum wage and penalty rates in this country," Opposition Leader Bill Shorten said when the Productivity Commission put minimum wages and tax credits on the table in its work-place issues paper for the government.

"It will be a weeping sore for the government,'' ACTU assistant boss Tim Lyons said.

Small wonder the idea has never taken root in Australia. Yet it comes with solid academic backing and is widely used around the world. In Australia in 1999, "The Five Economists" – including Hawke government adviser Ross Garnaut, Bracks government economic guru Peter Dawkins and former public service boss Michael Keating - advocated a minimum wage freeze offset with an "earned income tax credit" to lower entrenched unemployment.

The earned income tax credit or EITC – a payment to low wage earners contingent on them working – was in use in 17 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries in 2010, including the United States, United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands, the commission said. It's been a pillar of the safety net for America's working poor since President Bill Clinton dramatically expanded it in 1996.

Australia hasn't taken it up. But our minimum wage was third highest among 26 OECD nations in 2013-2014, according to OECD data cited by Richard Burkhauser, an Australian economist at Cornell and Melbourne universities, in a 2014 paper (Another look at the Economics of Minimum Wage Legislation).

Only Luxembourg – a tiny tax haven with incomes in the stratosphere – and chronically unemployed France had higher minimums. Adjusted using purchasing power parity rates to smooth out currency fluctuations these worked out at $US10.70 in Luxembourg and $US10.60 in France. Australia came next at $US10.20. These three were far above Britain and Canada (tied at eighth on $US7.90) and tenth-placed United States ($US7.10).

Translated at market rates (which have since fallen) Australia's then minimum was a world-topping $US15.10. By contrast US President Barack Obama is now battling Congress to raise the $US7.25 federal minimum wage to $US10.10.

Proponents say an EITC is a much better way to help the working poor because it costs a lot less than economy wide minimum wage hikes and targets poor households much more reliably. Since it's contingent on working, it boosts employment.

By contrast, many economists say, raising the minimum wage – the price of unskilled labour – reduces demand for unskilled workers and can increase unemployment.

This is hotly contested; just as many economists dispute these negative effects on employment.

Yet the idea should not be pooh-poohed on the basis of a largely US debate, says Deloitte Access Economics partner Chris Richardson, one of The Five Economists. Our minimum wage is not only higher than elsewhere, it is has more bite because of the wide coverage of the award system: "You are dealing with a different beast in Australia," he argues.superiority of the EITC

The superiority of the EITC over minimum wage hikes in reducing poverty is compelling to many economists.The EITC socialises the cost of paying unskilled workers more by shifting some of the burden to the broader taxpayer community. It makes it more affordable for business to hire them.

Burkhauser cites data from a 2014 Congressional Budget Office paper which controversially found Obama's minimum wage hike would destroy about 500,000 jobs – 0.3 per cent of the US labour force – at its best guesstimate. (The White House sent out its economics' advisers to rebut these findings, but applauded the CBO's finding that 16.5 million workers who remained in jobs would benefit from a raise.)

Less noticed, writes Burkhauser, whose paper is doing the rounds of Australia's workplace relations club, was other data showing that only $US5 billion of the $US19 billion economy-wide cost of the minimum wage increase would find its way into poor households. This is because most minimum wage earners live in middle or even high income households, not poor ones, and some working poor earn above minimum hourly wages but "just do not work full time." The EITC is more effective because it only raises the incomes of workers who live in poor households, writes Burkhauser.

"The US could dramatically improve the lives of the working poor if the real economic costs of the minimum wage were used instead to finance an EITC expansion," he writes.

Robin McKinney, director of the Maryland CASH Campaign has seen first hand the positive benefits of the EITC in the US.

Maryland CASH Campaign aims to increase the financial security of low income working families and helps file 18,000 tax returns free of charge each year.

"It really does lift people out of poverty and can become a game changer," McKinney says."It is absolutely an incentive and can help overcome the ' benefit cliff  '. "

One woman McKinney remembers who received the earned income tax credit a few years ago was paid about $US3000 after filing her tax return. "She used it to buy a used car so she didn't have to take the bus anymore. This meant she could drive to get a better job. So the next year she wasn't eligible anymore which was a good thing.

"It gave her that lump sum that she would never have been able to save at her low wage."

The EITC has been part of US policy since 1975 , supported and expanded by Republicans and Democrats from an initial $US400 credit to over $US6000, depending on income and numbers of dependent children.

Bill Clinton made it a major part of his 1993 budget, declaring: "[w]e will reward the work of millions of working poor Americans by realising the principle that if you work 40 hours a week and you've got a child in the house, you will no longer be in poverty."

Twenty-six states as well as Washington DC, New York City, and Montgomery County, Maryland, a liberal suburb of the nation's capital, top up the EITC from their own coffers.

Steve Holt, a veteran consultant on the EITC, calls it "one of the most successful social policy interventions we have seen over the last few decades". "There is strong evidence that it is getting people into and keeping people in the labour market," he says.avoided like the plague

Despite the EITC's wide international use, politicians here have avoided it like the plague. But the Productivity Commission will force them to at least consider it. The commission says that only 30 per cent of minimum wage earners live in the poorest households, and argues that "the cumulative effect of successive increases in the wage may still have impacts on unemployment" and that "while minimum wages do assist some low-income households, they may not necessarily target poverty and inequality very well".

Modern Australian politics lacks an advocate of the quality of Bill Clinton or former prime ministers John Howard and Paul Keating to carry the debate.

"It's not a debate that Australia's politicians are well equipped to handle," Richardson says ruefully.

Still, Richardson and several of the Five Economists remain keen on an EITC / wage trade off. Changes in budgets, taxes and minimum wage and award coverage mean the policy would have less "bite" today than in 1999, and funds are scarce. But effective marginal tax rates are still highest on the lowest earners, and the case is stronger than in many countries.

Society has two noble aims – prosperity and fairness. Australia relies heavily on minimum wages to deliver fairness – co-opting employers into the welfare system – because we tackled the issue early, when government was weak, Richardson says.

But business is much better at creating prosperity than fairness, especially for young workers, who are often the first workers laid off when times get tough because they are the least profitable. "That's the fault of decisions we've taken as a nation rather than the fault of those young workers," Richardson says.

You wouldn't do it this way if you had the luxury of starting with a clean slate, he adds. "Why not use the welfare system?"

For all that,he doesn't sound very optimistic. It's too easy to demonise advocates of such changes as cigar-puffing plutocrats.

"Australian can do better on the economics of the labour market. Where we always fail is in the politics of the labour market," he says.

HEADLINE: Abbott a 'very good captain': Abbott
INTRO: Prime Minister Tony Abbott says his internal rivals are popular and excelling because of his own strength as the government's leader.
TEXT:
Prime Minister Tony Abbott says his internal rivals are popular and excelling because of his own strength as the government's leader.

Mr Abbott vowed on Friday that he would "absolutely'' lead the Coalition to the next election while Treasurer Joe Hockey, whose tenure is also under a cloud, said the Coalition risked becoming dysfunctional like the previous Labor government if the leadership talk takes hold.

"Everyone's entitled to a view but I would just say to people we do not want to become a carbon copy of a bad Labor government, the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd government,'' he said.

Mr Abbott cast a cloud over his leadership with Monday's announcement that Prince Philip would be awarded a Knighthood of the Order of Australia.

Ministers and MPs are actively canvassing replacing both Mr Abbott and Mr Hockey if the government's fortunes do not lift in the second half of the year. Foreign Minister Julie Bishop and Communications Minister Malcolm Turnbull are the two replacements most spoken about. Mr Abbott said he had a very strong team, the key to which was his leadership.

"One of the reasons why so many members of the team are able to perform so well is because they have got a very good captain,'' he said.

"It takes a good captain to help all the players of a team to excel."

Mr Abbott described his decision to knight Prince Philip as a "stuff-up" but said he would no longer be distracted by the issue.

On Friday, Mr Turnbull was in the United States where he delivered a speech on shifting economic and military strengths i n the Asia-Pacific.

One of the rapidly increasing challenges caused by the rise of China and India was how countries such as Australia and the United States could remain high-wage economies with social safety nets, he said.

"Realistic governments in advanced economies can't be blind to the impact of convergence, technological catch-up, and growing competition across a range of sectors from the skilled, productive workforces and sophisticated, innovative producers we see in emerging Asia and elsewhere,'' he said.

"Many of the policies and premises of the past are already unsustainable.

"Leaders must be decision-makers, but they must also be, above all, explainers and advocates, unravelling complex issues in clear language that explains why things have to change and why the government cannot solve every problem."

Anxious Coalition MPs will be watching Saturday's Queensland state election for signs of any backlash towards the Abbott government. Mr Abbott has been asked to stay away from Queensland during the campaign.

Mr Hockey said if there were a swing against the Newman government, this would be due to a combination of a natural correction back to Labor, which lost heavily at the last election, and disquiet over the loss of 15,000 mining jobs caused by depressed commodity prices.

"I say to the people of Queensland don't abandon good government,'' he said.

HEADLINE: WICET 'on track' to load despite fall in coal price
INTRO: The Wiggins Island Coal Export ­Terminal will begin loading coal onto ships in April despite concerns over its ­financial future as its owners battle ­falling coal prices.
TEXT:
The Wiggins Island Coal Export ­Terminal will begin loading coal onto ships in April despite concerns over its ­financial future as its owners battle ­falling coal prices.

"Everything is on track," said Robert Barnes,  WICET's chief executive.

"The banks are not worried, we're still within the funding envelope, and still within the project schedule."

Concern over the sustainability of WICET's coal exports has emerged as some of the eight coal producers that own the terminal run into financial ­difficulties.

Cockatoo Coal's shares have been suspended on the Australian Securities Exchange for more than two months as it reviews its financing, with the ­company planning to update the ­market on Tuesday.

Another of the terminal's owners, Bandanna Energy, went into administration in September. A third owner, Glencore, suspended production for several weeks to avoid selling coal at a loss in an over-supplied market.Coal price down a third

Thermal coal prices lost more than one-third of their value in 2014 as ­production increased and demand from China weakened. China cut its use of thermal coal by 3 percent in 2014, said economist Ross Garnaut.

The coal producers are obliged to meet WICET's costs, whether they ship coal or not.

Cockatoo has made $39 million in payments, guaranteed by ANZ, to WICET for a take or pay agreement ­covering three million tonnes of coal annually, said its 2014 financial report.

If Cockatoo goes into administration, the six remaining coal producers that own WICET will need to ship additional coal or make extra financial payments to cover the shortfall.

WICET believes that its funding is secure because large producers such as Glencore, a multinational company based in Switzerland, will be able to support the terminal financially.

But Glencore,which is pursuing Rio Tinto for a merger, is reviewing its ­global coal operations as the outlook for its other commodities – including ­copper – worsens.  

Analysts have warned Glencore may get hit with a credit ratings downgrade, which would increase its funding costs at time when its stock price is sinking.

WICET has also been embroiled in disputes with contractors over completion of work at the terminal, including engineering group Monadelphous.

But Mr Barnes said the work ­undertaken by contractor John ­Holland, which, like Monadelphous has filed legal claims related to cost blowouts, was progressing.

"John Holland are performing really well," he said.

WICET expected to start unloading its first train of coal on March 13 and start loading coal onto ships between April 17 and April 23.

Mechanical completion of the ­terminal was expected by April 30.

WICET was now commissioning ship loaders, wharf and jetty conveyor belts, as well as a stockyard tunnel and stacker.

"All major project works have been completed and contractors are starting to demobilise," Mr Barnes said.

HEADLINE: Seven positioned to hatch oil and gas deals
INTRO: Seven Group Holdings has positioned itself to benefit from any future consolidation among Cooper Basin energy companies or a broader recovery in the battered oil and gas sector through its stake in ASX-listed Beach Energy.
TEXT:
Seven Group Holdings has positioned itself to benefit from any future consolidation among Cooper Basin energy companies or a broader recovery in the battered oil and gas sector through its stake in ASX-listed Beach Energy.

Seven Group, chaired and controlled by media billionaire Kerry Stokes, snared a 3.5 per cent stake in Beach Energy after-market on Thursday, as first revealed by afr.com. A second ­parcel of 30 million shares traded at $1 a share just before the close on Friday, with the buyer yet to be confirmed.

News of Thursday's move sent Beach shares up 6¢ to 96¢ on Friday, giving it a market cap of $1.2 billion with Seven's recent $200 million takeover of Nexus Energy raising questions about Seven's intent.

Both Seven and Beach declined to comment on Friday.

There has been no contact between the two companies.

Beach is understood to be unsurprised by interest in its stock at these prices although Seven is understood not to have any ambitions to build a controlling stake. The rapid collapse in oil prices has wrought havoc on the energy sector and Beach stock has shed around 40 per cent since July.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Andrew Williams said that Beach has strategically good long-term assets and it is struggling with the low oil price.

"At some point these assets get [value] realised. Either by the market or by a corporate. Perversely, weaker prices may be the catalyst to get some M&A going in the sector," he said.Anticipation of deals being hatched

There is widespread anticipation of deals being hatched among several players in the Cooper Basin.

"We think there should be consolidation in the Cooper Basin," Credit Suisse analyst Martin Kronborg said. "Cooper Basin players are some of the ones that have been hit very hard, which will mean there will be a lot of potential ­buyers sniffing around."

However, Seven's $1.1 billion of net debt means a run at Beach would be  difficult without a partner or an equity raising.

Mr Kronborg said Seven almost ­certainly doesn't have the fire power to acquire Beach on its own. "They'd have to take on a fair amount of debt . . . but it's not our understanding that [a takeover] is what Seven wants to do," he said.

Since Don Voelte, a veteran oil and gas man and a former CEO of Woodside Petroleum, became Seven Group boss in July 2013 the company has built a position in the energy sector with the aim of forming "a third ­operating pillar".

As of 30 June 2014 Seven held a ­portfolio of listed equity investments worth $915.6 million. The portfolio includes several energy investments and is understood to include Woodside as well as stakes in Cooper Basin operators Senex and Drillsearch Energy.

If Seven does have positions in Senex, Drillsearch and Beach it should do well if the Cooper consolidates.Investment closely watched

Beach Energy boss Reg Nelson is due to step down on July 1, and will be replaced by Woodside's Rob Cole, a former acolyte of Mr Voelte.

HEADLINE: Cashed-up Hegarty returns as deal-maker
INTRO: EMR Capital says its offshore backers are keen on corporate, not project investment.
TEXT:
EMR Capital says its offshore backers are keen on corporate, not project investment.

Fortescue vice-chairman and mining identity Owen Hegarty has re -emerged at the helm of a $US450 million ($577 million) war chest, as he seeks to buy into mining companies at a time of huge pain for the sector.

Mr Hegarty, a high-flyer who walked away with more than $8 million after the merger that created copper miner Oz Minerals, has raised one of ­Australia's biggest specialist mining private equity funds.

Melbourne-based EMR Capital, a private equity firm Mr Hegarty ­co-founded, closed its first fund on Friday at $US450 million, ahead of a target of $US400 million, after 14 months of ­fundraising.

It is targeting "strategic" stakes at a corporate level, rather than a project level, in miners across four ­commodities: potash, coking coal, ­copper and gold.

Most of the capital has come from large institutional investors in the United States, mainly endowments by universities and corporations, foundations, family offices and funds-of-funds. European institutions also invested.

For some, EMR was their first foray into mining, Mr Hegarty told AFR Weekend.

Resources exposure for private equity investors in the United States was often limited to oil and gas, Mr Hegarty said.

"And they've made good surpluses out of oil and gas. Yes they've been in resources, but not much on the ­minerals side."

EMR chief executive Jason Chang is confident the fund can better ­traditional private equity's typical ­internal rate of return, which is about 25 per cent.

"Mining offers an opportunity to go beyond that," Mr Chang, the former partner in charge of KPMG's Asia ­practice, said. "It's not easy, I'm not ­trying to be cavalier about this, but I think it does give you the opportunity simply because it is a relatively new ­sector for private equity."

Mr Chang co-founded EMR with Mr Hegarty in 2011.

EMR's fund has already made three investments.

EMR will look to buy into miners at the corporate level, rather than the project level, Mr Chang said.

"That's where management and IP (intellectual property) sit, so we ­typically try to buy at that level," he said. That mandate became more pertinent if the miner was diversified.

"Because if you are just buying an asset without the IP and management team, quite often there is a conflict between the mothership and the project company itself."

Mr Hegarty was managing director of Rio Tinto's Asian division, before founding Oxiana, which merged with Zinifex in 2008 to become Oz Minerals.

The mining sector is not short of ­private equity funds, after a string of new raisings over the 18 months.

EMR joins the long line of funds, led by Mick Davis' X2 Resources, trying to find the right resources buys for their mountains of cash.

Resources bankers have been ­staggered by strong interest from ­private equity, which has emerged as an alternative source of finance for the ­sector.

But despite all the talk and frequenting of data rooms, private equity has so far struggled to get over the line when it comes to buying mining assets. It is a big challenge to leverage up mining assets and get the right returns to meet private equity standards.

Despite the lacklustre hit rate in the space so far, Mr Hegarty and Mr Chang are confident they can find good homes for the EMR cash.

"The current market presents opportunity," Mr Chang said.

"Volatility is driving all the mining companies mad. You can't raise equity at the right time, and sometimes you can't raise debt," he said.

"Quite often the good assets sit in the hands of companies that can't raise ­capital."

And for privately-held miners, there was little incentive to go public now, Mr Chang said.

EMR has made three investments so far, including taking a $10 million stake in ASX-listed potash player Highfield Resources and stakes in two private companies. And Mr Hegarty said they were close to pulling the trigger on ­several deals.

Mr Hegarty is a non-executive ­director of Highfield.

The dire sentiment in public markets has seen many mining companies approach EMR for funding.

It is a good time to buy in.

Australia, along with other politically "stable" countries, is a key target.

But Mr Hegarty stressed that EMR was looking for "strategic" stakes.

"We need to have a measure of ­influence and control in those ­companies and things we invest in," Mr Hegarty said. "And that's important when it comes to not only to adding value, but it's particularly important from an exit ­perspective."

But even though bargains were aplenty now, and share prices depressed, Hegarty said it was important to remain cautious and be patient.

"It's a tough time in the resources market," he said. "The tide will come back, it will rise again as it always does, but we just want to make sure we ­continue to invest in quality assets.

"It's a good time to have access to the funds but it doesn't mean we will be splashing it about."

The US investors in EMR's $US450 million fund missed little when it came to due diligence on Hegarty, Chang, and their team of about 12.

"Following diligence from their office overseas, they would very often come to Melbourne to run due ­diligence on the rest of the team to meet them and see if their message was consistent with those of us who had gone on the roadshow," Mr Chang said.

"But that's logical, given they are committing 10-year money to us."

Mr Hegarty agreed, saying, "It makes sense for them to do that kind of due ­diligence – especially in mining – given it's an industry many don't have ­experience or connections in".

HEADLINE: Westpac's Kelly silent on career moves
INTRO: Outgoing Westpac Banking Corp chief Gail Kelly told staff on Friday she has yet to make any decisions on her next ­professional pursuit, as the most prominent woman in Australian banking prepares to embark on a three-month break in Africa.
TEXT:
Outgoing Westpac Banking Corp chief Gail Kelly told staff on Friday she has yet to make any decisions on her next ­professional pursuit, as the most prominent woman in Australian banking prepares to embark on a three-month break in Africa.

Friday was Ms Kelly's last day as Westpac boss, a position she has held for seven years. In her farewell email to employees, Ms Kelly noted Westpac "will move to the next level" under new chief Brian Hartzer and that she is keen to have a much-needed holiday with her husband, Allan.

"On our return in the middle of the year, I will be super refreshed and ready to decide how best to devote my time and energies. So, no decisions yet!"

Ms Kelly's reign as chief was not always smooth, and was kicked off by the acquisition of her former employer, St George Bank.

Ms Kelly's last email to the bank's employees also spoke of her focus throughout her tenure on customer and staff engagement. There was still more to do on that front too, she added.'I leave you with a word: Ubuntu.'

Of the big four banks, Westpac ranks second on consumer satisfaction, after Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

HEADLINE: Cheaper fuel prices 'equal two rate cuts'
INTRO: Lower petrol prices are worth the equivalent of two regular interest rate cuts to consumers, economists say.
TEXT:
Lower petrol prices are worth the equivalent of two regular interest rate cuts to consumers, economists say.

Deutsche Bank calculated Australians have received a $7 billion boost from cheaper petrol.

"That's equivalent to more than 50 basis points of interest rate cuts, or roughly 2 per cent of retail trade and one-third the size of the Rudd government stimulus payments," the broking firm said in a note.

Deutsche said it expected Australians to spend a large chunk of the extra money in supermarkets rather than on expensive products because consumer confidence remained stubbornly weak and the estimated $15 benefit per family was too small.

The NRMA said current prices, which are hovering around $1 a litre in most capitals, the lowest since 2009, are unlikely to fall much further.

Bank of America Merrill Lynch economist Saul Eslake said the lower petrol prices were one reason to keep rates on hold when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday.

"Retail petrol prices have fallen by around 48 cents per litre (32 per cent) since last July, which we calculate will save households an average of close to $50 a month – a similar saving to that which would result from a cut in interest rates of 45 basis points," he said.

Sam Tsiaplias, senior research fellow at the Melbourne Institute, which conducts the Westpac Melbourne Institute index of consumer sentiment, said cheaper petrol prices were more likely being saved than spent.

"Typically you would expect when prices fall substantially, sentiment would rise. In the last few months that hasn't really happened," he said.

Consumer sentiment remains low because of high unemployment and weak international sentiment, he said, and was 10 per cent lower than the same time last year, when the petrol price was around 50¢ a litre more expensive.

"Without that fall in prices, it probably would have been a bigger decline," he said.

Since petrol prices dipped below $1 a litre for the first time since 2009 in early January, only South Australia has experienced average prices below that mark. Motorists in Adelaide filled up at an average price of 99.6¢ for a litre on Friday.

NRMA president Kyle Loades said the fall in the dollar to just above 77¢ on Friday morning, and global crude oil prices rising marginally over the past two weeks were factors in petrol prices lingering at current prices.

"This may well be as good as it will get," he said. "Oil prices have risen and with the Aussie dollar dropping, these are new factors that have evolved over the past week or so. At best, we see the prices remaining the same."

Sydney fuel prices averaged $1.01 a litre on Friday, and Mr Loades said the fuel price cycle, usually marked by substantial peaks and troughs in price, had stretched out to a record 71 days of stable pricing. "It is unprecedented and unknown what all that means for the future; nobody can predict what the next cycle will entail," he said.

Brisbane and Gold Coast prices were closing in on Sydney and Melbourne levels, RACQ spokeswoman Renee Smith said. "We warn motorists the cycle could end any time and when it ends, the price could rise by 15¢ a litre."

HEADLINE: Hartzer comes out of the shadows to prove his mettle
INTRO: The tailwinds helping Westpac are easing, leaving a tough task for a new boss.
TEXT:
The tailwinds helping Westpac are easing, leaving a tough task for a new boss.

When Gail Kelly called up Brian Hartzer to offer him a job in 2011, he was in the middle of a sweeping overhaul of the Royal Bank of Scotland, Britain's second-biggest bank.

After RBS nearly folded in the global financial crisis, Hartzer "rebuilt nearly everything about the place" while he ran its vast retail network between 2009 and 2012, he once said.

The surgery involved deep cost cuts, including culling thousands of jobs and a dramatic streamlining of its product range – and it led to a sharp rebound in profitability in the division.

Former RBS chief executive Stephen Hester says it was a job in which Hartzer showed his abilities as a retail banker, but also brought a tough edge.

"Although I think he has an extremely good way around people and was very widely liked and respected, he also brings a tough edge and was very clear about the costs that needed to be taken out of the network, and set about doing that," Hester told AFR Weekend.

Now, the 47-year-old, United ­States-born Hartzer is poised to take over running Westpac, where he will start as chief executive on Monday after running its largest division for the last 2½ years. Like RBS, Westpac is the ­second-biggest bank in its country and has an enormous retail network. But it is there the similarities end between the banking giants.

Hartzer inherits the job of running a bank that has earned a reputation as a reliable source of shareholder returns and his task is more to optimise its ­performance, rather than rebuild from scratch.Bumper run

That he would succeed Kelly was widely anticipated and executives who have worked with him view it is a natural progression, citing Hartzer's track record at ANZ and RBS.

Nevertheless, analysts say he will need to outline a clear plan ­for maintaining the bank's ­performance in a slower economic environment, which will involve some tough calls.

Westpac had a bumper run under Kelly. Share price gains and dividends delivered investors returns of about 10 per cent a year during her seven years at the helm.

But the softer economic ­environment facing Hartzer could make it harder for the country's oldest bank to continue churning out such healthy returns.

CLSA analyst Brian Johnson said Kelly was able to deliver above-peer ­dividend growth during her leadership, but it was assisted by a series of one-off factors. These include deferred tax assets from the merger with St George, optimising the capital models and write-back gains from the institutional bank. "What were basically tailwinds for Kelly intuitively could become ­headwinds for Hartzer," he said.

Against this backdrop, Hartzer has pledged to make no major shifts in strategy, but has emphasised two closely-related priorities: a relentless focus on customers, and digital technology.

The two goals go hand in hand and have been recurring themes in his banking career, which began at ANZ in 1999, having arrived in Australia in 1994 after starting professional life as a ­business consultant in New York.Winning customers

Jenny Fagg, a former senior ANZ executive who had Hartzer as a ­manager in the 2000s, said his focus on customer service was a "mantra".

"It was all about how do we ­differentiate ourselves in the eyes of the ­customer and how do we give the best service and products in the way that the customer will value," she says.

"People sometimes say that. It can be said without a lot of follow through but it was absolutely the clear focus," says Fagg, now an executive in Toronto at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.

The approach – also emphasised by ANZ chief John Macfarlane – paid off for the bank. During Hartzer's time at ANZ between 2004 and 2008, ANZ's ­customer satisfaction rating rose from the high 60s to the high 70s, according to Roy Morgan.

Winning the hearts of retail ­customers will be a key battleground for Westpac today, after it briefly ­overtook Commonwealth Bank as the highest-rated big bank in the eyes of customers last year, a title CBA has since regained.

Increasingly, this battle for ­customers is fought in the digital world and it is here where analysts believe Hartzer, a former teacher of computer coding, faces his biggest challenges.

Macquarie analyst Mike Wiblin ­estimates Westpac needs to ­spend ­$3.7 billion upgrading its IT systems to catch up with its closest rival, the ­Commonwealth Bank, for instance.

There is a view the need to invest more in IT will inevitably require less spending elsewhere. Fagg says, under Hartzer, ANZ put a heavy emphasis on innovative payments technology, and this required saying no to other projects.

"That sort of focus and being ­tenacious actually means that you have to say no to things," she says.Backers

Former colleagues at ANZ also describe Hartzer as an engaging ­manager, but by no means a soft target. With his background in consulting, he was seen as a slick marketer able to ­capitalise on complex changes the bank had made to its back-office ­systems by lifting its reputation with customers.

However, it was not always smooth sailing. Hartzer's position as ANZ's credit card boss in the early 2000s came at a time when credit card profits were being crunched by an ­overhaul of ­interchange fee ­regulations, and ANZ's credit card arm was dogged by ­operational problems.

Hartzer was behind some ­unpopular moves, such as decision to cap how many frequent flyer points credit card users could rack up, at a time when ANZ was the biggest card issuer in the country.

But his handling of these challenges earned him plaudits among the top rungs of management, and he was­ ­catapulted to be Australian head of ­personal banking at the age of 37, and seen as a serious successor to ­McFarlane as chief executive.

McFarlane was a key backer of Hartzer at ANZ says he has been ready to step up to being CEO for some time.

"He is incredibly smart, with a strong leadership bias, gets results, and is a natural with people.
