He honed his marketing skills as a consultant in banking at First Manhattan in New York before joining ANZ and is well suited to a ­business in need of growth and expansion," McFarlane told AFR Weekend.

The former ANZ boss and next chair of Barclays is close to Hartzer – he reportedly sang The House of the ­Rising Sun by The Animals at Hartzer's ­wedding in England.

However, despite the big wraps on Hartzer, he was overlooked for the top job at ANZ, which went to Mike Smith, and soon after Hartzer left Australia to run RBS's retail network.

It was a job that involved deep cost cuts to a bank that had just received a taxpayer bailout, as well as the ­structural changes sweeping through the industry as finance becomes increasingly digital.

Hester, the chief executive who hired Hartzer at RBS, describes him as an executive who was "thoughtful and strategic" in his approach and able to make tough decisions. He also says Hartzer took a broader view beyond the narrow confines of the business he was running.

"In addition to running his part of the bank, he always spent time thinking about and talking about what was going on in other banking markets and in other parts of the bank and thinking about the broader strategic issues," Hester says.Technology looms

Hartzer announced he would leave RBS to return to Australia in 2011 for "family reasons" – his marriage had broken down and his former wife and four children were in Australia. He has since married again and his current wife, Georgy, has two children to whom Hartzer is a stepfather.

Since he was recruited to Westpac in 2012 to run its largest division, ­including its retail and business bank, St George and BT, with an $8.6 million sign-on bonus, he has been seen as a CEO in waiting.

Now that he is finally taking the reins from Kelly, the question is how he will change a bank that prides itself on ­taking a conservative approach.

Assembling a senior management line-up is normally one of the first items on a new CEO's agenda and the market expects a reshuffle, with the likely departure of highly-regarded ­institutional boss Rob Whitfield, the board's second choice for CEO.

Hartzer is also expected to overhaul the bank's structure so his previous position is redundant and the key ­executives, including retail head Jason Yetton, St George boss George Frazis, and BT boss Brad Cooper report directly to him.

Technology also looms large, as the market believes Westpac has spent ­significantly less than CBA on ­upgrading its IT systems and it will need to catch up if his main focus is on ­digital banking.

As with any CEO change at a ­company the size of Westpac, there will surely be other suggestions for what he needs to do to its performance. Just how Hartzer responds to these tasks remains to be seen. But after spending more than two years being viewed as Kelly's successor, it is fair to assume he has a plan in mind.

HEADLINE: Shell dumps $20b Arrow LNG project
INTRO: Royal Dutch Shell has officially scrapped plans for a new $US20 billion-plus liquefied natural gas project in Queensland in the latest fallout from the oil price slump, with the gas set to feed rival export plants instead.
TEXT:
Royal Dutch Shell has officially scrapped plans for a new $US20 billion-plus liquefied natural gas project in Queensland in the latest fallout from the oil price slump, with the gas set to feed rival export plants instead.

Global chief executive Ben van ­Beurden said the proposed greenfield Arrow LNG project with PetroChina was "off the table", while other ventures would be slowed as priority was given instead to Shell's North American LNG projects.

The comments came as US majors ConocoPhillips and ­Occidental ­Petroleum also cut back spending budgets to help preserve ­dividend ­payouts to shareholders.

Chevron was expected to follow a similar line in its fourth-quarter update late on Friday, while several local ­companies have advised of capex cuts over the past few days, including Oil Search and Beach Energy. Crude oil prices are trading near their lowest since March 2009, with Brent crude, the global standard, near $US49 a barrel on Friday. Brent was trading at $US115 a barrel as recently as June.

The Arrow greenfield project is ­formally "cancelled", Shell said at its fourth-quarter results in London, which cited several ventures that were being deferred or abandoned in the wake of the collapse in oil prices.

However, work is still going ahead on the development of the Arrow coal seam gas reserves, which would just not be commercialised through a ­separate LNG project.

"Work continues on development of Arrow's substantial gas resources in the Bowen and Surat Basins," Shell ­Australia spokesman Paul Zennaro said. "Shell continues to be driven by value and finding the best development option for Arrow gas. ­Discussions are ongoing on ­collaboration opportunities."

Prospects for a stand-alone LNG project by Arrow were already seen as near-zero due to the escalation in project construction costs. But until now, it had formally remained an option for Shell. Many in the market already regarded it as more likely that Arrow gas would find its way into one or more of the three LNG projects already under construction or ­operating in Queensland.

BG Group's $US20.4 billion Queensland Curtis LNG project, which started exports earlier this month, is short of gas feedstock, as is Santos' $US18.5 billion GLNG project. Arrow gas could potentially also supply Origin Energy's $24.7 billion Australia Pacific LNG project and underpin an expansion.Priorities

Mr van Beurden told investors in London that other international gas projects were also being slowed, casting doubt on Shell's eagerness to pursue the Browse floating LNG project in ­Western Australia, which has already been delayed by six months.

Shell on Thursday announced a three-year, $US15 billion ($19 billion) cut in spending as a result of the ­collapse in prices. But Shell still lists Browse among the final ­investment decision "choices" for 2015-16, meaning Woodside's target of starting engineering design work in mid-2015 could still be met. Shell still has several major investments under way in Australia.

These include the $US54 billion ­Gorgon LNG venture in WA, in which it has a 25 per cent stake and is due to begin ­production later this year, and its Prelude floating LNG venture in the Browse Basin, due to begin ­production in 2016-17.Woodside Petroleum stake divestment

Key points Arrow LNG project scrapped as Royal Dutch Shell looks to North American projects, but coal-seam gas drilling continues. Several ventures deferred or abandoned in the wake of the collapse of oil prices.

HEADLINE: Rate cut would boost housing investor activity
INTRO: A Reserve Bank of Australia decision on Tuesday to cut the cash rate would boost housing. It always does, one way or another, as the RBA well knows.
TEXT:
A Reserve Bank of Australia decision on Tuesday to cut the cash rate would boost housing. It always does, one way or another, as the RBA well knows.

The big danger would be the re-ignition of investment demand, particularly in Sydney. But a cut could also boost housing activity outside Sydney and Melbourne, in cities and regions where price growth has so far been sluggish.

The general view is that house price growth is slowing due to both declining affordability and the weakening economy and labour markets.

In that view, a cut to the cash rate would simply delay the slow down.

But January was a suprisingly strong month, according to CoreLogic RP Data's research director, Tim Lawless. The CoreLogic RP Data Home Value Index, to be released on Monday, will show national house price growth in excess of 1 per cent for the month.

Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have had record January price growth so far, CoreLogic reports, while values have fallen in Adelaide and Perth.

Century 21 Australasia real estate franchise chain owner Charles Tarbey hopes the Reserve Bank does not cut the cash rate. "In Sydney it would definitely create more interest in the investor market; that would be an issue."

Westpac senior economist Matthew Hassan, said housing was famously sensitive to interest rate moves, with Sydney the most sensitive because it is the most leveraged.

"A rate cut does alter the proposition for investors; housing becomes slightly more attractive for investors not seeking capital gains, but security of income," he said.

The Australian Prudential and Regulation Authority has warned of macroprudential restrictions should investor lending rise by more than 10 per cent a year – a figure that was marginally exceeded in 2014.

LJ Hooker National Research Manager, Mathew Tiller said a cut to mortgage rates would have a positive effect on major property markets around the country and especially those that are attractive to investors and first home buyers.

"A fall in interest rates would see investor activity grow as the potential total return (capital growth and income return) from property would be higher than other interest rate-reliant investment assets," he said.

Not everyone thinks a small cut on Tuesday would change the long-term picture. ANZ senior economist David Cannington expects two rate cuts this year. But he still expects house prices to rise more slowly than in 2013 or 2014. In Sydney the rise will be about 8 per cent, in Melbourne, about 6 per cent and near 4 per cent in Brisbane.

"We have seen some slowing in housing. due to sluggish income growth, the soft labour market and more difficult affordability," he said.

HEADLINE: Decision time for the RBA
INTRO: To ease or not to ease, that is the question . . . in times of outrageous misfortune.
TEXT:
To ease or not to ease, that is the question . . . in times of outrageous misfortune.

After 18 months of what gradually became almost boring predictability, the Reserve Bank of Australia on ­Tuesday will make arguably its most dramatic policy decision since the aftermath of the global financial crisis.

Faced with low inflation, sluggish growth and global uncertainty, the RBA has scope and reason for its first cut in the 2.5 per cent cash rate since 2013.

If the bank doesn't cut on Tuesday, some pundits argue, it will prepare the market for a March reduction with a marked shift in post-meeting language away from a neutral stance promising a "period of stability" in interest rates.

At the very least, say the most bullish economists, interest rates will remain on hold, but the language will change to reflect the slightly gloomier economic outlook for this year, the heightened risk of global financial turbulence, and continued softness in commodities.

"We expect the RBA Board to leave the cash rate at 2.5 per cent next week but change the guidance by dropping 'period of stability' and inserting either 'appropriate for the time being' or 'scope for easing'," said ANZ Friday.

Bank of America Merrill Lynch's chief economist Saul Eslake agrees.

"Even if the RBA doesn't cut, which is my position, I think they will change the language in their statement much more than they have in previous meetings where they've decided not to cut," he said. "Simply cutting and pasting from last month's statement probably is not going to satisfy markets who want to understand what the RBA's monetary policy is."

Amid all the speculation, at least one RBA-watcher is clear on the bank's direction: Herald Sun commentator Terry McCrann blind-sided the market and economists late on Wednesday night with a column declaring a 25 basis point cut virtually a done deal.

He later qualified himself to say the Reserve Bank's staff would recommend a cut to the central bank's board.

Market odds on a cut, which had just dropped to 7 per cent after stronger-than-expected core inflation data, ­rocketed to just below 70 per cent, while the dollar, freshly-fortified on the ­consumer price surprise, went into free-fall. A few economists felt obliged to alter their predictions at once.

"The strong signalling of an ­imminent cut has seen us reluctantly shift to factoring in two 25bp rate cuts in February and May and then no change until a couple of modest hikes in the ­second half of 2016," wrote Barclays economist Kieran Davies.

On Friday, JP Morgan's economist for Australia Stephen Walters joined the new doves, switching his call from an"on-hold" to a pair of cuts, in May and June.

Mr Eslake, however, remains unswayed. He typifies economists who see a surprising drop in the December unemployment rate and signs of a pick-up in non-mining activities such as house construction, financial services and tourism as proof that the falling dollar and lower oil prices are already doing the job of monetary easing.

Nor does he subscribe to the re-emerging "currency war" scenario, by which the RBA will be forced to cut the rate because monetary easing around the world – include unconventional ­quantitative easing in Europe – will drive the dollar back up to ­uncompetitive levels.

State Street Global Advisors' head of investment for Asia Pacific, Kevin Anderson, is another who says talk of such a race to the bottom is premature.

"I think it would be too early yet to say we are in currency wars," he said. "I think what we're seeing at the moment is domestic or national central banks reacting to a number of factors, some of which have surprised them – for example, the effect of the oil price on some are making them adjust their policies.

In the case of energy exporter ­Canada, the central bank recently cut its benchmark lending rate from 1 per cent to 0.75 per cent as a pre-emptive strike against continuing revenue weakness.

Australia, as a net energy importer, needs no such stimulus, argues Mr Anderson.

"Australia's got that two-speed ­economy, and [interest rate] cuts are somewhat blunt tools," he said.

HEADLINE: High-end childcare not spitting the dummy over changes
INTRO: Shopping mall giant Westfield might be an odd inspiration for a childcare business, but Only About Children founder Brendan McAssey admits he came to the early education industry first as a businessman.
TEXT:
Shopping mall giant Westfield might be an odd inspiration for a childcare business, but Only About Children founder Brendan McAssey admits he came to the early education industry first as a businessman.

The former investment banker has created a completely new segment in the $9 billion childcare sector by imi­tating Westfield's strategy of favouring the higher end of the retail market, a preference for prime locations and its build it up, sell it on, lease it back model.

McAssey's 28-centre network – ­peppered throughout ­high-income suburbs such as Sydney's Neutral Bay and Melbourne's Armadale, and growing rapidly – offers premium childcare and is not afraid to charge for it.

Parents want the best for their children and if they can, are prepared to pay. In this vein the rise of a premium operator should be no surprise. But OAC's success is also down to the dire shortage of care. For women who want to return to work after childbirth, ­paying a high price is either what's required to advance their career, or needed to keep their family afloat.

For rates of up to $170 a day, parents can head off to work, calm in the know­ledge that little Johnny and Lulu are indulging in food prepared under the supervision of a nutritionist, have sight and hearing monitored with regular checkups, keep active with Zumba classes and are learning a second language. They can even check in on the kids throughout the day via a smartphone app developed by the company.

In contrast, rates at the country's ­largest operator Goodstart Early ­Learning, a non-profit, range from $63 a day in the country to $140 a day in Sydney's Bondi Junction.

But McAssey, a 53-year-old father of two, is unapologetic. Innovation in childcare will only occur "at the ­premium end of the market," he says.

"We have the capital to experiment and try new things."Expansion approach explains capital

That capital comes from McAssey's approach to expansion. The 20-year Morgan Stanley veteran – who first ­dabbled in the sector in 2002 and made a motza from selling centres to Eddy Groves' failed ABC Learning – is picky about the right locations for his centres. They have to be in areas where ­childcare demand exceeds ­supply, and incomes are high.

OAC buys sites, designs and develops the centre, then sells it onto a property trust, from which the company leases it back. "I've sold over $80 million-worth of property," he says.

"We will continue to recycle capital in that sense. We are in areas that can afford higher fees, so we can therefore afford to pay higher rent. The [rental] yield on our properties . . . makes them an at­tractive investment proposition."

The strategy is in contrast to listed childcare plays G8 Education and Affinity Education, which acquire existing centres, but McAssey says his approach is generally cheaper.

Shares in G8, the sector's largest ­private operator, have increased 29 per cent in the past year raising the ­company's market value to $1.5 billion.

The $220 million Affinity had a ­volatile start to listed life, but is now worth 42 per cent more than its ­Dec­ember 2013 listing value.

Investors have an appetite for childcare but McAssey says he has no plans to float OAC, which will have revenue of $90 million this financial year. One ­reason is that childcare operators have to make "uneconomic" decisions from time to time, he says. "Investments in things such as sight, speech and hearing – which are clearly uneconomic in the early days – are things I can afford to do . . . because I don't have to report quarterly to my shareholders."

McAssey entered the childcare ­sector with the hard-nosed intuition of a banker, but claims he has softened since he had children: Gabriella, 7, and Stirling, who is 3 years old. Gabriella was the catalyst for implementing hearing check-ups at OAC centres after her parents missed a problem four years ago. "I thought: 'if I missed it, and I'm in childcare, how many other children are we looking after that have some sort of developmental problem?'," he says.Coalition family policy expected

However McAssey may have to sharpen his business edge in response to the Coalition's family policy, expected to be announced by new Social Services Minister Scott Morrison next week. A recommendation from the Productivity Commission to means-test the 50 per cent rebate on childcare, which is capped at $7500 a year, will definitely hit OAC's high-earning families if it is taken up. McAssey says this is not fair, because it does not take into account the higher cost of living for families in richer suburbs.

"[Means-testing] would no doubt impact on my families materially."

He is out on his own on this front, with the policy finding support from G8 and Goodstart Learning. Childcare ­subsidies cost the government $5 billion a year and there is pressure to ensure funding is enhancing supply.

In a submission, Goodstart proposed dropping the level of the rebate for very high income families. "It would help fund increased assistance for low to middle families, and they're the ones where you're going to get the biggest workforce benefit," Goodstart advocacy manager John Cherry says.

G8 chair Jenny Hutson says means-testing the rebate would not affect too many of the company's families, and believes a separate recommendation to bring together the childcare benefit and rebate under one payment "has administrative appeal for everybody".

"If [the means-testing] is what we saw in the draft Productivity Commission report, that looks ­balanced," she says.

McAssey might be fighting a losing battle against means-testing of the rebate, but it is talk of government ­subsidies of nannies he is most worried about. "What I see is a drain of staff out of the childcare space into the nanny industry," he says. Taking workers out of the industry would have a dramatic effect on the cost of labour, he argues.Labour costs not surprising

At OAC, labour already accounts for 75 per cent of the cost base, which is not surprising given the employment of nutritionists, fitness experts and healthcare professionals.

In contrast to G8, which has an ­occupancy rate of about 84 per cent, OAC centres are completely full. This leads to incredibly long waiting lists, but also gives the company capacity to offer its extra services, McAssey argues.

But it also puts the company at risk of falling profits should a policy change push families to rethink their expensive care, or increase OAC's labour costs.

McAssey is not perturbed. He plans to open 15 sites in the next year, many of which will be in Melbourne.

He admits that some families are just copping the high rates because it's the only option in their suburb, but says parents are also discerning.

"If I'm full and I think that it's only about the location of the centre, then why would I provide all the extra ­services that I do?" he says. "I know that my parents demand high quality care and they're prepared to pay for it."

HEADLINE: Nicholls shaping as LNP successor
INTRO: Queensland Treasurer Tim Nicholls is the likely replacement for Campbell Newman if the Premier loses his seat in Saturday's election.
TEXT:
Queensland Treasurer Tim Nicholls is the likely replacement for Campbell Newman if the Premier loses his seat in Saturday's election.

With the odds shortening for Labor's Kate Jones to reclaim the inner-Brisbane seat of Ashgrove off Mr Newman, the Liberal National Party has no choice but to begin considering the plan B scenario of finding a new Premier to lead the second-term government.

The senior LNP leadership team of Mr Nicholls and Deputy Premier Jeff Seeney have refused to contemplate the possibility of Mr Newman losing his own seat, which he holds on a margin of 5.7 per cent.

They have rolled out the well-worn line of "you can't win government, without winning Ashgrove", despite only a 5.7 per cent swing needed to lose the seat. But Mr Nicholls and Mr Seeney are shaping up as the most likely successors, along with Health Minister Lawrence Springborg, one of the strongest performers in the LNP government over the past three years in a tough portfolio. Mr Springborg's history as opposition leader, who lost three consecutive elections in 2004, 2007 and 2009, will count against him. Interestingly, Mr Springborg has rated highly in opinion polls in Brisbane seats, including Ashgrove, as an alternative to Mr Newman, despite hailing from a regional seat.

Education Minister and former LNP leader John-Paul Langbroek is also being touted as a contender.

Despite international precedents showing Mr Newman could remain Premier for a few months without holding a seat in state Parliament until a safe seat is found, this option is highly unlikely. "The electorate won't accept that," an LNP insider said.

There are many LNP supporters who believe Mr Newman is the main cause of the LNP government's popularity and would welcome a chance for a new start.

If Mr Newman is defeated, it could re-open old wounds between former Liberals and Nationals in the LNP that were largely resolved when the parties were merged in 2008.

Mr Nicholls' carriage of the $37 billion privatisation program and his relatively high profile would make him the obvious choice to take over.

But LNP insiders are confident they can hold Ashgrove despite betting agencies putting a victory for Ms Jones at $1.30, while Mr Newman has slipped away to $3.30.

The LNP is confident voters in Ashgrove will swing behind Mr Newman in the same way they did in 2012 when he launched a bid for the state's top job from outside state Parliament.

Regardless, they deny there is a specific plan to action if Mr Newman loses on Saturday. "There is no plan B," an insider told AFR Weekend.

Primary vote preferences from the Greens and other minor parties are expected to flow to Ms Jones. In the 2012 election, Mr Newman won 51.81 per cent of the primary vote, with Ms Jones on 36.6 per cent.

If the LNP is returned for a second term in office but Mr Newman loses his seat – or even if it's too close to call - it will make an interesting victory speech at the LNP election function on Saturday night.

HEADLINE: Newman battles to save his own seat
INTRO: Labor's vague plan for Queensland has been the weak spot for the Opposition Leader.
TEXT:
Labor's vague plan for Queensland has been the weak spot for the Opposition Leader.

Queensland Premier Campbell Newman launched a last minute assault on Labor's economic credentials ahead of Saturday's election but refused to ­discuss who will lead the LNP government if he loses his own seat.

With opinion polls showing a likely victory for the LNP across the state but not in Mr Newman's seat, he used his last campaign appearance to defend his government's agenda including a $37 billion privatisation plan and public service overhaul.

For the first time in the campaign, Mr Newman directly addressed ­criticisms about his abrasive leadership style which is expected to contribute to a loss of up to 25 to 30 seats.

"When you undertake reform it's often contentious," he told a leaders' debate in Brisbane. "Yes, I occasionally get fired up but that's because I'm working my guts out for this state."

Mr Newman criticised Labor's plans to sell assets to repair the state budget and pay down $80 billion in state debt and build much-needed infrastructure.

"We can fund the future. In contrast, we can see chaos and job destruction from Labor because they don't have a plan and they can't fund it," he said.

Labor's vague plan for Queensland has been the weak spot for Opposition Leader Annastacia Palaszczuk who made an embarrassing gaffe on ­Thursday when she could not name the rate of the goods and services tax.

Ms Palaszczuk, who is hoping a ­protest vote against the Newman ­government will return Labor to office, stuck to Labor's key message about not selling assets and defended her modest election promises worth $1.6 billion.

She targeted Mr Newman's record in government where he cut 14,000 public service jobs and picked fights with key constituents including the legal ­community and doctors.

"When Mr Newman talks about the future, remember the past," she said. "Queenslanders have to think – do you want three more years of this? I want to work with Queenslanders, not divide them. We are going to be a party of job creation. There is a better way for Queensland."

During the debate, Mr Newman returned to his controversial claims motorcycle gangs were backing Labor because of the LNP's tough bikie laws.

Ms Palaszcsuk rejected the claims as "rubbish" amid jeers from the crowd.

With the LNP's privatisation plan the main difference between the ­parties, Mr Newman reaffirmed his view the port and electricity assets would return to government ownership at the end of the 50 or 99 year leases. He said the state government would not pay companies that lease long-term assets, even if they make ­billions of dollars in capital injections.

"They will be coming back [into ­public ownership]," he said. "People won't be buying their assets back because we are not selling them in the first place. We are leasing them."

He was less forthcoming on his ­political future if he loses Ashgrove. "My firm belief is Ashgrove will go with government. I'm absolutely convinced of that," he said. "The battle in my ­electorate is the same as across the state." Labor needs a swing of 12 per cent to win government and ­Mr Newman only needs a swing of 5.7 per cent to lose Ashgrove.

The LNP has promised $18 million for the inner-Brisbane seat to try and shore up support for the premier but it may not be enough to hold the seat.

The LNP holds 73 out of 89 seats in the unicameral parliament, while Labor holds nine seats.

Prime Minister Tony Abbott, who was in western Victoria on Friday, has steered clear of the campaign, but ­federal Treasurer Joe Hockey on Friday urged voters to stick with the ­LNP government.

He said he expected Saturday's ­election would result in a ­"natural ­re-balancing" of the Queensland ­parliament, but he said the ­Newman government had been a good government.

"Do not walk away from the only political party, the LNP, that ­actually has a plan for the future of Queensland that is actually going to ­create jobs," he said.

HEADLINE: Murdoch frank and unfiltered
INTRO: Half a million fans are following the News Corp chief's daily doings.
TEXT:
Half a million fans are following the News Corp chief's daily doings.

Cuddles with baby farm animals, hijinks with life-size robots, sightseeing in Bejiing, cooking omelettes on his Aga: there's more to media mogul Rupert Murdoch's social media exploits than just fiery political tweets.

Six weeks away from his 84th birthday, this media mogul has taken to the democratic world of social media like a native and doesn't rely on his media outlets to make his views heard.

While Mr Murdoch's candid tweets to his 558,000 followers over the past three years have attracted the most ­controversy, it is his online diary "Murdoch Here" that reveals a more human and kooky side of the News Corp ­executive chairman.

The diary is collated by chief of staff Natalie Ravitz on the multimedia blogging platform Tumblr.

"This is what not catching any ­Yabbies looks like, #happy," reads a caption of a smiling Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch in casual bushwalking gear at the Murdoch property outside Yass, 10 days before Christmas.

Murdoch has one of the highest ­profiles of the relatively few household business names that have taken to social media in such a personal and unfiltered way.

Instead of portraying a shadowy puppet master controlling his media empire to manipulate the outcome of world events, "Murdoch Here" shows the multibillionaire pursuing his passions: technology, winemaking, ­travelling and wearing loud socks.

Social media experts say "Murdoch Here" and Murdoch's controversial political tweets are rare examples of a business leader engaging genuinely and honestly with his customers.

"Watch out Gordon Ramsay . . . Rupert Murdoch is coming for you," says a blog entry about Murdoch ­making bacon and eggs.

In September, as he visited his ­London-based tabloid The Sun, Murdoch posed – grinning and eyes closed – with editor David Dinsmore in the paper's photo booth, producing a mock front page that screamed "Freddie Starr Ate My Hamster".

A few weeks later, there were pictures of Murdoch enlisting his chief technology officer Paul Cheesbrough to try out his new drone at Laguna Beach, to the alarm of local seagulls.

Emma Lo Russo, chief executive of social media analytics company Digivizer, says Murdoch's passionate tweeting is ultimately good for the ­Murdoch brand.

"He shows it's not all about the business, it's not just about numbers, because he cares about issues and I think there's something great about that," Lo Russo says.

Murdoch, like many others ­grappling with the 140-character ­Twitter artform, still struggles to be ­understood.

After the Charlie Hebdo attacks, he was forced to backtrack on a tweet that said: "Maybe most Moslems peaceful, but until they recognise and destroy their growing jihadist cancer they must be held responsible."

Hours after the tragic end to the Sydney seige, Murdoch tweeted his ­congratulations to the Daily Telegraph for its coverage, praise criticised as insensitive. He also made himself the target of internet critics this week when he said Prime Minister Tony Abbott's chief of staff Peta Credlin should do her patriotic duty and resign. "@rupertmurdoch keep your Yankee arse out of our affairs!" said someone called @RedJules4. And then there was the mystery "Po" tweet of January 26, retweeted 1356 times without anyone the wiser as to its meaning.Other high-profile tweeters

Murdoch is not the only mogul active on social media, lifting the veil on their movements, meetings and thoughts.

CNN founder Ted Turner, with only 2362 followers, joined Twitter seven months ago and has confined his tweeting to environmental messages and restaurant openings, but has promised to tweet "until the world ends".

Oprah Winfrey, with 26.5 million followers, is a regular tweeter with more than 10,000 tweets since January 2009. Like her media empire, Winfrey's tweets are full of uplifting messages and plugs for Oprah-related products.

Only Donald Trump, who has been tweeting since 2009 and has 2.7 million followers, beats Murdoch for online ­followers and controversy.

In January, Trump suggested if Charlie Hedbo journalists had guns, "they would have had a fighting chance".

Lo Russo says that in the United States it is much more common for ­senior ­executives to use social media to talk outside their usual business ­interest.

As many as 75 per cent of "C levels" – that is chief ­executive, chief financial officer, chief information officer – are active on social media.

HEADLINE: National briefs
INTRO: ASX addresses risk
TEXT:
ASX addresses risk

The Australian Securities Exchange said companies need to consider market perceptions that insider trading could occur as much as actual breaches when granting executives and directors trading rights. The update of its trading guidance on Friday is widely seen as a direct response to trades by former David Jones directors in late 2013, three days before sales figures were released. The ASX said the changes were due to lessons from market developments since the last update in January 2012.

The document says trading policies need to minimise the risk of actual insider trading and avoid the appearance of insider trading and reputational damage. Shaun Drummond

BBY fined $180,000

Sydney-based stockbroker BBY was slapped with a fine and ordered by the Australian Securities Exchange to improve its risk-management systems. The ASX chief compliance officer said it would impose an $180,000 fine for three contraventions of ASX clear operating rules. They relate to events in 2014 and a margin call in Aquila Resources that BBY was unable to settle. In June, BBY was advised that to prevent it from committing an event of default and suffering a "possible insolvency event" ASX would delay the payment while imposing conditions on BBY. Joyce Moullakis

HEADLINE: Australia continues the hunt for MH370
INTRO: The Australian-led search for missing Malaysian Airlines plane MH370 will continue regardless of an official Malaysian declar­a­tion that all 239 people who were on it are presumed dead.
TEXT:
The Australian-led search for missing Malaysian Airlines plane MH370 will continue regardless of an official Malaysian declar­a­tion that all 239 people who were on it are presumed dead.

The Australian government has set aside $90 million in the federal budget for the search, which has so far failed to uncover any remains of the aircraft.

"There is no change to the search operations," said a spokesman for Infrastructure Minister Warren Truss.

"Australia, Malaysia and China remain committed to the search. We remain cautiously optimistic the aircraft will be found. The search for MH370 continues and there are now four ships participating in underwater search activities. About 18,000 square kilometres of the sea floor have been searched, which is about 30 per cent of the priority search area."

The search, which has been going since the flight disappeared from radar screens on March 8 last year, is focused on the southern Indian Ocean.

The Australian government estimates its sweep of the under­water search area where the aircraft is thought to be should be finished by May, discounting any delays.

On Thursday, Malaysia formally declared that the plane's disappearance was the result of an accident and that all on it should be presumed dead.

The declaration will trigger compensation payments of an undisclosed sum from Malaysian Airlines for the families of victims.

Six of those on the flight, which was travelling from Kuala Lumpur to ­Beijing when it disappeared, were ­Australian.

There were angry scenes in Beijing, as families of Chinese passengers ­protested outside the Malaysian embassy. Some relatives accuse the Malaysian government and its flag ­carrier of a chaotic and bungled response to the plane's initial diversion, which allowed the jet to disappear, and a subsequent cover-up.

Kuala Lumpur and Malaysia Airlines strenuously deny these charges.

Of those on the plane, 154 were Chinese nationals. The Malaysian government is due to release a report into the incident on March 7.

"We understand that the families of those on board MH370 are experiencing enormous grief, heightened by not knowing the circumstances under which the aircraft disappeared," a statement from the joint task force leading the search said on Friday.

"Providing support to those families, particularly at this difficult time, will continue to be a priority."

with AAP

HEADLINE: RBA faces hard decision on euro hoard
INTRO: While the Reserve Bank board faces a tough decision on Tuesday whether to cut the cash rate, the pointy heads at Martin Place will be mulling another dilemma - what to do with the $15 billion in euros it holds in foreign currency reserves.
TEXT:
While the Reserve Bank board faces a tough decision on Tuesday whether to cut the cash rate, the pointy heads at Martin Place will be mulling another dilemma - what to do with the $15 billion in euros it holds in foreign currency reserves.

With negative interest rates on euro denominated cash and bonds, central banks are losing money by holding the second most liquid currency in the world. And as it did when it halved its zero yielding gold assets in 1997 (attractive in these times) it may be time to trim down on loss making investments.

The RBA holds around $41.7 billion of foreign currency reserves of which 35 per cent are hold in euro denominated assets. Like most central banks, it takes an ultra cautious approach to its foreign currency holdings - which it keeps in shorter dated maturities and cash so as to not risk capital losses that may result from rising rates. But most euro denominated bonds that are safe enough to hold currently have negative yields out to five years. Worse yet, the major custodians such as BNY Mellon have introduced additional fees on euro cash deposits adding to the drag.

To avoid negative returns on European bonds, the RBA has actively engaged in the swaps market, switching its euro denominated debt into Yen allowing it to earn a slight positive return of about 0.20 percentage points versus a similarly negative amount. But as more large investors do the same - the gains are being eroded, making it even harder to avoid negative returns from holding euro denominated assets.

The challenges of low rates is afflicting many central banks of which most have turned to high yielding Australian government bonds to boost returns. The RBA said in its annual report that it was only able to earn a running yield of just 0.2 per cent on its $47 billion foreign currency portfolio, compared to about 4 per cent in 2007, before the financial crisis.

The world's central banks and governments hold a combined $US11.7 trillion ($15 trillion) of foreign currency reserves and as the US embarked on its program of quantitative easing which had the effect of devaluing the dollar, there was a major diversification shift into euros. But in more recent months as negative returns really started to bite and the prospect of European quantitative easing became more likely, central banks have dumped their euro holdings, driving the currency down.

Data from the International Monetary Fund, cited by MNI showed a decline in central bank holdings of €129 billion ($186 billion) in the third quarter of 2014. If central banks such as China that don't report numbers are included the sell down is around €200 billion.

Most recent data shows reserve managers still hold around 23 per cent in euros of the $11.7 trillion total, suggesting there's still plenty more to sell. And that's before European Central Bank president Mario Draghi has formally begun his €1.1 trillion quantitative easing program. With the prospect of even lower rates and a weaker yet euro there's a tidal wave of money fleeing Europe. Which brings us to the more immediate decision facing the RBA. Lower rates and a weaker currency may be the RBAs' only way of stemming the tide.

HEADLINE: CBA leads big week for banks
INTRO: Investors enjoyed another bumper week as the Australian sharemarket soared, underpinned by the big banks and Telstra amid growing expectations of an RBA rate cut as early as Tuesday.
TEXT:
Investors enjoyed another bumper week as the Australian sharemarket soared, underpinned by the big banks and Telstra amid growing expectations of an RBA rate cut as early as Tuesday.

The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 Index and the broader All Ordinaries Index each rose 1.6 per cent and 1.5 per cent to 5588.3 points and 5551.6 points respectively for the week. On Friday, both major indices rose 0.35 per cent, chalking up a seventh straight session of gains. In the month, the S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 3.3 per cent as the All Ordinaries went up 3 per cent.

The week's performance capped off a solid month for the sharemarket despite a short slump mid-month caused by falling commodity prices and global central banks' easing. The ASX 200 was at a four-and-a-half month high, beating the S&P 500 which was down 1.8 per cent for the month with one session to go, the Nikkei which only managed a rise of 1.7 per cent. The DAX however did well on the back of the European Central Bank's $1.2 trillion quantitative easing program, rising 9.5 per cent.

In the Australian market, the lure of more easing overseas and domestically buoyed investor mood, with banks the big winners.

"The key thing to note is the resilience of our market. There is volatility globally but our market has bucked the trend. While mining stocks have fallen, the falling dollar provided cushion and the banks held up the market even after US stocks fell," AMP Capital's portfolio manager, Nader Naeimi, said.

The further decline in materials and energy stocks in the month as commodity prices took another hit meant the stock market has become more heavily weighted towards financials.

Commonwealth Bank continued to power the market on Friday touching the $90 mark briefly, an all-time high. It rose 4.3 per cent in the month to $89.33. Westpac Banking Corp was up 3.9 per cent to $34.46, ANZ Banking Group rose 2.8 per cent to $33, and National Australia Bank jumped 6 per cent to $35.63.

"Relative to the rest of the stock market, the banks have never been this high in the history of the ASX200," Allan Gray's portfolio manager, Simon Mawhinney, said. "This type of thing cannot carry on indefinitely. If you fast forward the index, this is physically not possible. I hate to say the banks are overvalued but there is relatively more value elsewhere."

Economists urged investors to enjoy the spoils from the last two weeks ahead of the RBA meeting on February 3 which could set the market in an unexpected direction. Gold stocks were winners in the month of as investors flock to safe haven asset. The spot price of gold rose to $US1261.48 per ounce an ounce, up 6.5 per cent since the beginning of the month. Telstra leapt 8.9 per cent to reach a 13 ½ year at $6.50. Fortescue Metals Group dipped below $2 this month - the first time since 2009 - as iron ore price falls added concerns about the group's debt levels. It rebounded to close on Friday at $2.36 but still lost 13.9 per cent in the month. The spot price for iron ore, landed in China, was $US63.27 a tonne.

HEADLINE: $A slides again, pressure builds for rate cut
INTRO: The Aussie's lost about 18pc in six months.
TEXT:
The Aussie's lost about 18pc in six months.

The Australian dollar touched fresh 5½-year lows on Friday as solid US jobs data added further momentum to the long-running greenback rally and bets mounted on a local interest rate cut next Tuesday.

In late local trade, the Aussie was fetching US77.95¢, after having dropped to US77.22¢, its lowest point since mid-2009.

This compared with US78.74¢ at the same time on Thursday, and US80.06¢ at the end of last week.

The currency has now lost about 18 per cent in the past six months, its sharpest slide over that time frame since the global financial crisis.

In the three months from mid-July 2008, the Aussie plunged a massive 40 per cent as global credit and money markets seized up and governments and central banks sought to shore up failing lenders. During that upheaval, the local unit flirted with US60¢.

The Aussie broke down through US78¢ in international trade late on Thursday AEST, after a precipitous local decline driven partly by a newspaper report, which declared that a 25 basis point cut in the 2.5 per cent cash rate at next Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia monthly policy meeting was a done deal.

A sharper than expected decline in Australia's fourth-quarter terms of trade also prompted selling of the local unit, while a big drop in US initial jobless claims, to the lowest weekly level since 2000, added fuel to the US dollar's long-running rally.

"The Australian dollar's fall over the past 24 hours has been nothing short of stunning," National Australia Bank currency strategist Raiko Shareef said in a note on Friday morning. "Earlier [Friday] morning, it looked at risk of gaining a US69¢ handle," he said.

"The weight of expectation around next week's RBA meeting continues to mount, such that a nasty snapback beckons should the RBA fail to adjust its language towards an easing bias."

Whether or not the RBA eases next week, economists see the currency remaining below 80¢ for the rest of the year, as Australia's declining terms of trade continue to feed through, and demand for the currency for direct foreign investment - mainly into resources - falls away.

"What I think you can say with a very high degree of confidence is that the inflows into the mining sector are going to fall away to zero, because of what we know of the profile of the work still to be done on the LNG plants, which is all that's left of it," Bank of America Merrill Lynch chief economist Saul Eslake said.

"So, I think the currency is going to fall further - our official forecast for some time has been US77¢ at the end of this year and US73¢ at the end of next year."

The search for fixed income yield, further fuelled by quantitative easing in the European Union, will hold up some demand, although positioning ahead of an expected start to monetary tightening in the US will continue to draw investors into greenback assets. This divergence, marked by further monetary easing around the world, has made the US dollar a crowded trade, BK Asset Management's managing director for foreign exchange strategy said.

"If there is one take-away from the recent price action in the foreign exchange market, it should be that buying US dollars is still the best bet in the global currency war," she said.

"The Federal Reserve's short and sweet monetary policy statement on Wednesday contained no changes in forward guidance, leaving the Fed on track to raise interest rates in 2015.

"Meanwhile, the race to ease is heating up with the European Central Bank rolling out quantitative easing, the Monetary Authority of Singapore reducing the slope of its policy band and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand dropping its tightening bias.

"Next week, the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to fire the next shot by lowering interest rates for the first time since August 2013," she said.

HEADLINE: Timing is everything in $50b power play
INTRO: Plans to privatise billions of dollars worth of power assets are a key issue in Saturday's Queensland election. If Premier Campbell Newman clings on to power, the outcome will set the wheels in motion for what will be the world's largest auction of infrastructure assets.
TEXT:
Plans to privatise billions of dollars worth of power assets are a key issue in Saturday's Queensland election. If Premier Campbell Newman clings on to power, the outcome will set the wheels in motion for what will be the world's largest auction of infrastructure assets.

With NSW heading down the same road there will be more than $50 billion of electricity transmission and distribution assets up for sale over the next two years.

This puts Australia centre-stage for the hoards of pension and sovereign wealth funds globally seeking to mark their money into long-life assets which can guarantee returns for their members in 20 to 30 years time.

But getting the timing right will be a major challenge for the states and their advisers who have started mapping out a staged process which seeks to avoid congesting the market.

Newman is looking to sell around $30 billion of electricity assets, kicking off with the $8 billion sale of Powerlink this year if the election goes his way. NSW Premier Mike Baird, who is expected to retain power when the state goes to the polls on March 28, wants to lease 100 per cent of high voltage electricity transmission business Transgrid, and 50.4 per cent of Ausgrid and Endeavour Energy. UBS and Deutsche Bank are advising on that process.

While Queensland will have first-mover advantage, the NSW government is confident this will not dampen demand for its assets when they hit the market.

The Powerlink sale process is expected to be launched in February with final bids due by July. TransGrid will be first cab off the rank in NSW with final bids expected in the fourth quarter of this calendar year.

About three to four consortiums are expected to look at both assets. The sheer size of the multi-billion dollar assets means there is a finite number of bidders able to stump up the multi-billion dollar equity cheques needed at the same time.

International pension funds have increased their allocation to infrastructure assets since the global financial crisis. These bidders will range from Australian and Canadian super funds to Chinese state-owned enterprises and Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds.

A PricewaterhouseCoopers study out on Friday says the proposed leasing of the Queensland and NSW networks will be among the top-five largest transactions of their kind this year, easily eclipsing the value of the largest electricity deal globally in 2014 which was $US12.1 billion.

Exactly how much the bidders are willing to pay is less clear and the armies of investment bankers, lawyers and accountants are working on how to structure a deal to extract the most value for taxpayers.

The way that these assets are regulated has changed and bidders need certainty around how much of a return they can expect to get on their capital and the estimated cost of running the assets.

The Australian Energy Regulator (AER) issued a draft decision in late November that means NSW's four network power companies will have to cut prices by up to 36 per cent, dramatically cutting electricity bills. While this decision cuts the revenues the networks, which operate in a monopoly, can earn it also provides them with the regulatory certainty around the pricing they need to bid for the assets.

The AER's final decision on pricing for NSW is due on April 30. That decision can be appealed though, which means the outcome of what is known as a merits review might not be known until September. The NSW government is confident that this will not disrupt the sale process as it will still give the bidders clarity before the outcome of any final bids. Queensland distributors will have to wait longer for the outcome of the AER's determination with a draft decision due in April and a final decision due on October 31.

The philosophy behind the asset sales is that the NSW and Queensland networks are not efficient. Governments will argue the sale will generate cost savings which flow through to consumers. Critics such as unions and the NSW opposition warn it will drive up electricity prices and there will be job losses over time - something that will probably happen either way. The future will also have to be able to invest in innovation to stay ahead of disruptive technologies.

Future electricity demand will also determine which assets receive the most attention and both NSW and Queensland will argue their assets offer the most. The NSW government will pitch TransGrid, Ausgrid and Endeavour as the "marquee" transmission and distribution assets in the country. NSW's population is expected to increase by 2 million by 2031, requiring 1 million new homes.

Thinking like start-ups

Brian Hartzer offered some insight into how he might run Westpac seven months ago when he said banks had to think like start-ups to stay ahead of the technology race.

He said in a speech that Westpac was trying to "think and act like a 200-year old start-up company" to meet the changing demands of customers. Technology will be a major focus for Hartzer who steps up to the plate on Monday.

The bank's new chief is not expected to make any wild promises or make a major strategic announcement on day one. However, investing in digital technology and customer service will be key priorities.

As reported in The Australian Financial Review this week, Hartzer will announce an overhaul of the bank's management structure. The head of retail, St George, BT Financial and the bank's chief information officer will report directly to him.

Andrew Thorburn at National Australia Bank announced a reshuffle of his senior team on his first day last year which raised the bar for new chief executives wanting to be seen to be moving decisively and swiftly as they put their mark on the company.

Unlike Thorburn, Hartzer does not have a big mess to clean up but will be focusing on improving the bank's existing strengths in customer service and technology. His mantra will be customer satisfaction and emphasising the role of big banks to support the economy, business and consumers rather than being a target of public hostility. Outgoing chief Gail Kelly, meanwhile, will be heading off to Africa with her husband and children for a month of adventure and a well earned rest.

Timing is everything

Some badly-timed share trades by two former David Jones directors last year were the trigger for a review of the Australian Securities Exchange's guidelines on share trading.

The ASX did not name David Jones in the updated version of its listing rules guidance issued on Friday. But they have been designed to avoid a repeat of the events which led to Leigh Clapham and Steve Vamos buying stock in the retailer ahead of the release of sales data and a day after a merger proposal was received from Myer.

The ASX guidance notes have been tightened as a result. While there are existing rules designed to prevent insider trading, the ASX guidance focuses on ways to avoid the appearance or perception of insider trading and the reputational damage that can occur as a result.

This also applies to trading in derivatives, which also comes under the ASX's latest guidelines. About 300 of the 2200 listed entities on the ASX have derivatives.

The ASX says the market is "particularly sensitive" to directors and senior executives trading in the lead-up to financial reports or an announcement of market sensitive information, and good governance demands companies have a fit-for-purpose trading policy. Clapham, Vamos and former DJs chairman Peter Mason might still have their jobs if they heeded that advice.
