HEADLINE: Vision lost in folie de grandeur
INTRO: Tony Abbott's gaffe in knighting the Queen's husband strikes a bad note in Australia's efforts to balance relations with partners in Asia Pacific.
TEXT:
Tony Abbott's gaffe in knighting the Queen's husband strikes a bad note in Australia's efforts to balance relations with partners in Asia Pacific.

Back in 2006, Tony Abbott wrote a foreword to constitutional monarchist David Flint's Her Majesty at 80 in which he stated: "The monarchy is profoundly at odds with the spirit of this age (and gloriously impervious to the fads of all times)." A decade later you might regard this observation as even more of an understatement than it was then, and yet, provocatively, the Prime Minister of all Australians chooses to elevate Prince Philip to a knighthood in the Order of Australia on Australia Day of all days.

No rational explanation can be advanced for Abbott's folie de grandeur unless you believe the Prime Minister is unhinged, a situation not entirely without precedent in the recent past. Let's put aside the obvious criticisms of the inappropriateness of installing the Queen's consort in the pantheon of Australian honourees on Australia Day and focus instead on what this tells us about Abbott's vision for the country. And, for that matter, what does this extraordinary turn of events suggest to our neighbours about the sort of country we aspire to be - colonial relic or a modern, outward-looking Asia-Pacific entity with middle-ranking leadership aspirations.

What has resort to dishing out baubles to one of the least popular royals got to do with those reasonable objectives? The short answer is not much beyond a prime-ministerial obsession. One shudders to think what Abbott might have in mind for the Queen's Birthday honours to fill his self-proclaimed quota of four honourees for the year.

All those who have accepted his vice-regal blandishments - Governor-General Sir Peter Cosgrove, former governor-general Dame Quentin Bryce and former chief of the defence force Sir Angus Houston - have been demeaned.

Too late, Bryce has asked she not be referred to as Dame Quentin, or Houston as Sir Angus. Both could have declined, and others may well if they've got any sense.

Abbott's successors will not perpetuate the farce. But back to the more serious question of what all this tells us about the sort of Australia the Prime Minister wants to project in a bustling region that is creating its own realities separate from the past. When Abbott wrote in his book Battlelines - this was crafted well before he had any reasonable expectations of becoming Liberal leader, let alone prime minister, and he saw Australia as part of a like-minded Anglosphere - people indulged this whimsy. After all, the observation is historically accurate. By virtue of our birthright, language and alliances we are part of an English-speaking world, but the Anglosphere brand is misleading since it conveys an impression of exclusivity.

This is the very impulse we should avoid in our attempts to balance regional relationships with those of our traditional allies and newfound partners, and not more so than in this latest period when our positioning becomes more delicate between our cornerstone ally, the United States, and our economic sheet anchor, China. Abbott's Anglosphere - populated by knights and dames - sits uneasily with these aspirations. What makes all of this a bit disappointing is that the Prime Minister seemed to be asserting a reasonably steady hand in the foreign policy space, marred somewhat by an indifferent performance at the G20 in Brisbane where his domestically focused address to a leaders' retreat fell on stony ground.

The question now becomes after Abbott's detour into the world of Monty Python whether he is capable - in the face of ridicule from friends and foes alike - of reasserting his authority, not simply in the domestic sphere but more broadly. Tensions, now in the open, between Abbott and his deputy and foreign minister, Julie Bishop, will need to be cauterised if the government is to regroup. We can't have the sort of childish squabbling that accompanied Bishop's attendance late last year at a climate change conference in Lima, Peru. Abbott's insistence the deputy leader of the Liberal Party and one of its better performers be "chaperoned" by climate change sceptic, Trade Minister Andrew Robb was insulting to Bishop, and demeaning for the government generally; and, worse, reflected a schism between those (like Bishop) who believe anthropogenic climate change is a problem and those (like Abbott) whose scepticism verges on denial.

But back to Abbott's strange attachment to an Alice in Wonderland-world of knights and dames. Abbott falls back from to time in his justification for his monarchical preoccupations on Pascal's observation the heart has reasons that reason cannot know.

These metaphysical observations may be all very well in an intellectual discussion, but have not much to do with the world around us, or with practical day-to-day politics.

Tony Walker is The Australian Financial Review's international editor.

HEADLINE: Volatile politics a real threat to PM
INTRO: Has so much trouble ever come from something so trivial? While Tony Abbott's Australia Day pick of Prince Philip as a new antipodean knight was ridiculous, it was symbolic in the extreme. And so this indulgence crystallised the problems now undermining Mr Abbott's leadership and his government. Some of these are specifically of the Prime Minister's own making. Others stems from the broader trivialisation of politics into 24/7 infotainment. Together, they point to a bipartisan dysfunction of politics that bodes poorly for the challenges facing Australia.
TEXT:
Has so much trouble ever come from something so trivial? While Tony Abbott's Australia Day pick of Prince Philip as a new antipodean knight was ridiculous, it was symbolic in the extreme. And so this indulgence crystallised the problems now undermining Mr Abbott's leadership and his government. Some of these are specifically of the Prime Minister's own making. Others stems from the broader trivialisation of politics into 24/7 infotainment. Together, they point to a bipartisan dysfunction of politics that bodes poorly for the challenges facing Australia.

On Friday, The Australian Financial Review's chief political correspondent, Phillip Coorey, revealed senior figures in the government were discussing post-Abbott contingency plans, some of them focusing on deputy Liberal leader Julie Bishop and former leader Malcolm Turnbull. This is extraordinary, given the central lesson of the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd Labor governments was that dispensing with a popularly-elected prime minister is party political suicide. Surely what voters want now from government is stability. Yet, Mr Abbott's poll readings are so low the prospect of a one-term government no longer seems fanciful. Even the Prime Minister's staunchest supporters in the conservative commentariat have turned against him.

Again, this is extraordinary, given Mr Abbott's first year-and-a-half in government have not been marked by ministerial scandal or political crisis. There have been internal grumblings about the ultra-tight control of his chief of staff Peta Credlin. Mr Abbott has been slow to promote the younger talent on his backbench. The government has seriously misfired with its first budget. And, like the expensive paid parental leave entitlement scheme that undermined Joe Hockey's budget message, Mr Abbott has too often promised to consult with his colleagues only to seek forgiveness after the unfortunate event. Mostly what's missing is a clear, credible and consistent political narrative that explains why difficult decisions need to be made now to protect their children's prosperity. And it requires a sharpening of incentives to help restore productivity growth and help offset the loss of national income from our sharply falling iron ore and coal export prices. Yet, Mr Abbott's woes also conform to the new volatility of Australian politics: the internal assassination of Kevin Rudd, the minority Gillard government, the circus of the current Senate, the defeat of a one-term Coalition state government in Victoria and the prospect that one-term Premier Campbell Newman could lose his own seat in the Queensland election. At best, Mr Newman faces a large reversal of his 2012 landslide against a Labor opposition that proposes paying for its voter handouts by increasing the tax on jobs.

Governments have started poorly before. Bob Hawke's setbacks cost him seats in the 1984 election. John Howard's first term was marred by the departure of seven cabinet ministers over code of conduct issues. But Mr Hawke and Mr Howard were able to grow into the job. Mr Abbott could do the same under the old rules that governments elected with solid majorities could count on at least two terms. Amid today's volatile politics, Mr Abbott may have only six months to turn things around. Yet, this is also the six months where Mr Abbott needs to have a second go at getting a budget repair package through the Senate, to mount the case for tax and federal-state financial reform, and to prepare for a huge fight over workplace reform. The loss of political authority from his Australia Day "stuff up" will only embolden his opponents. The extra alarm, of course, comes from the fact that the party political alternative has refused to reform itself after being humiliated and discredited from its most recent term in office. Yet, this Labor alternative could be in government again too soon if Mr Abbott and the Coalition do not quickly rebuild their political stocks.

HEADLINE: Shortcuts in great rate guessing game
INTRO: Bartiromo said Bernanke was pointing out that the Fed might pause and start raising them again later.
TEXT:
Back in 2006, not long after he became chairman of the US Federal Reserve, Ben Bernanke got into trouble for leaking.

Well, maybe not leaking in the sense the word has been thrown around this week. For him it was a casual remark about interest rates that he made to Maria Bartiromo at a dinner on a Saturday night. For Maria, however, the CNBC financial journalist also known as "The Money Honey", it was definitely a leak and the scoop of a lifetime.

Perhaps, then, not all leaks are created equal, but the dinner was at the White House in Washington and it was the Correspondents Association annual shindig, so some banter was to be expected for sure.

It all got serious though on Monday afternoon when Bartiromo reported on air that she had bumped into Bernanke at the dinner and he said that Wall Street had misinterpreted his congressional testimony the week before.

After listening to the speech, investors and traders had all assumed the Fed had just one more rate hike left up its sleeve and then that would be it: game over when it came to interest rates for this cycle. On cue, assets were priced accordingly. But Bartiromo said Bernanke was pointing out that the Fed might pause and start raising them again later. Everything depended on the data, he said. (As it always does.)

Well, financial markets went into overdrive. Not used to hearing what the chairman thinks from a TV journalist, stocks got slammed at the very thought there might be more rate hikes, bond yields spiked to a four-year high, and the US dollar was pushed higher.

A month later Bernanke, at a Senate Banking Committee meeting, said it "was a lapse in judgment on my part," and "In the future, my communications with the public and with the markets will be entirely through regular and formal channels."

At the time it was thought Bernanke probably assumed the conversation was off the record.

But officials at the dinner said all conversations were on the record, unless the official made it clear they aren't.

These sorts of leaks, if they can be called that, don't happen very often. But they do happen. For instance, former Fed chairman Alan Greenspan also caused a kerfuffle soon after he too was in the top job for the first time. It was just before Black Monday on October 19, 1987, when he was interviewed on national television and suggested there wasn't much the Fed could do to stop inflation if consumers expected it. Greenspan never again granted a television interview while head of the Fed.

The topic of leaking was in the spotlight this week when News Corp's Terry McCrann wrote a column stating the Reserve Bank would cut the official cash rate when it meets next week. It came after the latest inflation report that wasn't as low as many expected, with most thinking a low number was needed to get another cut across the line at the RBA.

Just like economists, journalists can talk to the RBA to make sure they are on the right track with what they are writing. Nothing wrong with that. The real skill is asking the right questions to get the so-called right answers. When it comes to central banks there is plenty of reading of the tea leaves, perhaps too much, but with rates so low, forward guidance and statements have taken on a life of their own.

A leak, however, suggests the RBA has told someone what they are doing. That doesn't happen, although if it looks that way, so be it: it can definitely help someone's credibility when it comes to the great interest rate guessing game.

What can happen is a discussion regarding all the issues and getting a feel for what is really worrying them and what is needed for them to make a move on monetary policy. The outcome can also depend on whom inside the bank you are talking to. There's every chance of some disagreement among the senior staff who are allowed to talk. The same senior staff, however, eventually have to come together to agree on a formal policy recommendation on the Wednesday before the bank meets.

Attracting just as much chat on trading desks this week was why the RBA were talking at all in the media "black-out" the week before board meetings. The inflation data came out on Wednesday and the black-out would have been put in place the day before.

Talk of a rate cut next week has gained traction quickly, but there have been a few experts talking up the possibility of one well before this week's "leak".

Stephen Koukoulas of Market Economics has probably been the most vocal, but Westpac's Bill Evans and Macquarie Group's James McIntyre also share the same view.

If nothing else, all the talk about leaks and who will be right or wrong has definitely made next Tuesday's meeting a lot more interesting than it was looking just a few weeks ago.

HEADLINE: What should be done with all that oil?
INTRO: Over the past four weeks, US oil imports have averaged 7.2 million barrels a day. That means imports have fallen just 1 per cent from where they were a year ago, even though domestic oil production is up 1.1 million barrels a day over the same period and US oil refineries are drawing the same levels of product currently as they did last year.
TEXT:
Over the past four weeks, US oil imports have averaged 7.2 million barrels a day. That means imports have fallen just 1 per cent from where they were a year ago, even though domestic oil production is up 1.1 million barrels a day over the same period and US oil refineries are drawing the same levels of product currently as they did last year.

Why does that matter? Well, because the only logical conclusion from this little suite of data points is that US oil inventories must be rising. And, indeed, they are. The US added 21 million barrels to its crude oil inventory over the last four weeks, an increase that is three times the seasonal norm.

Last week alone the US added 9 million barrels to inventory, taking the national stockpile to 407 million barrels. That is the highest level since the US began keeping official records in 1982. Some have noted, in fact, the stockpile now is bigger than at any point since the open years of the Great Depression.

That might well be true, but the relevance is slight because of the massive change in consumption patterns over the intervening 84 years. Back when Herbert Hoover was president, the national inventory held better than 150 days of domestic production. Today's stockpile, on the other hand, is equivalent to just 45 days of growing US output.

But why does any of that matter anyway? Well, because, as is the case in the iron ore market, the weight of inventories being established by big customers at this low point in the pricing cycle is going to act as just another anchor on any potential recovery.

So, sure, the pruning of US shale oil capital programs should eventually see some sort of retreat in its domestic oil production. And, fully appeased, the Saudi's might finally blink in the face of the financial crisis low oil prices have triggered in some of the lesser member nations of the OPEC and the cartel's production ceiling might be trimmed from its current 30-million-barrel-a-day ceiling.

But the pricing effect of any meaningful change on the supply side of oil's global matrix will be delayed by the latent energy sitting in stockpiles around the US, Europe and Asia.

In other words, this supply overhang means we are looking at lower oil prices for longer while a divided petroleum world works out a way of rebalancing supply with demand.

This is all part of the New Oil Order, according to Goldman Sachs.

In work published this week on the US gas market, the US investment bank pondered some of the complications of the profound swing in the balance of petroleum power caused by the maturing shale oil revolution. If the Saudi ambition really is to relax the US embrace of shale by demonstrating the market realities of the higher production cost of unconventional oil and gas production, then the Goldman Sachs view is the WTI oil price is going to have to orbit the current $US44.50 a barrel for quite a deal longer.

"We forecast that WTI prices will need to stay lower for longer to incentivise the sustained reduction in drilling necessary to significantly slow US shale oil production growth," Goldman Sachs reported.

Big and small oil have always reacted with real-time speed to these sorts of pricing shocks and this time has proved no exception. Ambitions are being reined in all around the petroleum globe. But the story so far has been all about maintaining production while pruning capital-spending programs in defence of precious, but suddenly reduced, cash flows and their capacity to sustain dividends.

So it is that US shale drilling programs have been cut by the likes of our own BHP Billiton, which will spend at least $US1 billion less than planned in 2015-16 and beyond.

But, over the short and medium term, BHP has not changed its shale production targets.

Like most of the best shale operators, it is banking on doing more with less financial and human capital and driving its shale wells at peak production levels for considerably longer than anyone could have hoped just two or three years ago.

That is how fast the technical understanding of shale oil and its manufacturing is moving. That is why it is very difficult to put a firm time frame on just when, or even if, this slow-down in new drilling will result in lower US shale oil production in anything like the near term. And it is why the immediate fate of oil prices seems to sit firmly with those who triggered this current calamity back on 27 November.

Either OPEC bites the bullet on production cuts or we have to wait until lower oil prices generate the spike in demand that history and economic theory says they should.

Given Australia depends almost exclusively on the seaborne market for its oil supplies, perpetuation of the stand-off between OPEC and the non-OPEC oil world would seem to be nothing but beneficial. But there are shareholders aplenty in our wealth of petroleum finders and extractors that might not receive it that way. The Australian petroleum story is pretty much all about gas and this week has bought more evidence of what survival in the New Oil Order is going to take. There have been spending cuts and job losses confirmed at the likes of Senex, Beach Petroleum, Oil Search and Santos. And there has been opportunistic activity on the Beach register with Seven Group securing a 4.9 per cent stake at a 50 per cent discount from Copper Basin explorers' recent pricing peaks.

Just on that, it is hard to see how Seven might on its own be able to comfortably consume a business the size of Beach. Throw a 30 per cent control premium on top of Beach's eroded market capitalisation and you have a $1.56 billion price tag. At last report, Seven had about $160 million in cash and some $300 million tied up in minority stakes in oil and gas businesses and would likely be out of the money right now. It had net debt of $1.069 billion which translates into gearing of 26 per cent.

Given Seven boss Don Voelte has more that being a minority shareholder on his mind here (and I would not be taking that as a given), the only way forward here would seem to be with a partner. What the broader oil market is telling us is that, whatever Omaha's own has under construction here, there would seem to be absolutely no need for him to be in any sort of rush. Either way, this one could be a lot of fun to watch.

HEADLINE: Architectural statement is a drawcard for UTS
INTRO: Frank Gehry, one of the world's leading architects, has not given Sydney its best educational building or his best piece of work, says veteran architect Ric Thorp.
TEXT:
Frank Gehry, one of the world's leading architects, has not given Sydney its best educational building or his best piece of work, says veteran architect Ric Thorp.

Despite its $180 million price tag and distinctive curving, brick walls, the Gehry-designed business school at the University of Technology, Sydney, was more concerned with its outside appearance than its inside function, said Mr Thorp, named this week as a member of the Order of Australia for his services to the profession.

"I don't think that it's the best educational building in Sydney," Mr Thorp said. "It's much more about being a look-at-me building from the outside in terms of an unusual facade than it is about an innovative physical teaching or learning space."

UTS says Mr Gehry, who will be present at the building's opening on Monday, designed the inside first, then the facade. Mr Thorp, a designer of Canberra's Parliament House, said he had not yet seen inside the UTS building. He declined to say which educational building was the city's best but well-known educational designs include BVN's Ravenswood School for Girls, fjmt's Scientia building at the University of NSW and Hassell's National Institute of Dramatic Art.

"There's no shortage of academic or educational buildings in Australia," Mr Thorp said. "They may not have on the outside the daring-do 'Look-what-I-can-do-with-bricks' that the UTS building has."

The 12-storey structure built out of 320,000 customised hand-laid bricks also had to tweak its design after Mr Gehry's initial plan angled the bricks too much and had to be reduced; nor is it as good as the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles - one of Mr Gehry's most famous buildings - which he visited last year, Mr Thorp said.

So does Australia short-change itself by hiring big-name starchitects?

"If the money spent by UTS on this particular building and this particular architect raises the level of debate within the country and the discourse on the importance of good architecture, then that could be a good thing," said Steve Kennedy, national president of the Association of Consulting Architects Australia.

But it's not all good. "There is a certain degree of getting starry-eyed about starchitects and there's a concern about being willing to spend whatever it takes to have a starchitect do something when maybe other people could have done other things more cost-effectively," Mr Kennedy said.

Conversely, clients hiring big-name architects were less likely to compromise to cut costs than they would with a local, Mr Thorp said.

And the new structure, the Dr Chau Chak Wing building, played a crucial role for UTS, he said. "What a university really wants to have is an architectural statement, because that looks good in their brochures, in attracting people and students from other countries. UTS is going to achieve that with the Gehry building. It's a big deal."

HEADLINE: BRIEFS
INTRO: Westfield boost
TEXT:
Westfield boost

Westfield Corporation hit a high of $10.04 on Friday, helped on a strong day, by some analyst chatter from The Netherlands that European shopping centre heavyweight, the $35 billion Unibail Rodamco was running the numbers on the Australian group. Unibail has had a great year, with a recent spike in the stock price and a 7 per cent rise in earnings per security based, according to Morgan Stanley, on 3.8 per cent rental growth and very low debt.

ROBERT HARLEY

Mirvac wins approval

Mirvac has gained approval for a $140 million Bondi apartment project, its first in Sydney's east for some time. The development, on the former Benevolent Society site in Ocean and Wellington Streets, will consist of 190 apartments in five "mid and low rise" buildings, as well as the restoration of the heritage-listed Scarba House. Mirvac group executive, residential, John Carfi, said the project had been oriented to maximise views to Bondi Beach and Sydney Harbour, and would exceed the BASIX sustainability requirements by 25 per cent. Prices have not yet been disclosed but will be released after the opening of a sales office in mid-February. Assuming Mirvac gains the required level of pre-commitment, construction will start later in the year for completion in 2017.

The $336 million 360 Capital Industrial Fund has put off until next week lodging its bidder's statement for a proposed takeover of rival fund Australian Industrial REIT, which is managed by Fife Capital. The delay follows an announcement by the $220 million Fife fund that it has upgraded its 2015 earnings and distribution guidance. The 360 Capital fund has made an all-scrip offer for the rival fund. A similar offer, proposed as a merger agreement, has been rejected by Fife.

The unlisted Australian Unity Retail Property Trust has sold the Ballarat Homemaker Centre for $4 million. The sale price represented a net yield above 9 per cent for the new owners. HEADLINE: Hotels set for $2.6b bonanza
SUBHEAD: Tourism Biggest construction boom since 1980s expected
INTRO: Australia will experience its biggest hotel construction boom since the late 1980s this year with about $2.6 billion worth of projects to begin construction, BIS Shrapnel forecasts.
TEXT:
Australia will experience its biggest hotel construction boom since the late 1980s this year with about $2.6 billion worth of projects to begin construction, BIS Shrapnel forecasts.

This is just the tip of the iceberg - investment house CLSA identified a $7.4 billion pipeline of accommodation projects and a further $20 billion in mixed-use developments that will have a hotel component, in a new tourism investment report, The Next Wave.

Two years ago hotel commencements totalled less than a $1 billion. Last year they doubled to $2 billion, as the first wave of projects started to come out of the ground, BIS Shrapnel figures show.

Behind it all is offshore and domestic investor capital: a new CBRE Asia Pacific Hotel Trends report ranked Australia second behind Japan in attracting the surge of Asian capital. "The fact that there is more money than deals can only mean upward pricing pressure in the coming quarters," said Art Buser, executive director of CBRE's Asia Pacific Hotels business.

Accor, Mantra Group, TFE Hotels, Amalgamated Holdings, Meriton and serviced apartment group Quest all have projects under way in 2015 and 2016 ranging from budget accommodation to five-star luxury developments. Of the $2.6 billion of hotel projects to start in 2015, almost a third by value are in Queensland, a quarter are in NSW and more than a fifth in Victoria.

"Hotels are now a mature asset class," said Simon McGrath, Australia and New Zealand boss of Accor, the biggest hotel operator in Australia with more than 26,000 rooms. Accor will open three new economy hotels in 2015 - an Ibis Styles in Perth and one on the NSW Central Coast and a Mercure in Mackay in regional Queensland.

Mr McGrath said Australian room rates had risen over the last five years to the point where it made hotel investments attractive to investors. "Pricing supports new hotel builds. Six years ago a hotel market like Sydney was the 10th or 11th most expensive rates in the region, now it's third behind Singapore and Hong Kong."

Sydney hotels ended 2014 with revenue per available room rising to $178 a night - the highest level since 1995, according to STR Global figures. Nationally, room rates rose 9.4 per cent to $160 with occupancy levels rising 2.9 percentage points to 81.6 per cent.

Higher returns make hotels attractive to large property companies, Mr McGrath said. "It's become so competitive for office towers and even bulky good stores, that it's forcing these companies to think about tourism investments." Another key driver, he said, was the government's view on the sector. "In the government's thinking, tourism is now a tier-one industry. Tourism is front and centre of any federal or state election."

The last big hotel construction boom was in the late 1980s, part of a bigger commercial property boom led by Japan, when more than $3 billion was invested in new hotels, resulting in a notable oversupply of rooms, according to BIS Shrapnel.

Mr McGrath said he was confident there was more than enough demand - both from rising visitor numbers from the Asia Pacific and from local tourism - to absorb the new stock. "Certainly there won't be an oversupply in Sydney or Melbourne," he said.

Asian investors from China, Singapore and Malaysia, with big balance sheets, are a major part of the new wave. Last year Toga Group formed TFE Hotels, a $450 million joint venture with Singapore's Far East Hospitality, Quest struck a $500 million partnership with hotel operator Ascott, a subsidiary of Singapore-listed CapitaLand, and Mantra and Accor have partnered with Asian and Middle Eastern investors on new projects.

All this has been supported by Tourism Australia and Austrade. Tourism Australia has a goal of growing overnight hotel room spend from $80 billion to $140 billion by 2020 and has been shopping 40 investment-ready tourism projects to Asian investors.

"There is very strong interest from investors in China in Australian hotels. They feel they are underweight and are keen to increase their exposure," Austrade tourism and investment director Tim Beresford said.

BIS Shrapnel forecaster Timothy Hibbert said another factor spurring the big rise in investment was the strong upturn in apartment building nationwide, with many towers incorporating short-term accommodation as part of their mix. And precinct developments such as Barangaroo and Darling Harbour in Sydney, and Elizabeth Quay in Perth, all include hotels.

The new hotels are also bringing with them the latest global innovations, forcing owners of dated hotels to invest in their upgrade. Innovations include state of the art business lounges, lobby spaces that can be adapted for different uses, larger rooms with self-catering and traditional hotel amenities, free Wi-Fi and a sprucing up of food and beverage offerings.

"The needs of the business traveller continue to change in line with rapid evolutions in technology," Quest CEO Zed Sanjana said. "Access to Wi-Fi for multiple devices has been important to our guests for some time now; however, the speed of internet access is becoming increasingly critical to business travellers." Millennials were predicted to outspend Baby Boomers on hotels in the next few years and the industry needs to ensure product and service meet and exceed expectations.

HEADLINE: Australian Unity seeking sovereign wealth fund investment partners
INTRO: Aged care and retirement living owner and operator Australian Unity is in talks with sovereign wealth funds and pension funds to invest as capital partners in new projects.
TEXT:
Aged care and retirement living owner and operator Australian Unity is in talks with sovereign wealth funds and pension funds to invest as capital partners in new projects.

Mark Pratt, general manager of Australian Unity's $1.9 billion property funds management business, said a priority this year was explaining the retirement living and aged care model to investors.

"We've had discussion with sovereign funds and pensions funds, although there has been no investment to date," he said. "We're looking for capital partners who can see the potential of the sector, rather than someone who will just invest in a fund."

Australian Unity has funded most of its retirement living and aged care facilities off of its own balance sheet, favouring a model that incorporates retirement living and aged care in one precinct in an inner city location - as is the model for new facilities in Rathdowne Place, Melbourne and in Bondi Junction, Sydney.

This co-location model has delivered internal rates of return of 11 to 12 per cent, Mr Pratt said.

He said there was growing institutional investor interest in the sector following the successful float of operators such as Japara Healthcare and Estia Health.

"We have been talking to investors about these alternative investments for a period of time. They are interested in diversifying their portfolio."

But investors are uncomfortable about the lumpy returns generated from retirement villages, which operate via deferred management fees earned when a resident moves out or passes away. Aged care facilities deliver more regular income streams similar to residential rents.

Another issue is the regulation of the sector: aged care is federally regulated while retirement villages come under state jurisdiction.

HEADLINE: Vertical villages are on the rise
SUBHEAD: Retirement Baby boomers seek out aged-care facilities
INTRO: Australia's retirement and aged-care providers are moving to develop mid-rise, apartment-style accommodation close to inner cities where residents have spent much of their lives.
TEXT:
Australia's retirement and aged-care providers are moving to develop mid-rise, apartment-style accommodation close to inner cities where residents have spent much of their lives.

The demand for such accommodation is set to rise as baby boomers, many of them accustomed to inner-city life, inch closer to retirement.

Major players such as Aveo, Lend Lease, Stockand and Australian Unity are gaining exposure in so-called "vertical villages". At Ashfield in Sydney's inner west, Stockland is developing medium-rise apartments at the Cardinal Freeman Retirement Village.

In Melbourne, more typical of the trend is Australian Unity's Rathdowne Place, a six-storey 162-unit aged facility in Carlton, a few blocks from the bustling Little Italy section of Lygon Street.

Behind the facility, two nine-storey retirement unit towers are planned, each with 90-odd units that will be priced from about $450,000 to $1.2 million.

In the aged-care facility, the refundable accommodation deposits vary from $380,000 to $1.3 million. The facility has a hotel-style feel, with foyers, dining and break-out areas on each level. A cafe, gym and pool on the ground floor are open to non-residents as well.

Derek McMillan, chief executive of Australian Unity's Retirement Living division, explained the benefits of co-locating aged care with retirement, despite the differing financial structure in each sector. With a $900 million portfolio of retirement and aged-care assets, Australian Unity has to make projects such as Rathdowne Place stack up against a high-return residential development.

"The risks are different, no doubt," he said. "You have to build all at once and it is more expensive.

"We take a lower development margin than most residential developments. We're in it for the long term and over the longer term the annuity type income that comes from the deferred fees offsets the smaller development profit," Mr McMillan said

The property industry has embraced "vertical" retirement projects nationwide, in line with the broader market trend towards multi-storey living, said Mary Wood, executive director of the Property Council of Australia's Retirement Living Council.

"Older Australians are much more used to apartment living than previous generations, as is the general community. This explains why a lot of the innovation in retirement living is in urban, high-density areas.

"Baby boomers want services and care brought to them. So retirement village operators are increasingly offering a suite of services, not just units in attractive locations."

Andrew Giles, of One Fell Swoop, is consulting on and marketing at least 12 vertical style projects in Melbourne and other capitals.

"Almost all of those are being done in inner-urban areas and almost all are being done by church and charitable groups," Mr Giles said.

HEADLINE: Chinese to invest $25b overseas
INTRO: Chinese investors are set to fork out $US20 billion ($25 billion) on offshore property this year, up 21 per cent on 2014 as more domestic real estate developers and insurers internationalise their holdings, Jones Lang LaSalle said on Monday.
TEXT:
Chinese investors are set to fork out $US20 billion ($25 billion) on offshore property this year, up 21 per cent on 2014 as more domestic real estate developers and insurers internationalise their holdings, Jones Lang LaSalle said on Monday.

Chinese offshore property investment had increased 46 per cent to $US16.5 billion last year on the year before, with nearly 70 per cent going to commercial real estate, the property consultancy said in a report.

Outbound spending on commercial property, including office buildings, for the first time outpaced domestic investment, the company said.

"The easing of restrictions over the last few years by the Chinese government has [made it] ... much easier for institutions as well as individuals to move money overseas," said David Green-Morgan, the Singapore-based head of global research for International Capital Group at JLL.

Chinese property developers, including Dalian Wanda Group, have moved to globalise their portfolios to ensure long-term returns as China's property market cools.

On Monday Dalian Wanda Group announced a $US1 billion investment to purchase two buildings at Sydney Harbour, the Chinese conglomerate's second investment in Australia.

Big Chinese insurers, including Ping An Insurance Group of China and Anbang Insurance Group, have also emerged as buyers in global markets.

This month Ping An, China's second-biggest insurer, bought the Tower Place office block in London for £327 million ($622 million), having previously bought the Lloyds of London insurance building.

Last October, Anbang agreed to buy New York's Waldorf Astoria hotel for $US1.95 billion.

Driving China's outbound insurance investments are 2012 rules changes by the country's insurance regulator that allowed companies to invest in real estate outside of the mainland and Hong Kong.

As of the end of 2014, Chinese insurers invested nearly $US24 billion outside China, accounting for 1.4 per cent of the industry's total assets, said Zhou Yanli, vice chairman of the China Insurance Regulatory Commission at a press briefing last Friday.

Retail sales in the malls owned by Federation Centres rose by 1.3 per cent in the year to December, improving on the 1.0 per cent growth in the year to September. Federation chief executive Steven Sewell said the best performers were the mini-majors, where sales rose 4.5 per cent in the year, and the specialty stores, where sales rose 2.3 per cent. HEADLINE: ICAC efforts hang on Cunneen
INTRO: At least three inquiries by the Independent Commission Against Corruption and findings of corrupt conduct against 26 people are at risk if the watchdog loses a High Court appeal to be heard on March 4.
TEXT:
At least three inquiries by the Independent Commission Against Corruption and findings of corrupt conduct against 26 people are at risk if the watchdog loses a High Court appeal to be heard on March 4.

The High Court appeal follows a Court of Appeal ruling in December that the ICAC did not have the power to investigate allegations that Crown prosecutor Margaret Cunneen encouraged her son's girlfriend, Sophia Tilley, to fake chest pains to avoid blood alcohol testing by police after a car accident on May 31. "It is of public importance for the uncertainty created by the decision to be resolved authoritatively by a judgment of this court," the ICAC's submission to the High Court says.

The case has divided the legal community.

Robert Newlinds, SC, said he did not believe the framers of the ICAC legislation meant for the watchdog to have the wide ambit of power that it sought. "The way ICAC is construing its power means that it is a standing crime commission which has the ability to investigate any alleged crime, with no connection to what the man in the street would consider corruption," Mr Newlinds said.

ICAC inquiries were having "serious consequences" for people who were not intended, Mr Newlinds said. "ICAC can destroy people just by naming them in an investigation or inquiry."

He said the main problem was that people could not appeal to a court on a question of fact. "ICAC has made serious findings of fact on many occasions based on evidence that would not be acceptable in a court," Mr Newlinds said.

But Sydney barrister David McLure said reducing the ICAC's jurisdiction was neither necessary nor desirable. "Whatever you might think of this or any other ICAC investigation, even ICAC's harshest critics would probably accept that it has been extremely effective at exposing conduct designed to deceive public officials."

"ICAC's role in preventing corruption is substantially achieved by it making public findings about corrupt conduct," he said.

HEADLINE: Law firms consider listing
INTRO: It's not until you put [your industry or firm] out to the market that you get an idea of what an independent class of people, investors, might think it is valued at. Graham Cowin
TEXT:
Intellectual property law could be on the verge of a revolution as partners at some of nations biggest specialist firms have watched Spruson and Ferguson shares almost double, and are seeking advice on their own options for an ASX listing pay day.

IP and patent law firms Davies Collison Cave and Phillips Ormonde Fitzpatrick have sought external advice on listing options.

Griffith Hack has not engaged advice "yet" and is happy with its current growth strategy but it is keeping a close eye on market developments.

In what is a conservative private and partnership-based profession, the Spruson's success has prompted serious consideration of listing options.

"It has presented an interesting set of opportunities and discussion points. Where it will lead us to, its difficult to say but I don't think we would be alone, I would have thought all major competitors would be at least contemplating what's involved in it," Ormonde Phillips Fox managing partner Graham Cowin said.

Mr Cowin confirmed the firm is actively seeking advice from several sources in a "fact-finding mission".

"We are seeking advice from different investment advisers, strategic consultants, different sorts of names like that. We have a partnership that needs to understand what the options are," Mr Cowin said.

"We haven't made a decision that's the course were are going along, but we have to understand what's involved, why it would be a good option - if it is a good option," Mr Cowin said.

According to Leon Allen, managing partner at Davies Collison Cave, his firm has retained Moore Stephens, among others, to explore listing options for the company.

"We'd be crazy not to, but at the present time it doesn't suit our particular plan for the business. I would like to take a bit of a wait-and-see look, primarily because there are not that many professional firms that have listed and some of them have been a spectacular disaster."

In law offices up and down the country, both in intellectual property and in the broader legal profession, the IPH ticker (Spruson's holding firm) is said to be a mainstay on many partners computers screens, as partnerships consider the possibility of cashing in on the same sort of success that Spruson is experiencing.

When Spruson and Ferguson floated in November, the partners made an estimated $156.9 million from a 50 per cent sell down for the shares in IPH Limited, the holding company of the firm. The shares were floated at $2.10, but jumped by 50 per cent on debut. The price has risen since to be trading at a high of $3.80.

"Whilst before the float you could speculate about what your industry or your firm might be valued at, it's not until you put it out to the market that you get an idea of what an independent class of people, investors, might think it is valued at," Mr Cowin said

"I think everyone in the profession would have been surprised at the level of interest and value that was placed on it," he said

In the field of intellectual property, trademarks and patent, all firms in the sector are agreed, 2015 could precipitate new growth, as most figures suggest that Australian firms are behind the eight ball in identifying and protecting their intellectual property, particularly in the mining and tech sectors.

In the last IP Australia figures from in 2013, patents were up 12.7 per cent.

"In general, any professional services firm with a consistent track record, principals with significant skin in the game and strong market positioning in their fields of operations is always likely to attract investor interest," Morningstar equities analyst Brian Han said.

Griffith Hack chairman David Hughes said: "There is a huge amount of opportunity in respect of better management understanding and strategic planning in the whole area. We are doing boardroom lunches and things like that, if you compare Australia's position in regards to IP, we are not up to where other countries are."

On the Spruson model, Mr Hughes said clearly the market is considering "an opportunity for them to build on their model," but that Griffith Hack, a company of roughly similar size but with no Asian offices, does not intend to follow the listing path at this point.

"It's not in our current strategic plan, but you have always got an eye on for what's happening in the space," he said. "Our strategy is remaining in the current structure."

However, there is a concern that changing ownership arrangements could eventually undermine professional service incentive structures.

"Suddenly you have a potential for a difference in interests between the people with the shares and the people who do the work. In the boring old arrangement we currently have the partners are in control of the business and they do the work, but if you start to separate those two, I'm not sure how it works in the long term," Mr Allen said.
